title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
video_title: Relocates.io
video_transcript_excerpt: Finding a place for a family usually means juggling dozens of open tabs, trying to guess where everyone's daily life actually intersects. Relocates.io solves this geometrically. We input a family of four relocating to San Francisco. David commuting to Google, Sarah, Leah, and 8-year-old Tom. The agent parses the household and registers the profiles directly into client state. Now we define their daily mobility constraints. David needs transit within 30 minutes. Leah needs a 15-minute walk to high school. Tom needs 10 minutes to primary school, plus a nearby gym and park. The browser intersects these travel boundaries on device, 29.38 square kilometers across five candidate zones. Now the hard constraint. Sarah has an injured knee. Any pedestrian incline over a 6% grade is physically out of the question. That medical requirement is treated as non-negotiable, factoring San Francisco's elevation profiles into the pedestrian routes. >> The viable terrain immediately collapses by more than half down to 13.44 square kilometers. Hills eliminate most of the city. Instead of negotiating back and forth in chat, I open the drawer and adjust the sliders myself, granting Tom 17 minutes and tightening the park to six. Web MCP immediately detects my manual edits and synchronizes the agent state. The polygon updates dynamically to 11.88 square kilometers, highlighting five qualifying neighborhoods, including the Presidio. We drop straight into 3D terrain to verify street inclines before signing a lease. Compromise isn't an argument anymore. It's just geometry.

title: Sprintfy
pitch: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan.
about_excerpt: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Live: https://sprintfy.vercel.app — no account needed to see the whole idea. Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app, in ChatGPT mode : its built-in browser exposes WebMCP on its own, so the tools register with no flag and no extension. Desktop Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing works too, as does Chrome with the ChatGPT extension. One caveat: Codex mode in that same desktop app does not expose WebMCP , so the tools stay dormant there and the page will honestly say so — same app, two modes, two answers. Ask your agent for start_guided_demo , or press "Show me a demo", and you land in a real workspace with a proposal already waiting in the review panel and six tools live. Inspiration Every "agent-ready" app I looked at exposed the same shape of tool: create_task , update_task , delete_task . The model writes straight to the database. That is fine until the model is confidently wrong about your sprint plan, and then you are doing archaeology on a project board, trying to work out what it touched and in what order. Project planning is exactly the wrong domain for blind writes. A plan is an argument about sequencing and effort — it is the thing a lead is paid to have an opinion about. Handing that to an agent as unsupervised INSERTs gets you a plan nobody trusts and everybody re-checks, which is more work than writing it by hand. So I wanted to find out whether WebMCP could carry something other than commands. Can a tool call ask a question and wait for a human's answer? If it can, the agent stops being a thing you supervise and becomes a thing you argue with. What it does Sprintfy is a sprint planner — requirements, sprints, tasks, hour estimates — that exposes its workspace to agents over WebMCP. No agent tool writes to the plan. The loop has three moves: 1. The agent reads the room. get_project_context returns the plan and what the human is currently looking at: active view, selected sprint, status filter, which proposal is open. The agent plans into a context, not a vacuum. 2. The agent proposes a diff. Every write tool authors a change set — an ordered list of operations stored as JSON, rendered in the review panel as a real diff: additions in green, field-level changes as before → after, removals struck through. Nothing has touched the domain tables. An agent can propose a sprint and the twelve tasks inside it as one unit, using local ref ids that resolve to real primary keys only at apply time. 3. The human decides, and the agent hears the answer. apply_pending_changes opens the diff and blocks — the tool call's promise stays open while the person reads it. Approve applies the whole change set in a single Postgres transaction and the tool resolves with what landed. Reject resolves with the reason they typed, delivered back to the agent as the tool result. You do not start from an empty board either. You hand Sprintfy the thing you already have — a backlog note, a PRD as .md , .txt , .pdf or .docx , or a few paragraphs typed in — and it returns a plan sequenced by risk rather than by comfort. A real Turkish brief produced 8 requirements, 4 sprints and 38 tasks in 56 seconds, in Turkish, with the database migration ranked critical and placed first. Sprintfy's own planner is held to the same rule. It does not write the plan either: it authors a change set marked source: "planner" that lands in the same review panel, behind the same gate. How we built it Next.js (App Router) and React on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres, Auth and Realtime, and WebMCP for the agent surface. The architecture is one idea repeated: the write path is a data structure, not a function call. Tools append operations to a change_sets row. A single PL/pgSQL function, apply_change_set , applies them atomically and resolves ref placeholders to real ids as it goes. It is declared security invoker , so row-level security still guards every insert it performs — an agent cannot use it to reach another user's project. On the WebMCP side: Surface detection. The API moved during the spec's life and shipping browsers do not agree yet, so one adapter registers against document.modelContext.registerTool , navigator.modelContext.registerTool , or navigator.modelContext.provideContext , whichever exists, and the header badge reports which one it found. Page-scoped tool sets. Four tools before you sign in, six inside a project. The surface changes as the human navigates. Cancellation is honoured. The AbortSignal passed to apply_pending_changes releases the approval wait, so an agent that walks away does not leave the page stuck on a modal. Tools never throw at the browser. Failures come back as text an agent can recover from, including "these task ids don't exist in this project, call get_project_context again." Planning uses a strict JSON schema derived from the same Zod schema that backs the propose_plan tool — one schema, two authors, so a plan from the model and a plan from an agent are the same shape. Challenges we ran into Tool calls do not wait for React. Two bugs had the same root: an agent could not always see the proposal it had just written, and focus moved the human's view without get_project_context reporting it. A tool call can land before React has committed state, so reading a render closure returns the past. Tools now read from a ref that is written before the state, never from a closure. Both cases became eval scenarios so they cannot come back. Registering the same tool twice. Navigating between pages left the previous page's registration alive and the browser rejected the new one as a duplicate. Fixed with a module-level registry where claiming a name synchronously releases the previous holder. A machine asking a question and getting an HTML redirect. An unauthenticated POST to the planning endpoint was redirected to the sign-in page; Next then read the multipart body as a server action and answered 404. In an app whose premise is that machines are first-class callers, that was the wrong answer to give one. API routes now reply in JSON. The date picker that could not be used. The month grid was absolutely positioned inside a modal that clips its own corners and scrolls its body, so it was sliced off a few pixels below the field. It renders into a portal now, in viewport coordinates, flipping above the field when there is no room below. Knowing where WebMCP actually exists. Support is not a property of an application, it turns out — it is a property of a surface inside it. The ChatGPT desktop app has two modes, and only one of them exposes the API: in ChatGPT mode the built-in browser hands the page document.modelContext with no flag and no extension, while in Codex mode the built-in browser does not, so the same URL in the same application registers six tools or none depending on which mode you are in. I spent a while concluding the tools were broken before realising I had been testing in the wrong half of one app. That is why the page never assumes. It probes each surface, reports which one it found, and — when it finds none — still works and still explains itself, in its own voice, to a person who came in through an ordinary browser. Faking things. An early version showed timed loading stages — "Reading the brief", "Sequencing by risk" — while the model call ran. They were theatre, in a product whose entire argument is that you should not have to take an agent's word for anything. They were replaced with the true elapsed seconds. Accomplishments that we're proud of The blocking approval gate. Turning a WebMCP tool call from a command into a request is the part that is hard to fake, and it means the agent can be genuinely useful — proposing whole plans rather than timid one-row edits — without ever being trusted with the write. The evals. /evals.js runs seven scenarios against the actual ToolDescriptor objects the page registered, on the live site, from the console, with no account. Seven of seven pass in production. They assert the invariants rather than the happy path: a proposal writes zero rows; a rejection arrives as the tool's return value; approval applies a sprint and its tasks in one transaction with refs resolved; hallucinated ids are refused outright rather than half-applied. And the fact that Sprintfy's own planner goes through its own gate. A product arguing for review does not get to exempt its author. What we learned That a tool result is a channel back to the human , not just a status code. Once you treat it that way, "the agent asked and I said no, here's why" becomes a normal part of the protocol rather than something bolted on top. That the reviewable-proposal pattern belongs in the page, not in the model. The site knows what a legitimate change to itself looks like, so the site should render the diff and hold the gate. Any agent — any model, any vendor — inherits that

title: Hamburger Roulette with WebMCP
pitch: Turn food preferences into fun burger ideas with ChatGPT and WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Turn food preferences into fun burger ideas with ChatGPT and WebMCP.

 Three WebMCP site tools available directly to ChatGPT

 Rerolled #2 — ChatGPT replaced only the second result using WebMCP 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Hamburger Roulette started as a small Japanese web tool for a simple everyday problem: "What kind of burger should I make today?" 

 The original site lets users choose a meal or dessert mode, select preferences, and randomly combine bread, fillings, and seasonings. 

 When I learned about the WebMCP Challenge, I realized that this kind of tool could become much more useful when combined with natural-language interaction. Instead of manually choosing every option, a user could simply tell ChatGPT what they want and let the agent operate the existing website. 

 What I built 

 I added WebMCP support directly to the existing Hamburger Roulette website. 

 The site now exposes three tools to ChatGPT: 

 
 get_available_filters — returns the modes, templates, and tags supported by the site 
 burger_spin — applies preferences and runs the existing roulette 
 reroll_one — replaces only one result while keeping the others 
 

 For example, a user can ask ChatGPT to generate three meal burgers, and ChatGPT can use the site's own roulette logic to produce the results. 

 The user can then naturally ask to replace just one of the suggestions. 

 How I built it 

 The original application already had its roulette and filtering logic implemented in JavaScript. 

 Rather than creating a separate API or duplicating that logic, I exposed the existing functionality through WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 This means the same application logic is used whether a person operates the website manually or ChatGPT operates it through WebMCP. 

 The existing website remains fully usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. 

 Challenges and what I learned 

 The biggest design question was deciding what should remain a human interaction and what should become an agent tool. 

 Simply exposing a "spin" button was possible, but WebMCP became more useful when the agent could understand the available filters, translate natural-language preferences into those filters, and perform follow-up actions such as rerolling a single result. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can be added incrementally to an existing website without rebuilding the application around AI. 

 That was the most interesting part of this project: the website remains the source of its own functionality, while WebMCP gives an agent a structured way to use it.

 Inspiration 

 The Central Limit Theorem is a very robust and useful theorem in statistics. Like many others, we had a hard time understanding and appreciating it when we learned it for the first time. We felt that it would be nice to have a clear and easy demonstration. We realized that WebMCP can integrate AI, scripts, and data and thereby demonstrate this and many other theorems and theories.

 This is a WebMCP app hosted at our website, acctey.org. It remarkably makes it clear that the sample means are normally distributed and their mean tends towards the population mean.

 We could build a modern and useful web app that incorporates agentic AI.

title: colorwake
pitch: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended.
about_excerpt: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Canvas mode - select sketc Play mode Play mode - dance, fly, swim etc. colorwake in 20 seconds Kids color a character, then an agent directs it over WebMCP as it acts out their story onstage. A read-only get_guide tool works like a system prompt handed over by the page: an in-page playbook for guiding a child with choices, never a script. Successful write-tool results carry fresh, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after on-screen changes. No app backend or accounts: raw artwork stays local, and the agent receives only a compact state summary. A parent runs the agent; the child makes the art. Built solo by a first-time hackathon entrant with a product background. Inspiration Coloring apps end when the coloring ends. But the best part comes next, when a child holds up the drawing and says, “And then the rocket flies to the moon!” No app was listening. WebMCP changed that. The app’s state and tools live inside the page, letting a connected agent interact with the same canvas the child is touching and help the picture move as the child imagines. What it does Color — choose a sketch and paint it with a finger, mouse, or stylus. Play — finish coloring, and the same canvas becomes a stage. Tell ChatGPT the story — “The rocket flies to the volcano, and the robot dances!” — and through 10 WebMCP tools, the agent casts the characters, sets the place, time, and weather, and composes their movements. Young children shouldn’t need to formulate commands. The agent can read the state of play and offer one simple next choice — always choices, never a script. No artwork is generated for the child. The child makes the art; the agent plays inside it, in real time, on the same screen. Because ChatGPT is for users 13 and older (subject to local minimum-age requirements), colorwake is co-play by design: a parent operates the agent and relays the child’s ideas, while the child stays in charge of the art. How we built it colorwake is a static React 19 and TypeScript SPA built with Vite. It has no app backend or accounts; artwork and state persist in localStorage. Characters are rigged SVGs across five rig families, animated with the Web Animations API. Motion parameters are clamped to safe ranges for both whole-character and part-targeted moves. The WebMCP layer registers 10 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , typed with webmcp-types and validated with Zod: four read tools and six write tools. Three decisions mattered most: get_guide — an in-page playbook, delivered like a system prompt. A read-only tool can return more than app state. It can carry guidance: how the studio works, what the child can do in each state, and the house rules. An agent that reads it starts with a clear role as a playmate. A loop designed around WebMCP. On-screen button presses are not announced to the agent. Successful write-tool results provide current, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after manual interactions. The experience works best when the family continues through the protocol. Parity, with one boundary the agent cannot cross. UI-equivalent tools call the same actions as the on-screen controls, while motion tools drive the same play engine. The 20-picture and 8-step caps return actionable errors; the three-spot stage predictably swaps out the friend that has been there longest. There is deliberately no painting tool — coloring belongs to the child. Challenges I ran into This was my first hackathon, and I came to it with a product background rather than a traditional engineering one. The hardest part was translation : turning WebMCP’s technical properties into moments a family could actually feel. get_guide emerged from asking what happens when young children cannot type commands and turning that constraint into a feature. AI coding agents were my hands, but direction, taste, and QA were mine: round after round of on-device review, dozens of UI/UX fixes, and a 148-test verification chain. One technical lesson stood out: tool descriptions are UX writing. Agents behave only as well as the schemas and errors guiding them. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The promise works end to end: a picture colored a minute ago can walk across the stage beneath the weather the child chose. The page teaches the agent: get_guide gives it a playbook for becoming a good playmate. I shipped it solo for my first hackathon, with a local-first privacy model designed for families. What I learned Read-only tools can carry guidance — context, norms, and a role — not just app state. Designing for agents is UX design made of words: schemas, descriptions, and error messages are the interface. What's next for colorwake More sketches and motion families, sound, saved and replayable shows, and more languages — so more families can color together and more compatible agents can direct. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A simple tomato pasta can be the start of learning to cook, not just a recipe to finish. Mise explores how to make the next action manageable and add a cooking technique when the learner is ready. What it does Four cooking lines—pasta, rice, potato and one-pan oven—each contain ten recipe versions. Servings and dietary preferences change ingredients and directions together. People choose guidance, use one-step mode, pause and return, and keep approved preferences in their account. Why WebMCP The assistant acts on the same cooking workspace the person sees. Eleven page tools read current state, compose a session around multiple constraints, propose smaller actions, and request human confirmation. The assistant cannot award completed cooking through a tool call alone. Suggested memory stays pending until the person approves it. How it was built React, Vinext, Cloudflare Workers and D1, with imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration. Runtime schemas reject malformed inputs. Context tokens prevent stale recipe changes; per-account storage and revision checks protect saved progress. Challenges and lessons Testing found that paused sessions could be changed invisibly and that pending completion could outlive a servings change. Both were fixed and retested. A final beginner-rice correction made adding water, boiling and switching heat off explicit. Shared state and learner control matter more than simply awarding levels. Validation and boundaries 36 automated tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Actual browser checks covered shared state, persistence, pending approvals, invalid tools, mobile layout and keyboard navigation. Six cooking personas are simulations, not real-user research. Recipes are not professionally cook-tested or allergy-certified. This is browser WebMCP while Mise is open, not a remote connector in every GPT or Claude chat. title: Friction
pitch: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools.
about_excerpt: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools. Like Comment Story Updates Human-only patch review explains the evidence and proposed contract repairs. Baseline lab: paired human and agent traces expose a 50/100 parity score. Repaired scenario: clearer visible wording and a guarded completion contract. Ten real page-side WebMCP tools share state with the visible interface. Paired retest: the repaired human and agent journeys reach 96/100 parity. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Friction Inspiration WebMCP lets a live page publish named, structured actions instead of forcing an agent to infer buttons and forms. That creates a new usability question: does the agent receive the same information, consent gates, and final state that a person sees? Friction is a dual usability laboratory for answering that question. It pairs one visual journey with one WebMCP journey, exposes the differences, repairs both interfaces together, and proves the improvement with a retest. What it does The deterministic RelayConf event-registration scenario contains three intentional problems: a quiet-zone seat is hidden behind vague human-facing wording; the baseline agent result omits a $12 service fee and refund condition; an ambiguously described completion tool finalizes without the human review gate. Friction records both traces and scores outcome, information, consent, state, and effort parity. It produces evidence-backed findings and a four-part patch. A human must approve that patch through the visible UI—approval is intentionally not agent-callable. After approval, the human option becomes clear, the tool returns an itemized total and policy, and finalization requires a review token plus confirmed=true . The paired score rises from 50/100 to 96/100. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP generates one side of the experiment. The page registers ten tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; these are not a remote MCP server and do not automate the DOM. Tool handlers and visual controls share the same React state and durable browser storage, so agent mutations immediately change the visible trace, findings, and comparison. Without WebMCP, Friction could test only visual automation. With WebMCP, it can inspect the explicit contract a site offers to agents and compare that contract against the human experience. How humans and agents work together People complete and judge the visual task, report hesitation, and retain approval authority. Agents exercise the structured contract, analyze traces, submit findings, and propose interface changes. Neither side replaces the other: the agent contributes speed and structured analysis, while the person supplies subjective usability evidence and approves consequential changes. How we built it Friction uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn primitives, and ChatGPT Sites-compatible Cloudflare output. Ten page-owned WebMCP tools use restrictive JSON Schemas, runtime checks, read/write annotations, untrusted-content hints, feature detection, and registration cleanup with AbortController . The account-free demo persists locally in the browser, making the before/after experiment repeatable without credentials or external APIs. Deterministic tests cover the parity score, consent and information failures, approval transition, and repaired replay. Challenges we ran into The most important design challenge was avoiding a fake split between “human UI state” and “agent demo state.” Every interaction had to operate on the same live model. The second was expressing the repair as a real contract change: the completion tool’s description and JSON Schema are re-registered after human approval, and its handler independently enforces review and confirmation. Accomplishments that we're proud of A non-trivial ten-tool WebMCP implementation over shared visible state. A complete evidence → proposal → human approval → retest loop. A consent failure that is demonstrably blocked by the repaired handler. A polished responsive product requiring no accounts, secrets, or external APIs. Deterministic tests, type checks, linting, production build, and dependency audit. What we learned Parity is broader than whether both paths eventually produce the same record. A fast agent path can still be worse if it hides cost, weakens consent, or returns less context. Tool schemas, descriptions, results, and confirmation design are part of the product interface and need usability testing just as much as buttons and labels do. What's next for Friction Future versions could import OpenTelemetry-style traces, compare multiple scenarios, export regression suites for CI, and provide a lightweight SDK that lets other WebMCP sites embed paired parity tests while keeping approval policies application-owned. title: WebMCP Consent Layer
pitch: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters.
about_excerpt: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP lets any website register tools that AI agents can discover and invoke. Some runtimes already gate risky calls behind their own native approval UIs — ChatGPT's built-in browser shows a "Site tools" review panel, and the MCP-B Agent Chrome extension has per-tool approval settings. But most WebMCP clients don't provide any consent mechanism at all: every registered tool runs silently, whether it's a read-only health check or an irreversible production rollback. This project closes that gap at the package level. It adds a consent and annotation layer to @mcp-b/react-webmcp that any site using WebMCP can adopt — one hook, one provider — without every site inventing its own approval flow from scratch. How it creates a better user experience The consent layer is deliberately selective. Every tool registration carries structured metadata — scope, reversibility, risk level — and only actions flagged as requiring approval actually interrupt the user with a consent card. Low-risk reads (fetching service health, listing deployments) execute immediately and are logged silently in the audit trail. When a high-risk call like rollbackDeployment fires, the consent card shows exactly what's at stake: which systems are affected, whether the action is reversible, and what the agent wants to do. The audit log records every tool call — approved, denied, or auto-approved — so users can review the full history of what an agent did, not just the decisions they were asked to make. Cross-tab attention cues (a favicon badge and title blink) ensure pending approvals aren't missed when the user is in a different tab. For irreversible, high-risk operations, an optional WebAuthn gate (Touch ID, Windows Hello, or a hardware key) raises the bar beyond a simple click. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Without a consent layer, site authors face a binary choice: either don't register destructive tools with WebMCP (safe but crippled), or register them and hope the runtime provides its own gate (flexible but risky on runtimes that don't). With useGuardedWebMCP, an agent can be handed genuinely powerful tools — rollbackDeployment, deleteUser, revokeAccess — with a human gating only the specific calls that matter. The agent handles the routine reads autonomously; the human approves or denies only the irreversible, high-impact actions. The result is collaborative agentic work where the human's attention is spent on the decisions that actually need judgment, not on rubber-stamping every API call. Brief implementation explanation The core mechanism is a React hook, useGuardedWebMCP, that wraps the existing useWebMCP from @mcp-b/react-webmcp — it composes rather than forks it. Each tool registration includes a ConsentMetadata object (scope, reversible, riskLevel, requiresApproval, optionally requireUserPresence). The hook maps this metadata to standard MCP ToolAnnotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint) via toMcpAnnotations(), so native runtimes that do have their own gates receive real behavioral hints. When requiresApproval is true and no native gate is detected, the call suspends in a framework-agnostic ConsentBroker, which manages a queue of pending requests, session preapproval for reversible tools, timeout/expiry, and decision event streams. The React layer (ConsentBrokerProvider, useConsentBroker, usePendingConsentRequests) lets any component render approval UI against the broker's state. The on-page card includes an isTrusted guard to reject script-dispatched synthetic clicks — a best-effort defense, not a tamper-proof boundary, which is why hasNativeConsentGate() exists as an escape hatch to defer to real browser/OS-level permission prompts where available. The upstream PR (link) adds only the hook, broker, types, annotations, WebAuthn presence verification, and tests to @mcp-b/react-webmcp — the demo app is a separate workspace member, not part of the package. title: SurveyGuard
pitch: SurveyGuard helps people and AI agents collaboratively detect, explain, and fix survey quality, privacy, and bias issues before publication using structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
SurveyGuard helps people and AI agents collaboratively detect, explain, and fix survey quality, privacy, and bias issues before publication using structured WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 After corrections, SurveyGuard updates the findings and readiness score so users can verify the survey is safer and stronger. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP enables agents to inspect, validate, explain, correct, and verify surveys while keeping people in control. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SurveyGuard detects an unnecessary request for personal information, marks it as blocking, and recommends a safer question. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 After corrections, SurveyGuard updates the findings and readiness score so users can verify the survey is safer and stronger. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP enables agents to inspect, validate, explain, correct, and verify surveys while keeping people in control. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SurveyGuard detects an unnecessary request for personal information, marks it as blocking, and recommends a safer question. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 After corrections, SurveyGuard updates the findings and readiness score so users can verify the survey is safer and stronger. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Creating a good survey is harder than it appears. A survey can look complete while still containing leading language, double-barrelled questions, unclear timeframes, sensitive questions without an opt-out, conflicting response options, or unnecessary requests for personal information. 

 These issues are often identified through manual reviews, long checklists, and repeated back-and-forth between researchers, product teams, and stakeholders. The process takes time, depends heavily on reviewer experience, and can still produce inconsistent results. 

 SurveyGuard was inspired by a simple question: 

 What if a person and an AI agent could review and improve a survey together inside the same live workspace? 

 Instead of requiring an agent to interpret buttons, scrape page content, or guess how the survey application works, SurveyGuard exposes clearly defined survey actions through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the survey, identify risks, explain findings, and perform approved actions while the person remains in control. 

 What SurveyGuard does
SurveyGuard is a WebMCP-enabled survey quality workspace that helps people and AI agents collaboratively review surveys before publication. 

 The current MVP allows users to: 

 Create, edit, and delete survey questions
Configure question types and response options
Validate survey questions against defined quality checks
Identify personally identifiable information
Detect leading or loaded wording
Flag potentially double-barrelled questions
Identify sensitive questions that may need a “Prefer not to answer” option
Detect unclear reference periods
Flag exclusive options such as “None of these” in multi-select questions
Review findings by severity
Apply recommended corrections
Monitor a dynamic survey-readiness score
Generate a concise survey-readiness report
Findings are organized into three levels: 

 Blocking: A high-risk issue that should be addressed before publication
Needs review: An issue requiring human judgment or revision
Suggestion: A non-blocking quality improvement
SurveyGuard uses fictional survey content in the demonstration and does not depend on private company data, confidential research, or customer information. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit
Survey review is not just a question-and-answer experience. It requires an agent to inspect structured survey content, understand validation results, modify specific questions, add response options, and confirm how those actions changed the survey. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent may have to infer this structure from the visual interface and navigate the application indirectly. That approach can be slow, fragile, and difficult to verify. 

 With WebMCP, SurveyGuard exposes narrow and intentional tools that describe exactly what an agent can do. The agent works with the same survey and application state that the user sees. 

 The MVP includes the following site tools: 

 get_survey_summary
list_questions
validate_survey
rewrite_question
add_prefer_not_to_answer
generate_readiness_report
For example, a user can ask an agent to: 

 Validate this survey, explain the highest-risk issue, and help me fix it. 

 The agent can call the validation tool, return structured findings, explain the most important issue, and then use an appropriate write tool after the user approves the change. 

 This creates a more reliable experience than asking the agent to guess how to manipulate the interface. 

 Human-agent collaboration
SurveyGuard is designed around human review rather than unattended automation. 

 The application separates inspection from modification: 

 The agent retrieves the current survey structure.
The agent runs structured validation.
The agent explains the identified issues.
The user reviews the recommendation.
An approved change is applied through a specific WebMCP tool.
The interface updates so the user can verify the result.
SurveyGuard recalculates the readiness score and remaining findings.
The agent provides speed and consistency, while the user maintains responsibility for context, judgment, and final approval. 

 This is particularly important in survey design because whether a question is appropriate can depend on the research objective, intended audience, jurisdiction, and sensitivity of the subject. 

 How I built it
SurveyGuard was built as a React-based web application with a responsive three-panel review experience: 

 A question list for navigating the survey
An editor for reviewing wording, question type, and response options
A validation panel for displaying findings and recommended actions
The validation engine evaluates each question using transparent, deterministic rules. Each finding includes: 

 A unique issue code
A severity level
A short title
An explanation
A recommended correction or action when appropriate
The interface calculates a survey-readiness score based on the number and severity of unresolved findings. The score updates as users edit questions or apply corrections. 

 WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool defines: 

 A specific name
A focused description
A narrow input schema
Required parameters
Read-only annotations where applicable
An execution handler connected to the survey’s existing application logic
The tools return structured results so an agent can understand what happened and communicate the result to the user. 

 The application also preserves a normal visual workflow for people and can display a preview state when WebMCP is not available in the current browser environment. 

 Challenges I faced
Designing useful tool boundaries
One challenge was deciding how much authority each tool should have. A single broad tool that could change the entire survey would be flexible, but it would also be harder to control and verify. 

 I chose narrower tools such as rewrite_question and add_prefer_not_to_answer. This makes each action easier for the agent to select, easier for the user to understand, and easier to test. 

 Separating blocking issues from recommendations
Not every survey-quality concern should prevent publication. Treating every finding as equally severe would create unnecessary friction and reduce trust in the validator. 

 To address this, SurveyGuard separates blocking issues, review items, and optional suggestions. 

 Keeping the human in control
A technically successful agent action is not necessarily the right research decision. SurveyGuard therefore treats agent recommendations as reviewable actions and clearly communicates that human approval is recommended before publication. 

 Managing shared application state
WebMCP tools and the visible interface need to operate on the same current survey. Tool outputs, question edits, validation results, and readiness scoring must remain consistent after every action. 

 The MVP connects tool execution to the same underlying state used by the visual interface so changes can be seen and verified immediately. 

 Working within a short build window
The challenge required prioritizing a focused, demonstrable workflow. Instead of attempting to build a complete survey-authoring platform, I concentrated on the core WebMCP experience: inspect, validate, explain, improve, and verify. 

 What I learned
Building SurveyGuard reinforced several important lessons: 

 Agent-native applications need explicit actions, not just an AI chat box.

title: Redline
pitch: Your agent reads the contract, flags what will cost you, and drafts the fixes as redlines you can accept or reject. It has no tool that edits the document. Not by policy. By construction.
about_excerpt: Your agent reads the contract, flags what will cost you, and drafts the fixes as redlines you can accept or reject. It has no tool that edits the document. Not by policy. By construction. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone has signed a contract they didn't fully read. The current answer is to paste it into a chat window, which gets you advice about the document: a paragraph you then retype into the file yourself. We wanted the agent working inside the contract, with one hard rule: it can suggest anything and change nothing. What it does Redline is a contract review workspace for humans and their agents. The agent reads the agreement clause by clause, flags risks with severity and plain-English consequences, compares terms against a market-standard playbook, and drafts replacement language. Every change it suggests arrives as a redline — old text struck through, proposed text in green, reasoning attached, that a human accepts or rejects. Accepting is the only action that alters the contract, and no agent can take it. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Contract review is stateful, multi-step, and unforgiving of hallucination, exactly where screen-scraping agents fail and where a typed tool surface shines. Three things WebMCP makes possible that a chat upload cannot: The output is document state, not prose. A suggestion is an object anchored to clause 6 with an accept button, an author, and a status, not a sentence to transcribe. The document is live. Tools read the contract as it currently stands, so "re-check the clauses I just changed" works. An upload is a snapshot that goes stale immediately. The safety is structural. Any AI with write access is safe only while it behaves. Here there is no mutation tool registered, and the server refuses any write tagged as an agent. "Please don't edit without asking" versus "there is no API to edit" is the whole difference. Typed schemas help too: flag_risky_clause requires a clause id that exists, so the agent cannot cite clause 27 of a 13-clause contract the way chat routinely does. How it creates a better user experience You stop being a transcription layer between a chat window and a document. The agent does the reading, the comparing, and the drafting; you do the deciding, on a screen that shows exactly what would change, why, and who suggested it. Rejections carry reasons the agent can read back, so the review gets sharper as it goes. And because the tool surface is public, you bring your own agent, the one that knows your last eight contracts, your rates, and your risk tolerance. A document dropped into a fresh chat window knows nothing about the person dropping it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Work on the same legal document simultaneously, with a guarantee specifying who can change it. Before WebMCP, an agent either had no access (advice you retype) or full access (write permission you have to trust). Redline is the third option: full analytical reach, zero write capability , enforced by which tools exist rather than by how well the model behaves. The phase model makes that dynamic. In analysis, the agent has 8 tools and literally cannot propose. In redlining, it has 12. Once the contract is executed, it has 5, all read-only — a signed contract cannot be marked up, and the agent's own capabilities reflect that the moment the phase changes. How we implemented WebMCP Twelve tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback for older Chrome previews), unregistered via AbortSignal whenever the review phase changes: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "propose_edit", description: "Propose replacement text for a clause. This does NOT change the contract — it " + "creates a redline the human accepts or rejects.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { clauseId: { type: "string" }, proposedText: { type: "string" }, rationale: { type: "string", maxLength: 400 }, }, required: ["clauseId", "proposedText", "rationale"], additionalProperties: false, }, execute: async (input) => { const { proposalId } = await api.propose(reviewId, { type: "replace", ...input, via: "agent" }); return `Proposal ${proposalId} created. Status: pending_human_approval — the contract ` + `is unchanged until a human accepts it. Use list_proposals for the outcome.`; }, }, { signal: phaseController.signal }); Two design decisions did most of the work: Errors are written to be recovered from. "Error: no clause c27. Valid ids are: c1, c2, …" tells the agent how to fix its own mistake instead of leaving it to guess. Descriptions are prompts. Each says when to call the tool and what to read first, which is why agents chain them sensibly without being told the order. Stack: Express + vanilla JS, server-sent events for live sync across everyone reviewing, Upstash Redis in production so reviews survive serverless cold starts. Challenges we ran into Making the guarantee real rather than rhetorical. It isn't enough to omit an accept tool; the server also rejects any resolve request tagged via: "agent" , and phase changes are human-only. Defense in depth, so the claim survives a hostile reading. Writing tool descriptions models actually follow. Early versions had agents proposing edits to clauses they hadn't read. Explicitly saying so in the description fixed it. The WebMCP surface is still moving between document.modelContext and the earlier navigator.modelContext , so registration goes through a small adapter. What we learned Capability design is the safety story. Every guardrail you can move from the prompt into the tool surface is a guarantee instead of a hope — and phase-scoped registration means the answer to "what can this agent do right now?" is a list you can print, not a judgment call. What's next for Redline Upload your own contract; a shared playbook per organization so proposals match house style; multi-party review where the other side's agent negotiates back; and export to tracked-changes DOCX so the redlines land in the tools lawyers already use.  Inspiration 

 The meme "I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do my art and my writing..." and not the other way around. What does it look like to start employing robots to do work in our everyday lives so that we can be freed to do the parts that we enjoy more? 

 What it does 

 A simple cozy farm simulator game (think Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley)
Also: A detailed WebMCP inspector built into the game to give a transparent view to tool-calling under the hood. 

 How we built it 

 GPT 5.6 in Github Copilot, deployed on Github Pages, using 98.css for a retro feel that gives lots of popup explorable dialogs to have deeper insights into the WebMCP protocol and understand it on a more fundamental level. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting good artwork was a challenge. Eventually found the public domain Kenney set of artworks (TinyFarm, TinyTown, TinyDungeon) and was able to use that to cobble together enough assets for a complete-ish game. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Really happy with the debug view into WebMCP and being able to inspect and see what the LLM sees, and how it looks at the world.
Also happy that the human player and robot player controls go through the same basic interface. The only thing that matters is their source (keyboard or tool-call) -- but otherwise they're on an equal playing field. 

 What we learned 

 That there is a LOT that goes into a full / fun game. It's just a basic shell of a game, and there is not yet enough fun stuff to do. 

 Also learned that balancing the right number of tool calls for WebMCP is a tricky thing, and there is a LOT of tinkering that one can do with making a sensible interface for agents and humans alike. 

 What's next for VibeFarmer 

 Expand the simulator, add more things to do -- especially more time-consuming but fun activities (exploration, decoration, etc) and give a rich environment for collaborating on things that make sense to delegate to the agentic AI, and things that make sense to do yourself.

title: Crepusculum Dream: A Playable WebMCP Portfolio
pitch: An explorable HD-2D portfolio where visitors and agents share one live interface—walking the world, building goal-specific tours, and inspecting page-aware work through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An explorable HD-2D portfolio where visitors and agents share one live interface—walking the world, building goal-specific tours, and inspecting page-aware work through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Playable HD-2D home world—explore by keyboard, mouse, touch, or a WebMCP agent sharing the same live page state. A goal-specific tour appears in the live UI, giving visitor and agent a shared route through the portfolio. Research tools expose publication metadata and paste-ready BibTeX; copying stays an explicit human action on the shared page. The sanitized Mods page keeps the case study and external links while replacing bundled third-party artwork with coarse mosaics. The WebMCP interface separates global and page-specific tools and explains their shared visible state. Inspiration Most portfolios give every visitor the same menu, even though a recruiter, research collaborator, technical reviewer, and creative visitor are looking for different evidence. Agents also tend to receive a detached data view that the person cannot see. I wanted both participants to inhabit the same place: a playable portfolio whose visible page, navigation, and tool surface move together. Crepusculum Dream began as my personal HD-2D hub world. For the WebMCP Challenge, I meaningfully extended it into a shared human-agent interface and packaged the result as a separate, rights-safe competition edition. What it does Visitors explore a dusk-lit pixel world with keyboard, mouse, or touch controls. Landmarks lead to Projects, Research, Mods, Zine, and About. A WebMCP-capable agent can operate the same live interface through tools registered for the current route: Five global tools list pages, retrieve my biography, navigate, change language, and create a personalized portfolio tour. Home adds tools for walking the on-screen traveler to a landmark and reading its position. Every content page supplies its own version of get-page-overview and focus-page-section; the same tool name has page-specific sections and effects. Projects exposes the fluid-simulation work, Research exposes publications and a read-only, paste-ready BibTeX result, Mods exposes project details and a Workshop action, Zine exposes individual pieces, and About exposes photography captions. There are 16 distinct tool names. The live registry contains 7 tools on Home and 8 / 9 / 9 / 8 / 8 on Projects, Research, Mods, Zine, and About respectively, so an agent sees only actions that make sense on the page shared with the visitor. Human-agent collaboration The challenge-period centerpiece is create-portfolio-tour. The agent translates a visitor goal—recruiting, research collaboration, technical review, creative exploration, or a complete tour—into a visible liquid-glass route panel. Both participants see the same stops. Choosing one uses the site's real router; first arrival opens at the page introduction or abstract, while choosing a deeper stop centers and highlights that section below the persistent top bar. This is not a static API beside the website. Tool calls act on the mounted DOM and the same router used by the visitor. The URL, visible page, focused section, browser metadata, and registered tools change together. On Home, agent-driven movement controls the same traveler that the person can move directly. Information-retrieval tools can spare an agent from reading and re-grounding against an entire long page when the visitor needs one precise fact. Interaction tools provide semantic actions for navigation, movement, and focus instead of relying on fragile coordinate-based UI operations. Together, these tools can reduce unnecessary context and token use while lowering grounding and execution errors, potentially improving task-completion reliability. How I built it The application uses TypeScript and Vite without a frontend framework. Home is rendered in Canvas 2D at a low internal pixel-art resolution and scaled with nearest-neighbor rendering, combining procedural sprites and tiles with lighting, fog, embers, ash, depth blur, and color grading. Content pages reuse the animated dusk backdrop. Tools are registered through the standards-track document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Global tools stay registered for the session. Each route owns an AbortController; mounting registers contextual tools and unmounting cancels their work and removes them. This prevents stale tools after rapid navigation and lets shared tool names have route-specific schemas, results, and visible behavior. Every tool has a human-readable title, a strict JSON schema with additionalProperties: false, concise descriptions and results, trust/read annotations, and cancellation-aware execution when the host provides a signal. get-citation is a read-only information tool that returns a complete, paste-ready BibTeX entry for Overleaf; copying remains an explicit control in the shared page UI rather than an agent tool. The production build targets Chrome 149 or later. What I added during the challenge The playable world and an initial set of global, Home, and Research WebMCP tools predated the submission period; I do not claim them as new work. The latest public pre-challenge baseline is 5acdbc7 , dated August 17, 2026. Challenge-period work added the page-aware registry and route lifecycle, contextual overview/focus tools, exclusive tools for every content area, the Workshop action, a read-only paste-ready BibTeX retrieval tool with copying left to the visible page UI, strict schemas and annotations, cancellation support, Chrome 149 compatibility, route-specific metadata, structured WebMCP documentation, the visible goal-specific tour, shared-state focus behavior, and a repeatable six-route smoke test. The dated evidence is the original repository's 5acdbc7...5052cf2 comparison and the competition repository's CHALLENGE.md . Competition-safe edition The submitted repository is a clean export with new Git history so removed third-party source files are absent from both the tree and its history. It uses an anonymous blue-and-white pixel identicon, nonrepresentational coarse mosaics for redacted previews, CSS-only card/relic grids, and optimized runtime media only. Identity-specific game names, source artwork, a research PDF, the original publication teaser, and adapted literary mascots are not bundled. The Mods page retains ordinary external links to the separately maintained project and Workshop listing; their target content is not copied or proxied here. The audit compared all 31 retained image/vector/video files against 27 restricted baseline originals and found zero SHA-256 matches. Details and licensing boundaries are documented in ASSET-AUDIT.md , PROVENANCE.md , and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Challenges The hardest engineering problem was making page lifecycle part of the tool contract. An asynchronous registration can finish after its page disappears, so route cancellation and ownership must be explicit. Stable tool names also need page-specific schemas so an agent cannot request a section absent from the visible UI. The hardest experience-design problem was keeping collaboration observable: navigation, scroll positioning, fixed-top-bar clearance, highlighting, transition timing, and the tour panel all have to agree. A separate challenge was drawing a clear provenance and licensing boundary without weakening the working demo. Accomplishments One live router and DOM are shared by human and agent rather than parallel representations. Page-aware registration keeps the available actions precise across all six routes. Native Chrome and Codex in-app-browser checks pass, as does the automated WebMCP smoke suite. get-about-me is genuinely read-only; visible focus remains a separately modeled interaction. The public deployment, source, tests, metadata, and submission documentation describe the same sanitized build. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when tools express capabilities of the interface currently in front of the visitor. Page scope reduces ambiguity, visible effects build trust, and stable semantic actions let an agent help without taking the experience away from the person. Team Yunhao Luo led the overall site design and implemented the application, WebMCP integration, testing, rights-safe packaging, and submission materials. abcdefgJack contributed only through idea exploration and design discussion. What's next I would add evaluation datasets for tool selection, visitor-authored tour goals, deeper accessibility testing, and richer collaboration cues while following the evolving WebMCP standard. License and provenance The application source is MIT-licensed. Original site content and the limited third-party fonts/profile-link marks retained by the competition edition are separately documented. The original personal site and repository are linked only as the transparent pre-challenge baseline; the submitted live build and source are the sanitized competition edition. pitch: An educational AI evidence-reasoning app that helps students compare claims with evidence using bounded, explainable classifications.

An educational AI evidence-reasoning app that helps students compare claims with evidence using bounded, explainable classifications.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 ProofPath AI YES — Track 1: AI Application Development 

 Problem 

 Students often encounter claims online without a clear method for checking whether the evidence they have actually supports, contradicts, or is insufficient for the claim. ProofPath turns that reasoning step into a small, transparent educational workflow. 

 Solution 

 Users enter a claim and a piece of evidence. ProofPath classifies the relationship as SUPPORTED , CONTRADICTED , or INSUFFICIENT and returns bounded probabilities. It is intentionally limited to educational evidence assessment and does not claim to be a truth detector or scientific validator. 

 AI and technical design 

 The application uses a lightweight evidence-classification model behind a single analysis path. The same bounded analyze(claim, evidence) function is used by the human-facing interface and the structured WebMCP tool. This avoids duplicated verdict logic and keeps the same safety limits across interfaces. 

 Evaluation and testing 

 The project includes automated regression tests for the model and UI plus a real-browser WebMCP runtime canary. The canary discovered the analyze_evidence tool in headed Chrome, successfully invoked a normal evidence case, and verified that blank evidence fails closed instead of producing a confident result. 

 Responsible AI 

 ProofPath uses an explicit claim ceiling: EDUCATIONAL_EVIDENCE_ASSESSMENT_ONLY . Missing required input returns a BLOCK state. The project is not presented as a medical, legal, scientific-validation, or general automated fact-checking system. 

 User experience 

 The app remains usable as an ordinary web form. Students can enter a claim and evidence directly, inspect the resulting classification, and see when the system refuses to classify because necessary evidence is missing. 

 Track 1 submission package 

 The submission includes a slide presentation describing the problem, architecture, evaluation, responsible-AI constraints, and impact; a video walkthrough/live demo; source code and a live deployment; and the required packaged deliverables. 

 Built and verified with 

 JavaScript, HTML, CSS, lightweight machine-learning classification, WebMCP, GitHub Actions, headed Chrome runtime verification, and ChatGPT-assisted implementation/test/documentation workflows.

title: BenchPilot
pitch: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting.
about_excerpt: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hardware troubleshooting often becomes an unstructured stream of chat messages, photos, measurements, guesses, and repeated questions. The person can touch the physical system, but the agent can organize far more context than a person wants to track manually. BenchPilot gives both sides one inspectable workspace without letting the agent pretend it observed the hardware. What it does BenchPilot is a shared diagnostic canvas for safe low-voltage electronics. The human records symptoms and de-energized measurements. The app maps device topology, ranks evidence-linked hypotheses, maintains a safe test plan, preserves an append-only history, and produces a diagnostic report. In a WebMCP-capable browser, BenchPilot registers 12 typed tools over the same live case state. An agent can read the case and canvas, focus visible components, propose safe test steps, record only values explicitly supplied by the human, organize hypothesis updates, draft a cautious plan, and undo its own accepted changes. Every write is visible, attributed, reviewable, and reversible. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the product's collaboration layer, not a decorative integration. A troubleshooting agent needs structured topology, stable entity IDs, evidence provenance, unit and power-state validation, and a safe way to change the same workspace the person sees. Scraping page text cannot reliably provide those guarantees. BenchPilot's WebMCP tools use strict schemas and compact result envelopes. Human and agent actions share one command layer, so validation, revision checks, history, proposals, and undo behave identically from either interface. The site remains fully useful when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it BenchPilot uses Vinext/Next.js App Router compatibility, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Zod, @xyflow/react, Drizzle migrations, and Cloudflare D1 on OpenAI Sites. A deterministic NEMA 17 seed and rule engine make the flagship journey repeatable without an external LLM or physical hardware. Safety is enforced at the domain boundary: allowlisted test templates, strict type/unit pairs, disconnected-power requirements for resistance, session/case isolation, optimistic revision checks, rate limits, proposal review, actor attribution, and targeted undo. The release gate includes unit tests, WebMCP contract tests, production builds, and desktop/mobile browser journeys. Challenges The hardest design problem was balancing useful agent autonomy with human ownership of physical truth. BenchPilot lets the agent organize and propose while preventing it from silently inventing measurements or replacing canonical wiring. We also kept tool results compact while still returning revision, changed IDs, and a visible verification target. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve discoverable WebMCP tools operating on live shared state. A production-verified read, focus, proposal, human accept, and targeted undo loop. Deterministic D1-backed guest sessions with no login or paid API dependency. Unsafe energized resistance writes rejected at the API/domain boundary. Responsive manual fallback, accessible canvas list, and shareable report. Public MIT-licensed source with automated release gates. What we learned The best human-agent interfaces make authority boundaries visible. Structured tools help, but collaboration becomes trustworthy only when users can see why the agent acted, review the exact change, and reverse it without damaging human evidence. WebMCP rewards strong internal state design: stable IDs, provenance, revisions, and narrow commands improve both the agent experience and the manual product. What's next for BenchPilot Next steps include team case sharing, richer but still allowlisted device templates, instrument imports that preserve provenance, image-assisted label capture, and organization-level diagnostic playbooks. The safety boundary will remain deliberately narrow until each new procedure has explicit validation and review behavior.
