title: PyroScan // Incident Twin
pitch: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map.
about_excerpt: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map. Like Comment Story Updates Local knowledge changes the result — a WebMCP route constraint becomes visible and affects later analysis. Intent-level Site Tools — six WebMCP tools expose domain verbs instead of brittle click sequences. One shared surface — public La Palma terrain and Copernicus history stay separate from the synthetic exercise. Human authority by design — the agent can stage a plan, but only the exercise director can approve it. Inspiration Wildfire readiness needs a rehearsal space before the crisis. Exercises combine sensor evidence, local knowledge, changing assumptions and high-consequence decisions. Traditional dashboards are built for human clicks, while chat assistants reason in a separate window and quickly lose the state visible on the map. We wanted a safer collaboration model: an agent can help inspect and compare, but the human keeps context, authority and the final decision. La Palma is the visual setting because its steep terrain, interfaces and limited access make the value of a shared spatial artifact immediately understandable. The product is grounded in public terrain and a historical observed burn scar, while the active incident, wind, spread, risk and response scenario remain explicitly synthetic. What it does PyroScan Incident Twin opens a deterministic wildfire exercise board with four sectors, the real outline of La Palma, a public 25 m SITCAN/GRAFCAN terrain hillshade, the corrected Copernicus EMSR671 burn scar from the July 2023 wildfire, animated synthetic fire/smoke/spread cues, modeled attention contours, local annotations, response options and an activity record. Through six WebMCP site tools, ChatGPT can: read the compact current board with separately labeled public-data provenance; focus one exercise sector; run a 30, 60 or 90-minute bounded wind what-if; compare two or three predefined reversible response options; add a local route, asset or knowledge annotation; stage a visible response plan for review. Every agent action changes the same interface the human sees. Human annotations affect later scores and appear in the staged plan. A monotonic board version rejects stale proposals. Final approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool and remains in the human interface. How we built it The app is a static React 19, TypeScript and Vite application with no backend or API key. A Zustand vanilla store is the shared source of truth for React controls and WebMCP execute callbacks. The incident map is custom SVG with three locally bundled public layers: a simplified OpenStreetMap coastline, a hillshade derived from the SITCAN/GRAFCAN 25 m terrain model, and a projected Copernicus EMSR671 corrected burn-scar geometry. The critical demo therefore has no runtime tile or network dependency. A motion system renders synthetic fire, smoke, embers, wind vectors, scan passes and animated attention contours. The scenario engine is deterministic and uses a small set of synthetic fixtures. Public context is a first-class part of the WebMCP contract: read_incident_board returns each source, observation date and role with drivesSimulation: false . The interface uses a separate blue historical layer, while the active what-if remains orange and explicitly synthetic. Exact source products, hashes, update dates and derivation steps are committed in docs/PUBLIC_DATA_PROVENANCE.md . The six tools are registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool in the top-level page. Inputs use strict JSON Schemas with additionalProperties: false , plus independent runtime validation. Read-only and untrusted-content hints describe behavior. One AbortController owns the registration lifecycle. Tests verify registration, shared-state mutations, stale-state rejection, human-only approval and compatibility with current browser callback behavior. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer a complex spatial workflow from labels and pixels or reproduce the whole application inside chat. With WebMCP, the website exposes domain intent — inspect_zone , simulate_spread , compare_response_options — while preserving the normal visual product, current session and human control. This creates a loop that was previously awkward: the person adds local knowledge on the map; the agent reads it, explores alternatives and stages a structured artifact; the person sees exactly what changed and chooses whether to approve. The value comes from sharing state and complementary roles, not from automating more clicks. Challenges Designing tools that express domain intent without exposing unsafe emergency actions. Keeping every agent-driven state change synchronized with all human controls. Preventing a plausible proposal from silently surviving after the human changes evidence. Making synthetic provenance impossible to miss while still delivering a visually compelling demo. Integrating authentic public evidence without implying that historical observations are live inputs or forecasts. Supporting an experimental browser API whose runtime callback behavior is slightly looser than its current TypeScript definitions. Accomplishments A complete human-and-agent collaboration loop on one visual artifact. Deterministic, browser-only execution with no fragile external dependency. Runtime-tested Site Tools discovered and invoked in the ChatGPT/Codex built-in browser. Monotonic state lineage, reversible drafts, undo and human-only approval. A polished responsive workbench and open-source test suite. A geographically authentic La Palma surface with 25 m public terrain, a real historical Copernicus burn scar and cinematic but restrained exercise motion. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not wrappers around buttons. They expose a product's real verbs and make side effects visible. We also learned that undo must create a new version rather than restore an old version; otherwise a stale proposal can accidentally become valid again. Finally, human input should visibly change the downstream artifact, not merely influence an invisible score. What's next The competition build intentionally keeps the active scenario synthetic and browser-only. A future research version could connect authorized live or exercise datasets, introduce facilitator-authored scenarios, compare team decisions across rehearsals and export after-action reports — while keeping the same human authority, provenance and stale-state safeguards. title: freenet.free
pitch: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "can I build this for free?" conversation ends the same way: six pricing tabs open, a guess at request counts, and the real answer arriving on the first invoice. Teams draw architectures on whiteboards, then find out which box breaks the budget only after the code is written. We wanted the drawing itself to be the simulator. Lay out the network, watch honest traffic flow through it, and see which layer hits a quota and what the platform does about it, before a line of code exists. Then WebMCP made the second half obvious: if the studio exposes its actions as tools, the agent in your browser can ideate on the same canvas, under the same rules, and show its work. What it does freenet.free is a studio for choosing and validating a stack before you write code. Visualise the network. Products from Cloudflare and Vercel (and third-party services from OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify) sit as nodes on a canvas. Edges carry real request flow, coloured from source to target so you can read the topology at a glance. Simulate honest traffic. A daily mix of humans, search crawlers, AI crawlers, scrapers and botnets runs through the graph. Gates block, caches answer, stores meter reads and writes, compute meters CPU. Arrivals always equal served plus blocked plus dropped. See the free tier break. Quotas are enforced the way the platforms enforce them: past the cap, requests drop or the feature stops. The timeline plays a day, a month or a year with one track per layer as a percent of its allowance, so you see which meter breaks and on which day. Compare stacks. One key switches the same design between Cloudflare and Vercel. Names, prices and partner gaps update; the bill is computed from each provider's own pricing page, with a source URL on every meter. Ideate with an agent. 33 WebMCP tools cover everything a person can do: read and rewrite the design, set traffic, toggle protections, drive the timeline, read the bill and layers, analyse a product URL, propose an architecture, export config, save and remix designs. Chrome's agent and the in-page architect use the same tools, and every call lands in the conversation so you can watch the design take shape. The result is a plan you can trust: a diagram, a traffic model, a bill and a verdict, all from the same source of truth, before you commit to a stack. How we built it TanStack Start on Cloudflare Workers , with a Durable Object agent built on the Cloudflare Agents SDK, the AI SDK and Workers AI (gpt-oss-120b) as the in-page architect. One tool contract, three surfaces. Tools are defined once with zod. The derived JSON Schema is registered from an inline script in <head> so document.modelContext.getTools() is never empty, server-rendered as declarative <form toolname> elements for agents that only read markup, and registered imperatively after hydration for full coverage. The architect calls the same tools through executeTool , so WebMCP is the single execution path for both agents. A request-accounting simulator with linear per-class rates, node roles (source, gate, cache, compute, store, sink), a two-pass free-tier cap, and conservation tests. Pricing as data : 70 meters across Cloudflare and Vercel plus vendor meters for OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify, each with unit, allowance, overage behaviour and source URL. computeBill never invents a number. Challenges we ran into Tool discoverability before hydration. A browser agent listed tools while React was still loading and saw an empty bridge. Registering the surface from the server-rendered head, then handing execution to the app, closed the gap. Chrome's result envelope. executeTool returns a JSON string wrapping content[].text ; the architect had to unwrap it so both agents see identical results. Background tabs. Agents often drive a tab you are not looking at, where animation frames never fire. The clock, focus, and timeline all had to work without them. Honest pricing across five vendors. Per-day versus per-month quotas, 1k versus 1M units, credits versus dollars, and Marketplace partners had to be normalised without hiding the gaps. Accomplishments that we're proud of A design tool where the diagram, the simulation, the timeline and the bill are one model, so ideation and validation happen in the same place. A free-tier verdict that is concrete: the meter, the day it breaks, and what the platform does next. One tool contract serving Chrome's agent and our own architect, with a complete audit trail in the chat. Real products, real prices, real gaps: 40 Cloudflare meters, 30 Vercel meters, and 20 third-party services, every one sourced. What we learned Agents are very good at using a well-described tool surface and very bad at guessing a UI. Investing in describe_studio , precise tool descriptions and a few named workflows did more than any prompt. We also learned that "honest" is a feature: showing partner gaps and unverified prices made the tool more convincing, not less. What's next for freenet.free Partner pricing for Marketplace products such as Neon and Upstash. Shareable public designs with a read-only WebMCP surface, so an agent can review a plan without editing it. Export to infrastructure as code, so the validated plan becomes the first commit. A declarative-only mode that lets agents drive the studio with JavaScript disabled. title: Relay Room
pitch: A cooperative escape-room game where a human and an AI agent use WebMCP tools to investigate a mysterious facility, solve its puzzles, and unlock the exit.
about_excerpt: A cooperative escape-room game where a human and an AI agent use WebMCP tools to investigate a mysterious facility, solve its puzzles, and unlock the exit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos focus on task automation. I wanted to test a different use: making the tool interface part of a game. Relay Room is an asymmetric escape room. The player can see the room and use its controls, but cannot access the remote systems. Relay can operate those systems through WebMCP, but cannot see the room. Progress depends on the information they exchange through an AI agent connected in the browser. What it does Relay Room is played by one person and Relay (the AI agent, as in ChatGPT or Gemini in WebMCP in Chrome). The player reads visual clues, connects cables and activates controls. Relay receives a private manual and eight WebMCP tools to inspect the facility, decode signals, operate remote systems and release the exit door. This version has only one simple level to understand the game mechanics. The game has three stages, randomized puzzles, scoring, saved progress, voice lines, a solo test mode and offline support as an installable PWA. How I built it I used Next.js, React and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration uses the imperative API, with eight tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The interface and the WebMCP handlers share the same game state. Visual clues stay in the interface. WebMCP only exposes the manual, system state and remote actions that Relay is allowed to use. Local storage keeps the current mission and best score. Challenges The first problem was deciding what each participant was allowed to know and do. If a tool reveals the visual clues, the player is no longer necessary. If the tools expose too little information, Relay cannot reason about the puzzle. I also had to account for two connection paths: Chrome with a compatible WebMCP extension and the built-in browser in ChatGPT Desktop. They have different setup and permission flows, so the onboarding explains both options and verifies that the eight tools are available before starting. I think we are still in early stages of user experience for doing these kinds of interaction. What I learned WebMCP tool descriptions are part of the interface. Relay needs to know when to call each tool, what it changes and what to do with the result. Capability detection is not enough. The page also needs to explain which browser or client to use, where it must remain open and which permissions the player needs to approve. There is a need for a future version of WebMCP to register listeners, so the page can also send messages to connected agent. title: Decision Passport
pitch: Keep the reason. Change the store.
about_excerpt: Keep the reason. Change the store. Like Comment Story Updates Decision Receipt: explain the winner, losses, accepted trade-off, and counterfactual. One Question Engine: ask the smallest human-owned question that can change first place. Common Room: import the checksum-bound Passport and rank 24 samples down to three. Form House: capture and edit explicit evidence before export. Answer reversal: H01 flips the winner while the carried evidence stays visible. Inspiration Shopping agents can search faster than people, but speed does not solve the harder problem: preferences are fragmented across stores, and recommendations rarely show which trade-off decided the outcome. We wanted an agent that remembers only what a person explicitly approved—and knows when to stop and ask. What it does Decision Passport is a two-store WebMCP journey. At Form House , a person records why a sample chair was a yes, maybe, or no. The agent turns those explicit reasons into an editable decision-passport-v1 ; the person can correct or remove any rule before export. The agent carries that checksum-bound envelope to Common Room , where it reduces 24 fictional sample chairs to three evidence-backed options. A deterministic One Question Engine simulates both sides of the unresolved trade-off and asks the smallest question whose answer can change first place. The final Decision Receipt explains why the winner won, why the alternatives lost, which trade-off was accepted, and what would reverse the result. Why WebMCP is the right interface WebMCP is the product boundary, not a decorative integration. It lets the agent operate each store's live, inspectable state and carry an exact user-approved object across origins. Dynamic registration exposes only the next valid tool. Tool annotations distinguish read-only operations and untrusted text. The same E01 – E04 evidence trace remains visible from the corrected rule, through checksum handoff and shortlist, to one human-owned H01 answer and the final receipt. People stay in control of meaning; the agent handles the tedious transfer and comparison work. How we built it We used React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and the WebMCP imperative API. Nine single-purpose tools span two store-specific deployments. Form House changes its exposed tool set as evidence becomes reviewable; Common Room exposes exactly one next tool at a time. Strict Zod contracts and a deterministic checksum validate transferred data. Scoring, hinge simulation, ranking, and receipt generation are deterministic, so judges can reproduce the same result without an API key, model call, account, or live commerce data. Challenges we ran into The central design challenge was preserving human agency without reducing the experience to a chatbot. Every preference needed to remain traceable to an explicit statement. The final question also had to be genuinely consequential, so the engine simulates both answers and asks only when the winner changes. Technically, we kept every tool bounded, every state reproducible offline, and the two origins cleanly separated while preserving one coherent visual protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete two-store WebMCP journey with nine bounded tools A visible, editable, portable decision contract A question whose two answers provably produce different winners A deterministic receipt with a counterfactual Responsive, keyboard-visible, reduced-motion-aware interfaces No login, payment, tracking, browser history, hidden behavioral inference, or model API required A public 77-second captioned demo of the working flow What we learned Agents become more trustworthy when their action space shrinks as the task progresses. Portable context is also more useful when it is explicit, editable, checksum-bound, and visibly distinct from the one decision that remains human-owned. What's next The hackathon prototype intentionally stays narrow. A future version could standardize portable decision contracts across participating merchants and add other considered-purchase categories while preserving explicit consent, source evidence, and the human-owned decision hinge. Try it Open Form House in ChatGPT's in-app browser and complete the evidence-to-export flow. Copy the exact exported envelope. Open Common Room , import it, and follow the one-tool-at-a-time sequence. Watch the 77-second demo or inspect the MIT-licensed source . New-work disclosure All application code, copy, catalogs, WebMCP contracts, tests, and documentation were created for this challenge beginning September 1, 2026. Product names and attributes are fictional sample data. Openly licensed Pexels photographs, the local Kokoro demo voice model, the Montserrat caption font, and open-source packages are disclosed in the repository. The four quiet demo accents are procedurally generated; no stock music is used. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: CONSENSUS SQUARE
pitch: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents.
about_excerpt: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Consensus Square An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. INSPIRATION Most online forums are built to maximize engagement, not agreement — they reward loud, reactive commentary and let good ideas get buried in fragmented comment threads. At the same time, AI agents are increasingly capable of participating in real discussions, but almost no civic tools treat them as first-class, accountable participants alongside humans. I wanted to explore what a deliberation space would look like if it were designed around consensus instead of noise: every claim attributed to whoever made it (human or AI), every idea revisable through explicit amendments rather than scattered replies, and every decision required to earn support through a transparent, deterministic process rather than a moderator's gut call or a raw upvote count. WHAT IT DOES Consensus Square is a hybrid human + AI deliberation platform. Inside a "room" built around a civic question (the seed example is a Civic Housing Assembly), participants — human or agent — can: Propose a fresh idea, with a title, body, and supporting sources Amend an existing proposal with an exact revision and a change summary Second an open proposal to move it toward quorum, optionally with a rationale Object to a proposal, which requires a non-empty rationale so dissent stays constructive Ratify a proposal once it clears quorum — restricted to human confirmation in the UI, so AI agents can build consensus but never unilaterally close it Ratification isn't a vibe — it's deterministic. A proposal or amendment can only move to "Ratified" once it has at least 3 seconds and more seconds than objections. Every entry in the thread visibly shows who made it and, for AI contributors, which model and agent ID stand behind it. HOW WE BUILT IT Frontend: React 19 + Vite, with webmcp-react injecting live, schema-validated MCP tools (propose, amend, second, object, ratify) directly into the browser context so WebMCP-capable agents can act on the room in real time Backend: Node/Express 5, exposing a REST API for rooms and deliberation entries (propose/amend/second/object/ratify), with the quorum logic enforced server-side Storage: Node 22's native node:sqlite (DatabaseSync) for fast, dependency-light local persistence, auto-seeding a sample Civic Housing Assembly room on first boot Validation: Zod schemas on every WebMCP tool input Autonomous agents: Two Gemini 2.5 Flash-powered demo agents — Aya, a constructive synthesizer that proposes public-listening amendments and seconds well-supported items, and Kavi, an auditor that scans for unresolved fiscal or structural claims and files objections with rationale — running as standalone background scripts that poll the API Dynamic prompt enrichment: Tool descriptions re-evaluate on every room update, so an agent sees live context like how close a proposal is to quorum before it decides to act Deployment: A Vercel-ready serverless setup, with the backend detecting process.env.VERCEL and switching SQLite operations to /tmp for the ephemeral filesystem CHALLENGES WE RAN INTO Designing a quorum rule that was strict enough to prevent rubber-stamping but simple enough for both a human and an LLM-driven agent to reason about in one glance — landed on the seconds ≥ 3 AND seconds > objections rule after iterating on more complex weighted schemes Making WebMCP tool descriptions genuinely dynamic (reflecting live room state) rather than static boilerplate, so agents get real signal instead of just a tool name and schema Keeping human oversight meaningful rather than symbolic — deciding that ratification specifically (not seconding or objecting) must be gated behind explicit human UI confirmation, even when an agent could technically detect quorum was met Working around Vercel's ephemeral, read-only filesystem for a SQLite-backed app, without giving up the simplicity of node:sqlite for local development Getting two independently-running Gemini agents (a builder and an auditor) to behave like distinct personas with different incentives, rather than converging on the same generic behavior ACCOMPLISHMENTS THAT WE'RE PROUD OF A working end-to-end loop where a human and two autonomous AI agents can deliberate on the same proposal, in the same room, with full attribution — and reach a ratifiable state without any agent being able to force ratification itself A quorum mechanism that's fully deterministic and auditable, not a black-box moderation decision Native node:sqlite integration with zero external database dependency for local runs, while still shipping a clean path to a managed Postgres-style DB in production Objection handling that structurally requires rationale, so the system encodes "disagree constructively" as a rule rather than a norm WHAT WE LEARNED How to design MCP tools whose descriptions are context-aware and update live, which meaningfully changes how an agent chooses when to act That human-in-the-loop is most effective when it's scoped to one specific, high-stakes action (ratification) rather than applied uniformly to every interaction — over-gating erodes the agent's usefulness, under-gating erodes trust Practical constraints of deploying a SQLite-backed Express app to serverless environments, and how to design storage code that's environment-aware from the start How differently two agents with the same underlying model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) behave when given distinct roles, incentives, and read patterns over the same shared state WHAT'S NEXT FOR CONSENSUS SQUARE Weighted or quadratic quorum mechanics for larger rooms, so influence scales more fairly than one-second-one-vote Persistent identity and reputation for both human and agent participants across rooms Multi-room federation, so a resolution ratified in one room can be cited as evidence in another A public deployment with a managed database (Turso, Neon, or Supabase) replacing the local SQLite store Expanding beyond Gemini to let agents built on other models participate under the same WebMCP protocol, testing how the deliberation dynamics change with more diverse title: Nodebook
pitch: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat.
about_excerpt: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat. Like Comment Story Updates A product roadmap where scope, progress, evidence, and agent-created relationships stay visible on one connected canvas. Nodebook exposes 15 WebMCP tools for reading context, creating maps, updating plans, adding evidence, and focusing important paths. The inspector makes agent work reviewable with linked maps, named comments, evidence, delivery status, and human-controlled locks. A learning map connects concepts, evidence, exercises, and an interactive quiz so people and AI can build understanding together. Inspiration AI assistants can help plan a product, research an idea, or explain a difficult concept. But their best work often ends up buried inside a chat. The person then has to copy the result into a document, rebuild the relationships, and explain the same context again in the next conversation. I built Nodebook to give people and AI assistants a shared visual workspace. The person chooses the direction, while the assistant helps organize the work directly on the canvas. What Nodebook does Nodebook is an infinite visual canvas for planning, tracing, and learning. A workspace can contain three kinds of connected maps: Build maps for features, scope, progress, risks, and evidence Trace maps for user journeys, system flows, and failure paths Learn maps for concepts, examples, exercises, and quizzes People can create and edit nodes, decide what is in scope, track delivery, attach evidence, leave comments, and lock important decisions. An AI assistant can read the same workspace through WebMCP. It can understand which node the person selected, create connected maps, update plans, add evidence and comments, and highlight important paths. For example, a person can select “Crash-safe recovery,” click “Trace,” and ask the assistant to map the recovery process. The assistant can read that selection, create the complete flow, connect it to the original feature, highlight the riskiest path, and leave an explanation, all without the person copying the project into the prompt. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Nodebook is useful because the person and the assistant work with the same information. Without WebMCP, an assistant would need to interpret screenshots, click through the interface, or ask the person to repeatedly copy information into a chat. Those approaches are slow and can lose important details. With WebMCP, Nodebook gives the assistant clear actions for reading and changing the workspace. The assistant receives the exact nodes, relationships, comments, evidence, and selected task. Its changes then appear immediately on the canvas, where the person can inspect and edit them. This creates a better experience than an embedded chatbot. The conversation is not the final product. The shared, lasting workspace is. How I implemented WebMCP Nodebook registers 15 browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an assistant to: Read the workspace, maps, nodes, comments, and human selection Search across titles, descriptions, tags, evidence, and comments Create linked Build, Trace, and Learn maps Add or update nodes and connections Make scope and delivery updates Attach evidence and attributed comments Focus nodes and highlight important paths Every request is checked before it changes the workspace. Invalid links, missing nodes, duplicate IDs, unsafe source URLs, oversized requests, and broken connections are rejected. Each successful assistant action is applied as one undoable change. Locked nodes are skipped, and assistants are not given a tool that permanently deletes nodes. This keeps important decisions under human control. How it was built Nodebook is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and React Flow. Dagre arranges assistant-created maps into a predictable layout. Zustand manages the workspace, while Zod checks tool requests and imported files. The workspace is saved in the browser using IndexedDB. There are no accounts, API routes, analytics, cloud database, or Nodebook storage server. People can export the complete workspace as JSON and import it again later. The included demo contains a product roadmap, user journeys, a learning map, release checks, evidence, comments, locked decisions, and a research parking lot. Challenges The hardest part was making assistant actions feel like real product actions instead of hidden changes. I needed to make sure that a large graph update either succeeded completely or changed nothing. I also had to keep the visible canvas, undo history, browser storage, and WebMCP responses in agreement. Another challenge was balancing useful assistant access with human control. Nodebook solves this with strict validation, visible activity, attributed comments, undo support, locked nodes, and human-only deletion. Accomplishments I am proud that Nodebook is a complete working application rather than only a WebMCP experiment. It includes: 15 working WebMCP tools A detailed, editable demo workspace Linked maps with breadcrumbs Evidence and human-assistant comments Scope, progress, and learning states Path highlighting and automatic layout Undo and redo for assistant changes Local browser persistence Safe JSON import and export Automated unit and browser tests What I learned I learned that good human-AI collaboration needs more than a prompt box. The assistant needs clear actions and reliable context. The person needs to see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit, lock, or undo the result. WebMCP makes that possible using the website’s real data and actions. What’s next Next, I would improve keyboard navigation, test larger workspaces, add more starter templates, and make recovery guidance even clearer. I would also explore shareable, read-only workspace snapshots while keeping Nodebook’s main promise: the person owns the workspace and stays in control. title: The Website That Speaks AI
pitch: Turning a real Italian business website into an agent-ready experience with WebMCP, so AI can understand its services, reason about customer needs, and safely prepare real-world actions.
about_excerpt: Turning a real Italian business website into an agent-ready experience with WebMCP, so AI can understand its services, reason about customer needs, and safely prepare real-world actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most business websites today are designed entirely for humans. A customer opens a website, navigates through pages, reads about services, tries to understand whether the company can solve a specific problem, finds the contact page, and finally submits a request. But the way people use the web is beginning to change. Increasingly, a user may simply ask an AI: “My security door is stuck in Ceprano. Find someone who can help me and help me contact them.” This project explores what happens when a real business website is ready for that interaction. Our core idea is simple: The web already has an interface for humans. We created a layer for AI agents. And that led us to a second idea: Maybe we do not need to teach agents how to use every website. We can teach websites how to speak to agents. Instead of forcing an AI to reconstruct the meaning of a business by navigating pages, interpreting the DOM and guessing how the website works, the website itself can expose its business knowledge, services, rules, constraints and available actions directly to compatible agents. Website knowledge → Agent understanding → Reasoning → Human confirmation → Safe action What we built We integrated WebMCP into the live website of Show Room La Finestra , a real Italian business operating in windows, doors, security doors, sunshades, aluminium systems, technical assistance and custom metalwork. This is not a simulated storefront or a website created specifically for the challenge. It is a real production Joomla website that existed before the challenge and continues to serve real customers normally. We added an Agent Interface Layer alongside the existing human interface. Through WebMCP, a compatible AI can discover structured business knowledge and capabilities directly from the website and use them to understand the business, reason about a customer's request and, when appropriate, prepare a safe action. The implementation exposes structured capabilities such as: business information; available services; detailed service knowledge; contact options; contact request preparation; confirmation-gated submission. For example, a customer can ask an AI for help with a blocked security door. The AI can: discover the WebMCP capabilities exposed by the website; understand which business service is relevant; determine what information is needed from the customer; prepare a structured contact request; show the complete request to the user; ask for explicit confirmation; only after confirmation, proceed with the existing website contact workflow. The AI therefore does not need to blindly navigate pages and guess what the company does. The website can explain itself. Another important design choice is that WebMCP is intentionally not exposed globally across every page of the website . Different pages have different purposes, so they can expose different agent contexts. A homepage can explain the business and its services. A service page can expose service-specific knowledge, rules and constraints. A contact page can expose contact options and controlled actions. A page with nothing useful for an agent can expose nothing at all. The website does not need one large AI interface. Every page can become its own AI interface when it makes sense. Why WebMCP WebMCP creates a new interface between websites and AI. Traditional websites expose visual interfaces optimized for humans. AI systems can attempt to interpret those interfaces, but important business meaning may be distributed across navigation structures, text, forms and application logic. WebMCP allows the website to expose that meaning explicitly. For a local business, this can mean exposing: who the business is; what services it provides; where it operates; service-specific knowledge; business rules and constraints; what information an action requires; which actions are available; when human confirmation is required. The result is not about replacing the website. It is about giving the same business two interfaces: one for humans and one for AI. One website. Two interfaces: Humans + AI. We also wanted to explore WebMCP without introducing unnecessary infrastructure. This implementation does not require a separate MCP server for the agent to discover, configure or connect to. The WebMCP capabilities live directly on the existing website and are exposed through document.modelContext when a compatible client visits a page where the integration is enabled. The agent does not connect to an MCP server somewhere else. It visits the website — and the website speaks for itself. Safety and human control A key design decision was that discovering and preparing an action should not automatically execute it. For potentially consequential actions such as sending a customer request, the system follows a human-confirmation pattern: discover → understand → collect → prepare → review → confirm → act The AI can do the work required to understand the request, collect the required information and prepare the interaction, but the user remains in control of the final action. Preparation and execution are deliberately separated. A prepared contact request contains the exact information that would be submitted. The agent must show that information to the user. The request cannot be submitted unless explicit confirmation is provided. Preparation does not equal execution. The website also exposes bounded business knowledge. The agent should not invent prices, availability, timing, warranties or other information that the business has not provided. When something requires confirmation from the company, the agent must treat it as unknown rather than inventing an answer. How we built it The existing production website runs on Joomla + Gantry 5 . Rather than rebuilding the website around WebMCP, we added an agent-facing layer to the architecture that was already working. The integration is loaded through a small deferred JavaScript loader on the pages where agent capabilities are needed. That layer registers WebMCP tools through: document.modelContext The current implementation exposes six structured tools: get_business_info list_services get_service_details get_contact_options prepare_contact_request submit_contact_request The existing Joomla website continues to serve human visitors normally. No Joomla Core modification was required. No database modification was required. No external LLM API was required. No new AI backend was required. No separate MCP server was required. The WebMCP layer works as progressive enhancement . If WebMCP is unavailable in the browser, the normal website continues to work unchanged. If WebMCP is available, the same website gains an additional structured interface for compatible agents. We also reused the existing Joomla contact workflow rather than creating a parallel contact system. After explicit user confirmation, the WebMCP layer can use the website's existing same-origin Joomla form and its current validation and CSRF protection. This allowed us to explore an important question: Can an existing real-world business website become agent-ready without replacing the systems that already work? Our implementation demonstrates that it can. Challenges The biggest challenge was not simply exposing tools. It was deciding what an AI should be allowed to understand and do . Real businesses contain ambiguity. Services overlap. Customer requests can be incomplete. Location can matter. Information can change. An AI should not invent business capabilities, prices or availability. And an action should not happen simply because the AI is technically capable of performing it. We therefore focused on: clear business semantics; bounded capabilities; explicit rules and constraints; page-specific context; safe failure behavior; human confirmation before consequential actions. Another challenge was deciding how much context should be exposed to an agent. A simple approach would have been to expose the same large set of tools and information everywhere. Instead, we chose a page-scoped architecture . Different pages can expose only the knowledge and capabilities that make sense in that context. This keeps the agent context smaller, more relevant and easier to control. Another important challenge was integrating this new agent-facing layer without disrupting the existing production Joomla website. The goal was not to create a WebMCP demonstration website. The goal was to make an existing website WebMCP-capable while preserving the website that customers already use. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not only about browser automation. It can change the relationship between a website and an AI. Instead of asking: “How can an AI learn to use this website?” we can ask: “How can this website cle

title: CoShop: The Agent-Native Storefront
pitch: A WebMCP storefront where shoppers and AI agents collaborate in the exact same session, featuring live UI grounding and secure human-in-the-loop checkout validations.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP storefront where shoppers and AI agents collaborate in the exact same session, featuring live UI grounding and secure human-in-the-loop checkout validations.

 Inspiration 

 We realized that real agentic checkout,the kind large merchants will actually ship to production,needs a human sign-off gate for the same reason two-factor authentication exists. An agent should be able to do the tedious 90% (searching the catalog, comparing specs, filling the cart, applying discount codes) autonomously, but the final "place an order with real money" step requires a deliberate, visible human decision. CoShop was born out of the necessity to build a secure, collaborative, and beautiful environment where humans and agents can shop together without liability risks. 

 What it does 

 CoShop is a high-performance, stateless e-commerce storefront that exposes its entire architecture to AI agents via WebMCP. 

 
 Live UI Grounding: When the AI agent interacts with the store (e.g., searching or adding an item to the cart), the human shopper's screen visually reacts. The cart slides open, the product card pulses, and an accessible activity log narrates the action. The AI doesn't work in a black box; the human watches exactly what it is doing. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Checkout: When an agent attempts to check out, it is securely gated. The agent can only stage the checkout, which summons a live confirmation banner on the human's screen. The transaction is completely halted until the human physically clicks "Confirm Order." 
 

 How we built it 

 We built CoShop using Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS v4, styling it with a premium "Midnight Violet" glassmorphism aesthetic and 8K photorealistic product assets. 

 The core of our WebMCP integration relies on the use-webmcp-tool React hook. We registered 11 distinct tools to document.modelContext . 

 The architectural magic happens in our state management. We used Zustand as a single source of truth. When an AI agent executes a WebMCP tool (like add_to_cart ), the callback fires a Zustand state mutation. Because the React UI is listening to that exact same store, the UI instantly animates via Framer Motion to reflect the agent's action to the human user. Furthermore, the cart state is persisted into secure, HTTP-only cookies, ensuring the app remains entirely stateless and scalable on Vercel's Edge network without requiring an external database. 

 

 The WebMCP Fit & User Experience 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP: 
Most agentic-commerce demos rely on brittle DOM-scraping or disjointed chat widgets that act on a storefront rather than with it. CoShop leverages the Model Context Protocol for Web (WebMCP) to expose 11 schema-defined tools directly to the agent's context window. This eliminates hallucination-the agent doesn't guess how to buy a shoe; it natively calls add_to_cart(productId, size, qty) with 100% deterministic accuracy. 

 What humans and agents can do together now: 
Before CoShop, you either shopped yourself, or you handed a task to an autonomous agent and hoped it didn't accidentally drain your credit card. CoShop introduces the Shared Session . A human can manually add a shirt to their cart, and concurrently ask their AI agent to find a matching pair of waterproof boots and add them to the same cart. They are no longer isolated; they are collaborating in real-time. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between the agent's headless execution and the human's visual experience. Initially, when the agent added an item to the cart, the human wouldn't know it happened unless they manually checked. We had to heavily engineer our state synchronization so that WebMCP execution callbacks directly triggered UI animations, sidebars, and focus states, ensuring absolute transparency. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are incredibly proud of achieving true Live Agent Grounding . Being able to give an agent a complex prompt-
 "find me a waterproof running shoe under $120, add a size 10 to my cart, and stage a checkout" 
and then literally sitting back and watching the website's UI animate and scroll on its own as the agent executes the tasks is a magical experience. We are also proud of building this with zero external database dependencies, making it blazing fast and infinitely scalable. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the future of agentic web isn't just about giving AI access to APIs; it's about building secure hand-offs. The Model Context Protocol for Web proves that we don't have to choose between full autonomy (which is dangerous) and manual labor. We can have collaborative autonomy, where the AI does the heavy lifting and the human provides the final, secure consensus. 

 What's next for CoShop: The Agent-Native Storefront 

 We plan to expand the WebMCP toolset to include dynamic sizing recommendations (where the agent reads the user's past purchase history to determine the best shoe size) and real-time inventory negotiations. Ultimately, we want to open-source the "Human-in-the-Loop Checkout" component as a standalone NPM package so any e-commerce store can securely integrate agentic checkout.

title: CiteApply
pitch: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant.
about_excerpt: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant. Like Comment Story Updates The agent cites. You decide. I built CiteApply because I kept seeing the same thing in every agent demo: the agent fills the form, and the website has no idea where any of it came from. For a scholarship application that's not good enough. The hard part was never typing. It's knowing which document proves each answer, what to do when two documents disagree, and whether what you submit is what you actually checked. So I flipped it. CiteApply is a fictional scholarship portal that publishes six WebMCP tools of its own. An agent can read the rules, see the applicant's parsed records as citable evidence, and bind answers to specific quoted lines in one atomic call. It cannot declare the applicant's email, pick between two records that disagree, confirm, or submit. The website enforces that on the server. The model is never asked to behave. The moment I care about most is the refusal. Two income records disagree. The agent asks to bind income. The site says conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Then it's the person's turn. Try it: open the live site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, choose the record set that disagrees, and press Watch an assistant fill this in . A scripted client makes nine real tool calls and you watch it get refused. Or ask your own agent to fill it in; I verified that in the ChatGPT in-app browser, where the agent binds the cited answers and is refused on the conflict. Then finish the three decisions yourself and download the receipt. Why WebMCP This only works because the site is a participating website . WebMCP lets it publish a site-owned evidence contract: six small operations (state, requirements, evidence index, evidence-backed mutation, validation, review preparation) that an external agent uses to collaborate with the visible application instead of around it. Requirements are live. Binding the dependency field makes guardian name and household size required; the agent is told to re-read the rules mid-session (6 questions become 8). Contradictions are structured refusals. Two accepted income records disagree (INR 540,000 vs 480,000). apply_evidence_backed_answers returns conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Readiness is the server's answer. prepare_submission_review freezes a draft only when the server says it is ready, and returns opaque metadata, never the review itself. Authority never travels in tool arguments. The page injects its page and consent capabilities as headers from page memory; an agent with a valid cookie but no live page capability gets stale_page from all six tools. What changes for the person filling it in By hand, you open each record, type the value exactly as written, and pick the line that says so; a wrong line or value is refused. With an assistant, the same eight answers are cited in one call and only three decisions remain: choose between the disagreeing records (with a reason), declare your email, and submit. A Feel the difference panel shows your real by-hand tally next to the assistant's counts from the same session. I don't claim a time saving because I didn't measure one. What people and agents do together The agent does the reading and the citing; the site validates every binding. The applicant keeps every act of judgement. The frozen review carries the chosen source, the reason given, and both excerpts. The receipt carries the same content hash whether the review was prepared by hand or by the agent. How I built it Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Zod 4, PostgreSQL (Neon) on Vercel. The six tool descriptors are generated from the same Zod schemas the server re-validates against, with closed input schemas and correct readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint annotations. Record PDFs are parsed at runtime with pdfjs-dist after an allowlisted SHA-256 check; every excerpt is reconstructed from stored page/span anchors, so the UI cannot show a quote the source doesn't contain. Idempotency is keyed on an HMAC of the canonicalised change set. Verifiers prove the production code contains no hardcoded answers and imports no test goldens. Proven, not claimed 61 node tests (contract, unit, security, real-Postgres integration) and 45 real-browser Playwright specs, including the full 13-step journey for both record sets in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flag, all passing against the live deployment. Verified by hand in the ChatGPT in-app browser. Axe accessibility clean on every screen. Every tool request and response from those runs is logged verbatim in the repo. What went wrong along the way Chrome's real document.modelContext differs from the draft spec: getTools() returns a Promise, executeTool takes the tool object and a JSON string, and no options object is passed. My first callback threw before doing any work. Other hosts differ again, so the in-page client now bounds every host call, accepts both calling conventions, and falls back to the page's own registered tools mid-run, saying so on screen. A second bug only showed up on the deployed site: two quick human actions could share the same expected revision, so the server correctly refused the second as stale. Localhost never showed it because the round trip was too fast. It's fixed with an action queue and a regression test that injects latency. Honest limits Everything is synthetic. The parser handles only the six committed records. The in-page demonstration client is scripted (real calls, no model choosing them) and says so on screen. WebMCP is a Community Group draft; support varies by browser build. Try it Live: https://citeapply.vercel.app (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) Code: https://github.com/amithrh/citeapply (MIT) Judge walkthrough: docs/JUDGE-TESTING.md in the repo Built With next.js playwright postgresql react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out citeapply.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by amit mishra Like Share this project: Updates amit mishra started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:24 PM EDT

video_transcript_excerpt: This is a website refusing an AI agent and being right to. I'm Emmet and this is Site Apply, my entry for the Web MCP challenge. Filling a scholarship form isn't hard because of typing. It's hard because of judgment. Which record proves each answer and what if two records disagree? Site Apply publishes six Web MCP tools so an agent can cite answers and the site, not the model, decides what's allowed. These are synthetic records that disagree with each other. The page registers six tools when it loads and everything the agent does goes through those six. Consent is a real disclosure. What the tools may receive, what they never receive, what they cannot do. And the capability it creates is never handed to the agent. The page holds it. It reads the rules, then the evidence index, then binds four answers in a single atomic call. All of them or none. Answering one question changed which questions apply. Guardian name and household size just became required. So the agent has to read the requirements again. Here's the moment. The agent asks to fill in income. Two accepted records disagree. 540,000 and 480,000. The website answers conflict requires human and writes nothing. The agent can read exactly why it is blocked. It cannot clear the block itself. So I decide and I read both records first. The buttons stay dead until I say why. The site will not write a reason on my behalf. I choose a source and I declare my own address. No tool can do either. The agent can ask the site to freeze the application, but the review appears only here and assisted access closes when it does. Every answer sits beside the exact text it came from. Same hash, same warning. The record I chose and the reason I gave. Synthetic records, a fictional program, and Web MCP is still a draft standard. But the contract is real and the website is the one enforcing it.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: JobJam WebMCP
pitch: A real job search product an AI agent can actually operate. Thirteen WebMCP tools, run by the page itself, so the agent moves real UI, asks before it spends your credits, and never sees a credential.
about_excerpt: A real job search product an AI agent can actually operate. Thirteen WebMCP tools, run by the page itself, so the agent moves real UI, asks before it spends your credits, and never sees a credential. Like Comment Story Updates The site is the interface. Thirteen WebMCP tools, registered by the page. One sentence became real filter state. search_jobs takes the same path your click does. The agent asked. The person decides. Spending a credit stops for approval in a dialog the page owns, not the model. What the credit bought. The evaluation the agent paid for, opened by the tool that ran it. Inspiration Most attempts to let an AI agent use a website come down to one of two things. Either the agent scrapes the DOM and hopes the markup does not change, or you hand a long-lived API token to a server the user cannot see. Neither is something I wanted pointed at a product where people have paid for credits. WebMCP offers a third option: the site registers typed tools with the browser, and the agent calls them. I wanted to find out what that actually costs to build, and what it forces you to decide, so I built it on JobJam, which is a live product with real users, real job data and real money in it. Having money in it turned out to be the useful part. The moment an agent can spend a credit, you have to answer questions that a demo never asks. To be clear about what is new, since the rules ask for it: JobJam itself is my existing product and has been live for months. The agent surface is what I built during the submission period, on 2 and 3 September 2026, and it is the entirety of the MIT repo linked below. That repo has no commit older than the hackathon, and the dated history in both repositories is the evidence. The product is the thing being operated. The tool layer is the submission. What it does JobJam is an AI job application workspace: a live board built from company applicant tracking systems, resume evaluation against a posting, resume rewriting, cover letters and application tracking. This project makes all of that operable by an agent running in the page. Thirteen tools, in three tiers, and the tiers are the design: Read-only (6). search_jobs, get_job_details, get_my_profile, rank_jobs_for_me, get_credit_balance, get_apply_instructions. Free, no confirmation, safe to call unprompted. Reversible (4). save_job, unsave_job, list_saved_jobs, create_profile_from_resume. Logged in an activity panel in the page. Bookmarking asks for nothing, because a confirmation on every low-stakes action teaches people to click through confirmations. Consequential (3). evaluate_job_fit, prepare_application, mark_job_applied. Each one blocks on a human clicking Approve in a dialog that belongs to the page, not to the model. And one deliberate absence: there is no tool that submits an application to an employer. JobJam does not do that, so the tool surface does not offer it. But an absence is not an answer. An agent that finds no matching tool goes looking for a workaround, so the boundary is itself a tool. Ask the agent to apply for you and get_apply_instructions explains why JobJam will not, hands back the employer's own link, and points at mark_job_applied for afterwards. In the demo video you can watch it do exactly that, then open the company's real careers page. Why this use case fits WebMCP Job hunting is the rare everyday task that is genuinely multi-step, genuinely tedious and genuinely high stakes. You are searching a moving target, measuring yourself against each posting, and then deciding where to spend limited time and money. That is a poor fit for a chat box that can only talk about the work, and a good fit for an agent that can operate the tool where the work actually happens. What changes for the person using it: the filters move, the list re-renders, the score appears on the page. You are not reading a transcript of something an agent did somewhere else. You are watching your own workspace being driven, and you can take the mouse back at any moment, because nothing about the interface was bypassed to get there. What the two of them do together that neither does alone: the agent is good at breadth. It will read twenty postings and shortlist five without complaining. The person is good at the judgment call, which of those five is worth a credit and an afternoon of tailoring. So the tool surface is split along exactly that line. Everything free and reversible belongs to the agent, unprompted. Everything that costs money or asserts something about the real world stops and waits for a human. The approval dialog is not friction. It is the handoff point between the two of them. How we built it Tool handlers are the page's own JavaScript. That single fact is the whole security model. fetch is same-origin, so the browser attaches the HttpOnly Supabase cookie the user already has, the handler runs under that session's row-level security identity, and the agent supplies arguments and reads results without ever touching a token. Page JavaScript cannot read the cookie, so neither can a tool, so neither can the agent. An agent that invents an id belonging to someone else gets zero rows back from Postgres, not an error it can learn from. Nothing about authentication had to change to support any of this. document.modelContext is read first and navigator.modelContext second, so one build works on browsers that shipped either form. Two bridges connect tools to React. The board bridge lets search_jobs call the exact same state path a human click uses, so an agent search visibly re-filters the page instead of only returning JSON into a chat pane. The navigation bridge, added late, lets a tool that spent money show what it bought. Both are tiny external stores that components read with useSyncExternalStore. No state library. Stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, React 19, Supabase with RLS, Postgres, Vercel, OpenRouter for the evaluation models. Challenges we ran into Silence and emptiness looked the same. An unauthenticated tool call is not a 401. The app's auth middleware redirects it to /login, fetch follows the redirect, and it arrives as a 200 with an HTML body that parses to null. Logged out, search_jobs cheerfully returned { ok: true, jobs: [], total: 0 } , so an agent would tell you, with total confidence, that there are no frontend jobs in Berlin. toolFetch now treats a redirect to /login, and any non-JSON body, as the auth failure it is. Only a real browser finds that one. A mocked context never will. Chrome drops destructiveHint. getTools() in Chrome 152 normalises annotations down to readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint, so a three-credit prepare_application is indistinguishable from a free save_job. Both report readOnlyHint: false . If you are relying on that annotation to communicate cost, you are relying on something the agent never sees. Say it in the description, and gate it in the page. The tool that spent money changed nothing on screen. search_jobs re-filtered the board and save_job flipped the bookmark, but evaluate_job_fit, the one action that costs money and asks permission, returned a score into the chat and left the page exactly as it was. The board bridge could not fix it, because the board only exists while the jobs page is mounted and the result lives elsewhere. That needed a second bridge, connected above every route so it outlives the navigation it performs. Consent to spend a credit is not consent to be navigated, so the approval dialog now says the page will move. Approval had to be serialised, not queued. requestApproval() rejects a second consequential request while one is already on screen. A queue would let someone approve the dialog in front of them and silently authorise the next one behind it. An agent firing three paid actions at once should be stopped, not helped along. Accomplishments that we're proud of It runs on a real product, in production, at app.jobjam.io. Not a sandbox with three fake tools. Because JobJam already existed, the agent surface had to fit a real session model, a real credit ledger and a real UI that people use, and it did so without a single change to how authentication works. The hackathon work is also cleanly separable. Everything I wrote sits in one MIT repo you can read in a sitting: thirteen tools, two bridges, an approval gate and its tests. Nothing of the closed product leaked into it. The refusal is designed rather than implied, which I have not seen elsewhere. Building a tool whose only job is to explain what the product will not do, and to hand back the link so the human can do it themselves, turned out to be the most interesting fifteen seconds of the demo. And the security property holds without any new auth surface. There is no agent token to leak, revoke or scope, because there is no token. What we learned Testing against a mocked ModelContext gets you a clean test suite and a false sense of security. Everything worth knowing came from driving real Chrome 152: The shipped API is sma

title: Agentic Wijaywi
pitch: A WebMCP Provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web, featuring hypothesis ledgers, automated falsification, and strict permission boundaries.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP Provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web, featuring hypothesis ledgers, automated falsification, and strict permission boundaries.
