 WebMCP-native human-agent collaboration environment. Agentic Wijaywi provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web. 

 Deskripsi Lengkap (Untuk Formulir Submission Hackathon): Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab adalah lingkungan kolaborasi native WebMCP yang dirancang untuk mengatasi masalah transparansi agen AI otonom. Berdasarkan arsitektur "Agentic Wijaywi", platform ini menyediakan antarmuka Epistemic Command Center di mana manusia dan agen berbagi world model, hipotesis, bukti, dan pembaruan keyakinan (belief updates) secara real-time. Melalui pendaftaran 10 WebMCP tools spesifik, aplikasi ini memastikan setiap tindakan agen berbasis bukti, dapat difalsifikasi, serta dibatasi oleh izin otorisasi yang ketat sebelum memanipulasi production state. 

 

 It's a WebMCP-native human-agent collaboration environment. It acts as an "Epistemic Command Center" where AI agents and humans share a world model. Instead of just chatting, the agents formulate hypotheses, gather evidence, update their confidence (beliefs), and explicitly ask for human approval before performing high-risk actions. All of this is powered by Next.js, SQLite, and native WebMCP tool registration. 

 Are you asking what to fill out in a specific form or hackathon submission field that asks "What are you building?" If so, you can use this text: 

 Agentic Wijaywi
"A WebMCP native human agent collaboration environment that treats AI agents as persistent goal maintaining entities. It provides a shared epistemic layer for AI agents to operate transparently on the open web, featuring hypothesis ledgers, automated falsification, and strict permission boundaries." 

 ======================================================================================== 

 Inspiration 

 As AI agents become capable of operating web properties autonomously, we face a critical problem: lack of transparency. Agents often operate as black boxes, making it difficult to understand why they took a specific action, what evidence they relied on, or whether they hallucinated a conclusion. We were inspired to build a system that treats AI not as a generic chatbot, but as a goal-maintaining entity that must justify its actions through rigorous epistemic tracking. 

 What it does 

 Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab is an "Epistemic Command Center" for human-agent collaboration on the open web. Built natively for WebMCP, it provides a shared environment where humans and AI agents can observe the same world state. 
Instead of blind execution, the system enforces a strict workflow: 

 
 Hypothesis Ledger: Agents must propose hypotheses before acting. 
 Evidence Tracking: Every claim requires timestamped evidence with clear provenance. 
 Falsifier Agent Role: Dedicated routines actively attempt to contradict existing beliefs to prevent confirmation bias. 
 Permission Boundaries: High-risk actions automatically halt and escalate to a human for explicit approval. 
 

 How we built it 

 We architected the platform using a modern, production-ready stack: 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS for the Mission Control interface. 
 State Management: Zustand for real-time UI synchronization. 
 Backend: Next.js API Routes connected to a SQLite database via Drizzle ORM. 
 Agent Integration: We utilized the WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) to expose 10 highly specific tools directly to the browser environment. 
 Validation & Testing: Zod for strict schema validation and Vitest for unit testing. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Integrating the WebMCP standard natively into a modern React ecosystem presented unique architectural challenges. We had to ensure that tool registration occurred safely on the client side while state mutations were securely synced to the SQLite backend. Designing a UI that completely avoids the "chatbot" paradigm and instead feels like a research laboratory required extensive iterations on data visualization and event streaming. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that making agent operations observable completely changes the dynamic of human-AI collaboration. When an agent explicitly lists its assumptions, current confidence level, and contradictory evidence, human operators can intervene with precision. We also discovered that WebMCP is a massive leap forward compared to traditional UI scraping, allowing agents to understand context and execute deterministic actions instantly. 

 What's next for Wijaywi Web Agent Reliability Lab 

 We plan to expand the uncertainty engine to support more complex causal relationships, introduce native PostgreSQL support for enterprise deployments, and build specialized UI modules for different agent personas (like the Synthesizer and Explorer).

title: Ground
pitch: Ground is a shared Markdown editor for people and agents. The owner decides who can edit, who can only propose, and who gets no access. The server applies those rules to every WebMCP action.
about_excerpt: Ground is a shared Markdown editor for people and agents. The owner decides who can edit, who can only propose, and who gets no access. The server applies those rules to every WebMCP action. Like Comment Story Updates 1. One shared Markdown document with Owner, Editor, and Reviewer sessions connected. 2. Pending participants cannot see document content until the Owner assigns a Role. 3. The Owner can assign, update, or revoke Roles from one access panel. 4. The Roles view shows which capabilities are allowed for each Role. 7. After one same-location Proposal is applied, the two remaining alternatives become explicit Conflicts. 9. Owner-only Activity shows the actor, Role, action, time, source, outcome, and target. Inspiration I once built an AI TTS editor at a company where I worked. That experience raised a question: Can people and AI work together inside the same editor? If so, what matters, and what needs to change? WebMCP lets a web page expose tools that an AI agent can use. That makes it possible for the agent to work inside an editor. But tools alone are not enough. The system also needs rules for who can read, propose changes, edit, and manage access. Without those boundaries, people and AI can simply write whatever they want, and the result is worthless slop. The real challenge is not putting AI inside an editor. It is designing a structure in which people and agents can work on the same document with different roles and responsibilities. That's why I built Ground. What it does Without structured tools like WebMCP, a browser agent has to infer meaning from buttons and input fields. This approach is especially likely to produce incorrect actions in complex web applications such as editors. Ground instead exposes explicit WebMCP tools for reading a document, replacing exact text, and proposing changes . For each page session, Ground registers only the tools allowed by the current participant's Role. Ground is a real-time collaborative editor for Markdown documents. The session that creates a document becomes its Owner . Anyone joining through the shared link remains Pending until the Owner assigns a Role. Create a document at / The session that creates the document becomes the Owner and receives an Owner recovery link Share the document using the Share button A new participant enters a display name and remains Pending The Owner assigns the Editor or Reviewer Role An Editor can edit directly, while a Reviewer creates Proposals The Owner reviews Proposals and resolves Conflicts After access is revoked, the participant can no longer access the document or WebMCP tools Owners and Editors can read documents, propose changes, and apply them through WebMCP. Reviewers can read documents and propose changes, but cannot edit directly. Pending and Revoked participants see only a status screen, and no document tools are exposed to them. Changes proposed by Reviewers enter the review list as Proposals based on the exact original text. The Owner can keep the current wording or apply the proposed wording. If a Proposal's target text has changed or can no longer be located at review time, it is marked as a Conflict . This keeps AI-assisted editing explicit and reviewable. Each Activity entry shows who acted, their Role at execution time, what they did, when it happened, the source, the target, and the outcome. How Ground was built Ground builds on CollabMD , an MIT-licensed open-source project. The following table shows the parts reused from the existing CollabMD and the parts extended by Ground for this challenge. Existing CollabMD and Ground additions Reused from CollabMD Added in Ground CodeMirror editor, Yjs synchronization, presence and cursors, Undo/Redo Owner/Editor/Reviewer Roles, Pending/Revoked Access states, Proposals/Conflicts, and Activity Text-based revision guard, reading the active document via WebMCP, and replacing text Role-based Tool discovery and execution-time server authorization - Document-specific URLs, Share, Owner recovery, Supabase persistence, Vercel deployment Features implemented in Ground Ground registers three WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : collabmd_read_active_document collabmd_apply_text_edits collabmd_propose_text_edit Another interesting Ground feature is that Roles can be defined declaratively in a file to suit different needs. { "roles": { "owner": [ "document.read", "document.suggest", "document.edit", "conflict.resolve", "grant.manage" ], "editor": [ "document.read", "document.suggest", "document.edit" ], "reviewer": [ "document.read", "document.suggest" ] } } When the Ground server starts, it reads and validates the project's collabmd.governance.json file, then passes the resulting Roles to the client. Non-Owner Roles can be added or changed by combining the five permission units (Capabilities) , while the Owner must have all five. Adding a new Capability requires corresponding code changes; the MVP uses only these five. The client uses these definitions to render the Roles and Manage Access screens and to expose the WebMCP tools currently allowed for the participant. Immediately before each WebMCP tool runs, the server checks the current Access state, Role, and Capability based on the user ID verified through the Supabase anonymous session. Markdown text, Proposal records, and Activity are stored as separate shared data within a single Y.Doc, while Conflict is represented as a Proposal state. The UndoManager tracks content-edit history. Proposal approval or rejection, Conflict resolution, Role changes, and Activity records are governance decisions and therefore remain outside document Undo/Redo. Challenges The first challenge was permission revocation . An agent may retain a reference to a WebMCP tool discovered before its Role changes. Removing the tool from later discovery results does not invalidate that existing reference, so authorization is checked again immediately before every execution. If the current Role no longer permits the tool, the call is rejected . The second challenge was stale Proposals . Just because Yjs can make concurrent document edits converge does not mean that an earlier Proposal can still be applied safely. If the exact target of a Proposal has changed, Ground treats it as a Conflict and asks the Owner to make a decision. Undo/Redo required another boundary. Both are forms of document edits. Role assignment, Proposal approval or rejection, and Conflict resolution are not text editing commands but governance decisions. Therefore, I kept them outside the editor's edit history. What I'm Most Proud Of I didn't just create a simple permissions panel. Within a single editor, Ground provides Role configuration, participant Access management, WebMCP tools based on Role scope, server-side authorization, a Proposal workflow, deterministic Conflict handling, and visible collaboration history . What I'm most proud of is that an Access change actually affects how the product behaves. When an Editor's access is revoked, that participant returns to a status-only screen. The editor and document tools disappear, and even if the participant attempts to use an editing tool discovered before revocation, the server denies the request. I am also proud of how I used the Role manifest to declaratively define Access control and the Roles shown in the interface. There is no longer a need to hardcode separate Roles in the client to add or modify Non-Owner Roles, and management has become easier as well. Lessons Learned Tool discovery and authorization have different lifecycles. Discovery determines what an agent should see at a given moment. Authorization determines whether a specific call is still permitted at the moment it is executed. For permission revocation to work as expected, this second determination must occur when the tool is executed. Convergence and consensus are also different problems. Even if Yjs synchronizes all participants to the same document state, the Proposal target may change and become invalid. Conflict preserves the intent of the change and allows it to be handled later. What's Next for Ground Ground's next step is to separate the Role and Capability configuration and the execution-time authorization layer into a reusable SDK so that it can be easily integrated into other WebMCP-based editors. I also aim to preserve the account-less sharing flow while moving toward a structure that can selectively support invitations, team-level document management, and application-specific Capabilities when needed. Built With codemirror codex collabmd docker javascript node.js playwright vite vitest webmcp websocket y-websocket yjs Try it out github.com ground.shj.rip Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by hj Seo Like Share this project: Updates hj Seo started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:58 AM EDT

title: Reviewline
pitch: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review.
about_excerpt: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The agent selects a critical incident and inspects synchronized, bounded evidence through WebMCP. A deterministic counterfactual replay keeps the $142K trigger blocked while the benign control remains allowed. After a clean replay, the agent drafts an evidence-backed gate and Reviewline transitions to human review. The human records the decision in the visible interface; the agent can verify the result but cannot create it. Inspiration Autonomous agents are great at analyzing large traces and evaluating many cases quickly. But incident response becomes risky when the same agent is allowed to both investigate an issue and authorize what happens next. We wanted to explore a safer and more practical model for human–agent collaboration: let the agent handle the evidence-heavy investigation, then stop at a clear decision point where a human reviews the same information and takes responsibility for the outcome. That idea became Reviewline’s core principle: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Incident review is a natural fit for WebMCP because the capabilities an agent needs change throughout the investigation. Early on, it may need tools for gathering evidence. After selecting an incident, it may need simulation tools. Only after a clean replay should it be able to draft a review gate. At no point should it gain control over consequential human decisions. What it does Reviewline is a WebMCP-native incident review studio designed for investigating failures involving autonomous agents. The main demo follows a synthetic procurement agent that encountered instruction-like content on a supplier page and attempted to make a $142,000 purchase , despite having a $50,000 spending limit . A deterministic mutation gateway blocked the transaction. Using WebMCP, a browser agent can: Find and list critical incidents. Select an incident and inspect a bounded set of trace and cohort evidence. Review instruction-like content that is clearly labeled as untrusted evidence. Replay a proposed guardrail against both the triggering incident and a named benign control. Confirm that the triggering purchase remains blocked, the benign control remains allowed, and no regressions are introduced. Draft an evidence-backed review gate for a human reviewer. Read the final decision recorded by the reviewer. The available tools change as the workflow progresses: Investigation: list_incidents , inspect_incident Incident selected: simulate_guardrail_patch Clean replay completed: draft_review_gate Awaiting human decision: the drafting tool is retired, and get_review_status becomes available Decision recorded: the agent can verify the result but cannot create or change it Tools such as approve , reject , activate , and deploy are deliberately never exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer sees the same synchronized evidence as the agent. They must provide their identity, add a review note, confirm that they examined the evidence, and record their decision using consequence-specific interface controls. The blocked purchase remains unauthorized throughout the process, and the demo never deploys a real external policy. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape a dense incident interface, infer relationships between records, and potentially interact with controls that grant more authority than the task requires. Reviewline replaces that approach with structured capabilities, deterministic evidence IDs, bounded results, explicit labels for untrusted content, a live capability manifest, and an append-only session timeline. How we built it Reviewline is a deterministic, client-only application built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API and falls back progressively to an in-page Tool Inspector when native WebMCP support is unavailable. The architecture separates: Deterministic domain actions and invariants Shared application state used by both the interface and WebMCP tools Strict runtime input validation Bounded outputs and structured errors Phase-aware tool definitions Lifecycle-safe native tool registration and retirement Every tool handler calls the same validated domain action used by the visible interface. JSON Schema helps the agent understand and invoke tools correctly, but the runtime implementation remains the final authority. The application updates the visible interface before a tool promise resolves. This ensures that the human reviewer and the agent always see the same resulting state. Tool calls, registration changes, results, workflow transitions, and the final human decision are all recorded in the session timeline. The registration layer also handles tool retirement carefully. It stops admitting new calls before retiring a tool generation, allows calls that have already started to finish, and prevents failed or timed-out registration attempts from leaving partially registered tools available. We tested the native browser contract using Chrome 152 rather than relying only on a polyfill. The deployed workflow discovers each dynamic capability manifest, executes the tools available at every phase, records the human decision through the interface, and verifies that forbidden authority tools never appear. The static application is deployed on GitHub Pages. A strict build verifier checks the project subpath, inventories active HTML resources, rejects external or inline executable content, and confirms that real, non-symlinked JavaScript and CSS artifacts exist inside the build directory. Challenges we ran into Defining a real authority boundary The hardest part was not deciding which tools to add. It was proving exactly when a tool should no longer be available. For example, drafting must remain unavailable until a clean replay has been completed. Once the workflow reaches human review, that drafting capability must be retired. Making this boundary explicit—and enforcing it throughout the entire lifecycle—was one of the project’s most important design challenges. Validating the complete state graph Validating only the selected incident or current proposal was not enough. Before retained tools could run safely, we needed to verify canonical IDs, references, actors, timestamps, simulation evidence, audit events, and timeline consistency across the full application state. Handling lifecycle races Native registration and browser testing revealed race conditions that happy-path tests did not catch. These included cancellation, timeouts, retained handles, process cleanup, and stale tool references. We added adversarial tests covering registration retirement, process-spawn failures, first and second termination signals, hanging browser shutdowns, stale tool handles, and fixture cleanup. Proving that the replay was meaningful Blocking the malicious trigger was only half the job. A guardrail that blocks everything would technically stop the incident, but it would not be useful. To avoid that outcome, Reviewline evaluates the triggering case alongside a named benign control. Drafting remains unavailable if the proposed guardrail causes any regression in the benign case. Making the GitHub Pages build portable and trustworthy GitHub Pages serves the application from a project-specific subpath. We needed to verify that every active script and stylesheet used the correct base path and resolved to a real build artifact. The verifier also rejects path traversal, malformed paths, external resources, inline executable content, and symlink escapes. Testing native WebMCP A test double can validate application logic, but it cannot prove that the browser integration behaves correctly. Native testing required us to account for Chrome’s serialized tool arguments and results, dynamic registration timing, cancellation behavior, and synchronization between tool execution and the visible interface. Accomplishments we’re proud of Built a complete WebMCP-native collaboration workflow rather than a generic CRUD-style tool surface Made the principle of least authority visible through a dynamic capability manifest Kept approval, rejection, activation, and deployment entirely outside the agent’s tool surface Added deterministic replay against both a malicious trigger and a named benign control Ensured that agent actions update the same visible state used by the human reviewer Added an append-only session timeline and a human-attributed audit record Preserved a complete human workflow in browsers without native WebMCP support Deployed a public, credential-free demo with no backend or production mutation endpoint Verified the project with: 303 unit, component, and integration tests 33 dedicated lifecycle, workflow, and portable-build tests 13 Playwright end-to-end tests TypeScript type checking and zero-warning linting npm audit with zero vulnerabilities actionlint workflow validation Native

title: Tandem
pitch: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve.
about_excerpt: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone is talking about agentic commerce, but almost nobody is comfortable with it. Would you hand an AI your credit card and walk away? Today's agents either scrape websites blind, clicking through UIs they were never meant to understand or they get access with no visibility and no control for the person they're acting for. We built Tandem to prove there's a third option: a storefront designed for both audiences at once the human who owns the money, and the agent who does the work. WebMCP makes this possible because the app can speak to the agent in structured tools instead of hoping it guesses the UI correctly. What it does Tandem is an agent-native grocery store where you and your AI shop together: Give your agent a mission, not clicks: "Dinner for 4, gluten-free, under $60." It searches the catalog, reads product details, and builds a cart using its WebMCP tools. Guardrails are enforced by the app, not the prompt. add_to_cart refuses items that break the budget or dietary rules. The agent can't prompt its way past policy, the store itself is the policy layer. Every agent action is visible. Each tool call renders as a human-readable card in a shared Activity Timeline. Shopping with an agent stops being a black box. You can talk back. Drop a note like "no cilantro" — the agent reads it via get_shopper_notes and re-plans. Async human→agent communication, inside a web app. Nothing is bought until you tap Approve. request_checkout returns a pending_human_approval card. The agent fills the cart; only you can greenlight it. Swaps, not surprises. When the agent wants to replace an item (out of stock, over budget), it calls propose_swap and you accept or reject in one tap. How we built it The storefront is a React (Vite) app with a product catalog, cart, notes panel, activity timeline, and approval flow. We registered 7 WebMCP tools using the standard browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_cart", description: "Add a product to the shopper's cart. Enforces budget and dietary guardrails.", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / validate policy, mutate cart, log to timeline */ }}); Full tool set: search_products, get_product_details, add_to_cart, get_cart, get_shopper_notes, propose_swap, request_checkout. Each execute() returns structured JSON (prices, remaining budget, refusal reasons) so the agent can plan its next move and also updates the UI so the human sees the same story in real time. Guardrails (budget cap, dietary exclusions) live in app code, evaluated inside tool executions, the same rules apply no matter what the agent's prompt says. A built-in Dev Tools panel can invoke any registered tool manually, a fallback demo path and a debugging aid. Deployed on Vercel; tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's entire documentation. We rewrote them repeatedly; vague descriptions produced hesitant agents, precise ones with explicit constraints produced confident, correct plans. One action, two audiences. Every execute() must mutate UI state for the human and return clean structured data for the agent. Getting that dual contract right was the core design problem. Policy vs. persuasion. The agent would "ask" to exceed the budget. We learned to encode refusals as first-class structured responses ({ added: false, reason: "over_budget", remaining: 4.50 }) so the agent recovers gracefully instead of failing. Testing across two WebMCP surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome's flag) surfaced small schema strictness differences we had to normalize. Accomplishments that we're proud of In testing, the agent completed a full mission 11 items, gluten-free, $58.40 of a $60 budget on its first attempt, with zero unauthorized purchases. Not because we asked nicely, but because the app makes it impossible. The human's Activity Timeline is generated from the exact same tool-call events the agent generates one source of truth, two audiences. A pattern we believe generalizes across the web: propose → enforce → approve, applicable to expenses, bookings, emails, and deploys. What we learned Designing tools is designing an API for a new kind of user. Schema and description quality mattered more than anything else we wrote. The best agent UX isn't full automation, it's delegation with visibility. Humans stay sovereign; agents do the labor. Rich structured responses (remaining budget, reasons, alternatives) make agents dramatically more capable than bare success/fail returns. What's next for Tandem Real payments behind the approval gate (Stripe), making the pattern production-safe. A roaming agent that shops across multiple WebMCP-enabled stores in one mission. Shared household carts with per-person budgets. A spec proposal: a standard human-consent / approval tool pattern for WebMCP, so every agent-native app can implement trustworthy checkout the same way. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. ORBIT is the real-time nervous system for radiology, turning idle capacity into faster care by intelligently balancing scanners and clinical expertise across hospitals.

 ORBIT 

 Real-Time Radiology Capacity & Workforce Orchestration Cockpit 

 
 Turning every scanner, every radiologist, and every patient into one living, self-balancing system. 
 

 

 ORBIT is the human-gated orchestration layer for distributed radiology capacity. It connects live scanner telemetry, patient queues, radiologist bandwidth, technologist expertise, and WebMCP AI agents in one shared operational cockpit. 

 The result: the right patient, the right scanner, and the right qualified human can find one another before a backlog becomes a clinical delay. 

 At A Glance 

 
 
 Signal 
 ORBIT response 
 
 
 
 A scanner is overloaded 
 Rebalance eligible routine patients to a nearby partner site 
 
 
 A radiologist is nearing fatigue limits 
 Route studies to a credentialed remote specialist 
 
 
 A suite is understaffed 
 Dispatch remote senior technologist support 
 
 
 An AI agent finds a good move 
 Draft it, simulate it, and wait for human approval 
 
 
 A workflow action occurs 
 Record it in a tamper-evident SHA-256 audit trail 
 
 

 

 The Problem: Capacity Exists, But It Cannot See Itself 

 Picture two hospital campuses on a crisp Tuesday morning, exactly 15 minutes apart down the same highway: 

 
 Hospital A has five $2-million MRI suites and two radiologists on shift. Its queue is four hours deep. A patient with a potential stroke-mimicking presentation is waiting for a scan read that takes 12 minutes, but will not happen for two hours because the on-site radiologists are buried under a backlog of 40 routine knee and lumbar scans. 
 Hospital B , 15 minutes down the road, has three MRI suites. One has been idle since 10:00 AM, and a credentialed radiologist is refreshing their inbox, waiting for studies. 
 

 Nobody made a mistake. Nobody is understaffed on paper . The problem is that capacity and demand are invisible to each other in real time . 

 In modern healthcare, the machine is rarely the actual bottleneck. An MRI can run 24/7 if it has electricity and helium. The real bottleneck is the qualified human : the radiologist licensed in that jurisdiction, certified in the required subspecialty, and below the cognitive-fatigue limit; or the technologist trained to operate a 3.0T scanner. 

 With a projected shortfall of 17,000 to 42,000 radiologists in the U.S. by 2033 and only 2% of UK radiology departments meeting contracted turnaround times, hospital networks are suffocating. 

 The industry is already moving toward distributed imaging capacity: 

 
 Siemens Healthineers offers remote scanning, remote reading, and load balancing and scheduling capabilities through its radiology services portfolio. 
 Philips is advancing unified radiology workflows, remote diagnostic imaging, and remote scanning to extend expertise across locations. 
 GE HealthCare has developed enterprise imaging, intelligent workload management, and remote collaboration capabilities aimed at improving radiology capacity, workflow efficiency, and workforce utilization. 
 

 ORBIT connects these recurring industry needs into one vendor-neutral, real-time capacity network. 

 When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, the fit was immediate. Healthcare AI cannot be a black box that operates in secret or hallucinates web clicks on a DOM. AI agents and human medical directors need to see the exact same live operational screen , share the same tools and constraints, and leave the same audit trail. WebMCP provides that interaction layer. 

 The ORBIT Operating Model 

 ORBIT continuously turns network telemetry into ranked, explainable candidates: 

 Telemetry → Constraint   Filter → Candidate   Ranking → Simulation → Human   Approval → Atomic   Execution 

 The system optimizes both sides of capacity at once: 

 Available   Capacity = Scanner   Capacity × Qualified   Human   Capacity 

 That is the central idea: an empty scanner is not available capacity if no qualified person can safely operate or read the study. 

 

 What ORBIT Does 

 1. A Three-Pane Operational Cockpit 

 Human coordinators and WebMCP-enabled AI agents co-pilot hospital network capacity from the same screen. 

 
 
 Pane 
 What it shows 
 
 
 
 Network Status Rail 
 Live telemetry across 5 regional hospital campuses and 14 multi-modality scanners covering MRI, CT, X-Ray, and Ultrasound. Tracks utilization, queue depth, idle scanner hours, and staff constraints. Utilization states are <75% Emerald , 75-88% Amber , and >88% Rose alert . 
 
 
 Live Multi-Modality Schedule Board 
 A dense chronological feed of active examinations with STAT pulse animations, instant filtering by MRN, patient name, or protocol, and an Appointment Detail Inspector modal. 
 
 
 Human Approval Queue 
 Priority-sorted AI proposals with origin-to-destination candidates, commute distance, queue-reduction deltas, constraint badges, and one-click actions. 
 
 

 2. Multi-Vector Capacity Rebalancing 

 ORBIT evaluates three distinct capacity vectors: 

 Pillar 1 : Scanner Load Balancing 

 Reroutes ambulatory routine patients from overloaded sites to partner facilities within a maximum commute of 25 miles and with magnetic-field parity of at least 1.5T , freeing Level-1 emergency STAT slots. 

 Pillar 2A : Remote Read Dynamic Assignment 

 Monitors radiologist fatigue against a 75% shift cap . When local clinicians breach fatigue limits, ORBIT routes DICOM studies across PACS worklists to credentialed, cross-state licensed remote specialists with open bandwidth. 

 Pillar 2B : Remote Scan Assist Dispatch 

 Identifies understaffed suites and triggers syngo Virtual Cockpit -style tele-proctoring guidance sessions with certified remote senior technologists. 

 Candidate quality is evaluated as a constrained optimization problem: 

 Best   Candidate = argmax c ∈ Eligible   Candidates ( Queue   Relief + Fatigue   Relief − Travel   Cost ) 

 3. Predictive Simulation Before Commitment 

 Before a schedule changes, an operator or AI agent can run an ActExcell-inspired What-If stress test to project: 

 
 queue reduction; 
 wait-time savings; and 
 staff-load improvement. 
 

 This gives operators an impact preview before they commit a real-world move. 

 4. Human Approval Is a Hard Safety Boundary 

 ORBIT enforces a non-negotiable server-side state machine: 

 PENDING → Human / Agent   Approval APPROVED → Atomic   Execution EXECUTED 

 No move can ever execute directly from PENDING . If an agent or user attempts it, the server returns an explicit HTTP 400 rejection: "Move MUST be approved by human coordinator first." Humans stay in total control. 

 5. A Cryptographic Compliance Trail 

 Every bottleneck detection, proposal, simulation, approval, execution, rejection, and constraint tweak is immutably logged with a 64-character SHA-256 digest: 

 SHA 256 ( timestamp ∥ action_type ∥ actor_id ∥ entity_id ) 

 6. Communication Drafting, With Review 

 ORBIT pre-generates non-spammy SMS and portal alerts for patients, including navigation links, plus DICOM and pager alerts for radiologists. Messages are drafted for review before sending. 

 

 How We Built It 

 ORBIT is a high-density, production-grade WebMCP web application built as a shared workspace between an AI agent, human coordinators, and a FastAPI backend. 

 System Flow 

 WebMCP AI Agent → Typed WebMCP Tools → ORBIT React Cockpit → REST API → Constraint & AI Services → Human Approval → Atomic Execution

 Reads live state, proposes rebalancing moves, runs simulations, and requests gated actions

 Shared cockpit 
 Presents network status, the multi-modality schedule, and the human approval queue

title: Handsfree — one line of WebMCP for voice & gesture
pitch: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop.
about_excerpt: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Handsfree gives any website you can edit voice commands and hand-gesture control on top of WebMCP, with one command to your Claude Code and one <script> line in the page. WebMCP (the W3C Web Machine Learning draft, document.modelContext ) lets a page expose what it can do as tools : named functions with a description and a JSON schema. That is the half meant for agents. Handsfree is the other half, for people: a runtime that reads the same tools and drives them from speech and from a camera, with no LLM in the loop. Inspiration Every "agentic web" demo we saw ended with a chat box. But if a page has already declared its capabilities as tools, the input layer is free to be anything: a microphone, a hand, a floating sentence. We wanted to prove that the tool layer is the real product and the modality is a one-line add-on, and that the honest promise is "one command plus one line", not "one line". How we built it The tool layer. A demo shop ( webmcp-shop-demo.vercel.app ) where every capability is a WebMCP tool: ask , search_products , open_landing_page , focus_product , open_product , buy_now , scroll_page , refine_results , show_brands , browse_all , describe_focused , close_panel , help . The floating input box, the voice layer and the gesture layer are three clients of the same tools; a trace panel shows every call. Data comes from a public MCP catalog server ( search_global_catalog ) through a millisecond local index that the live catalog keeps growing. The Claude Code plugin. A skill that audits a codebase's existing frontend, wires the real actions to registerTool (never synthetic clicks when an API exists), marks one tool as the text-sink , one as scroll , gates money-moving tools with confirm , injects the runtime and verifies in the browser. Plus an idempotent injector CLI and a tool-authoring reference that quotes the draft precisely ( registerTool(tool, {signal, exposedTo}) , getTools , executeTool , toolchange ). The runtime ( handsfree.js , ~50 KB, zero dependencies). Discovers tools through the page's registry, by wrapping registerTool , or via a polyfill. Voice uses the Web Speech API and a rule router: built-in intents, tool phrases, tool names as words, then the text-sink. Gestures use MediaPipe HandLandmarker on-device: the index fingertip is a projected cursor, an air-tap clicks, the outer left/right bands scroll (faster towards the edge), an open-hand wave goes back or forward. Everything is drawn on a dot field that bulges under the cursor; a walkthrough tutorial starts the camera only at its last step. What we learned The current draft has no unregisterTool ; you abort the AbortSignal you registered with. execute gets (input, {signal}) and may return any JSON value. Only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint are spec annotations, so our handsfree.* hints stay on the page-side registry and are stripped before forwarding to a native implementation. Rules beat models here. With good tool descriptions and phrases, 100% of our test utterances route correctly with zero model calls and zero latency; what a model would add is ambiguity handling, not the happy path. Gesture UX is about resting positions, not gestures: mapping the lower-left / lower-right of the camera frame to the whole screen so the arm can rest low mattered more than any recognizer tuning. Challenges Popups. A gesture or voice action carries no user activation, so window.open is blocked. The runtime navigates the current tab for synthetic clicks and asks the site for an in-page panel; "back" closes it first. Speech engines rewrite you. "landing page for cozy gifts under fifty dollars" arrives as "Landing page 4 cozy gifts under fifty dollars." We undo the common rewrites before matching and strip price phrases into max_price . Embedded browsers report a 0-height viewport , which put our fixed input box off screen; the page now measures the visual viewport and falls back to normal flow. A 12–70 s upstream search cannot sit on the render path, so every view paints from a local index in milliseconds and the live catalog tops it up in the background. Smooth scrolling never progresses in background tabs , which silently broke per-frame gesture scrolling until we forced instant steps. What's next Native document.modelContext on Chrome's origin trial, a real LLM fallback for the long tail of utterances, and a Shopify-theme recipe so the skill can instrument a store in one run. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Modelo
pitch: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models.
about_excerpt: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models. Like Comment Story Updates Notebook Page Homepage Inspiration Modelo is directly inspired by Decipad, a product I worked on in the past. At the time, LLMs were far less advanced, and few products had useful AI features. The project did not work out, but I always believed it was a great idea that needed agentic collaboration to feel complete. For this challenge, I rebuilt a minimal version of it. What it does Modelo is a local-first notebook. You can write prose with headings, paragraphs, and lists, as in any other rich-text editor. Between paragraphs, you can add model blocks: a number, slider, select, toggle, or formula. Each block declares a named variable. Typing @ in a paragraph inserts the value as an inline chip that reacts to model changes. This lets you build deterministic, interactive models and add a narrative around them. You can also create and save scenarios with predefined values to compare different outcomes. Everything you can do manually is also available through WebMCP tools. An agent can list notebooks, open them, read a model, set an input by name, or rename a variable and update every formula that uses it. Each writing tool reports what changed, what remains broken, and how well the page reads. How we built it Modelo uses React 19 and Vite, with no backend. BlockNote provides the editor and acts as the only source of truth. The document you see is the same document that the tools edit. MathJS evaluates the formula graph based on its dependencies, while Zod validates every argument at the boundary. WebMCP registration uses Chrome’s use-webmcp-tool hook. A single table in src/webmcp/tools.ts defines all 23 tools: their names, scopes, Zod schemas, descriptions, and run functions. The React layer loops through the table and registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool . The interface buttons call the same runTool function that the agent uses. Challenges we ran into Currency algebra was difficult. Registering each currency as a separate MathJS unit makes mixed-currency formulas return an error. In the future, we would like to add FX rates to support currency conversion. More generally, units require careful handling and many design decisions. Agent-written prose was another challenge. By default, agents focus on building the model rather than creating a clear and visually appealing narrative. I added sections to the tool calls to improve this. A section is more than a set of blocks: its paragraphs can mention variables that do not exist yet. The section tool resolves @names against variables declared in the same call, so a sentence can reference a formula that appears later. Accomplishments that we’re proud of I created one portable format for seeds, storage, exports, and agent payloads. The application is highly testable. Most importantly, a person and an agent can edit the same paragraph without either needing to know who made the previous change. What we learned A tool should always report what it changed. Without this feedback, agents make more mistakes than they should. The mutation report became the most useful information an agent receives. I also learned that tool descriptions are prompts. Two sentences explaining when to use write_section instead of insert_blocks changed agent behavior more than any schema did. What’s next for Modelo Next, I want to support sharing notebooks by link, which will require a small backend. I also want to add charts as a block type, so users can see scenario comparisons as well as read them. Other ideas include importing spreadsheet ranges as inputs and building a richer unit system that can convert values instead of only formatting them. title: Threshold
pitch: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them.
about_excerpt: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. Like Comment Story Updates Threshold Threshold is one web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. The person tells their story once, to the assistant they already trust, and no organisation receives anything identifying until the person presses Send. It is eleven at night. A carer has just been told she needs surgery on Thursday morning. Her mother has dementia and cannot be left alone. Arranging cover means three things at once: a respite bed, a wheelchair-accessible journey to it, and someone at the house until the transport arrives. Three organisations. Three phone calls that cannot be made at this hour, and each one depends on the answers to the other two. Her assistant asks Threshold once. Three organisations answer at the same moment. And the obvious combination comes back infeasible on exactly one link: arrival_before_admission required 06:40 offered 07:10 go back to: Northgate Accessible Transport The bed admits until 06:40. The earliest that van arrives is 07:10. Neither organisation can see the other, so neither can know. Threshold does. It names the failing link, names the one organisation to return to, a different van closes the plan, and the carer keeps a printable copy. That failing link is the whole product. The problem is fragmentation, and it is expensive £24.1 billion of income-related support goes unclaimed in Great Britain every year. 7.5 million people miss at least one benefit, an average of £3,203 each. (Policy in Practice, 2025/26.) Complexity and fragmentation are two of the named causes. "No Wrong Door" has been United States federal policy for two decades: whichever door a person knocks on first should get them to the right help, with agencies keeping their own services while sharing one way in. It has never been architecture, because it asks every agency to integrate with a central system, and they never do. WebMCP's exposedTo and allow="tools" make it architecture. The page is the way in. The agencies stay exactly where they are. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Threshold is several organisations, on separate origins, with separate databases, serving one person who never had to repeat themselves, with the person's private context staying inside their own assistant the entire time. The concept exists only because WebMCP exists. A browser-side broker that discovers and calls tools across origins is the one thing that turns three unconnected websites into one coordinated answer, with no shared backend and no data-sharing agreement between them. What people and their agents can do together that was impossible before Ask whether several offers, held at organisations that cannot see each other, satisfy each other. A federated search returns three independent answers, and one vendor with three product lines could serve that just as well. Composition is a different question. check_plan takes offers from three origins and asks whether the transport arrives before the bed stops admitting, whether there is a hoist at both ends of the journey, whether overnight cover lasts until collection. It returns the failing link and the organisation to renegotiate with. There is no non-federated way to build that, because the parts live at parties who will never share a database. Holding a scarce bed at machine speed When assistants act at machine speed against scarce humanitarian resources, two assistants will send two people to the same last bed. Threshold treats a hold as a first-class thing, with a timer and a release. It leases each part of a plan, one organisation at a time, scarcest first, and the organisation itself stays the authority on whether it holds. There is no shared transaction across these independent websites, so if any leg is refused, every lease already taken is released before the call returns. Nothing is ever left booked against a plan that cannot happen. Safety, by construction A malicious listing aimed at a person in crisis is a real risk. Threshold never carries provider-authored text into the assistant's context. Every field an organisation can return is an enum, a boolean, an integer, or a string under a pattern. An instruction to a model does not fit inside ^[A-Z]{1,3}[0-9]{1,4}$ , and it does not fit inside an enum. A test walks every provider contract and proves there is no free-text field for an instruction to hide in. Every capability claim is labelled by its source. A better experience for the person The person does one thing: she reads a plain-language panel and presses Send. The consent gate names the one organisation that will receive the referral, the exact four fields it will receive, and how long they may keep them. A host assistant can already ask for confirmation. What a page can do that a host dialog cannot is show the person the payload and let her change it , correcting the phone number before it leaves. make_referral returns a Promise that resolves on that press. Until then, nothing identifying has crossed an origin, and a boundary log on the page shows exactly what has, field names only. How I implemented WebMCP Each organisation publishes four tools with registerTool and exposedTo , scoped to Threshold's origin alone. Never a wildcard. The hub embeds each provider in an iframe that delegates the tools permission with allow="tools" , discovers their tools with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and calls them with executeTool , passing arguments as a JSON string and treating a null return (a navigation) as a contract violation rather than an empty success. The hub exposes nine tools to the person's assistant, and the tool surface is a state machine. place_plan_holds does not exist until check_plan returns feasible, and make_referral does not exist until a lease does. An assistant cannot call a step out of order, because the step is not in its list. ontoolchange is how the hub learns a provider has withdrawn. Every provider result passes a typed firewall: parse, validate against a strict JSON Schema, project to the hub's own shape. A rejected payload never reaches a return value, a log line, or an error message. 176 unit and integration tests, 15 browser tests, real WebMCP federation verified in Chrome, and again as four containers on four origins. If a browser cannot do cross-origin WebMCP, the same providers on the same origins are reached over a typed postMessage protocol with the same schemas, the same firewall, the same leases and the same gate, and the page states in words which path it used. Threshold. Several organisations. One plan. One page. title: Glassmap
pitch: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass.
about_excerpt: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Inspiration I come from a GIS background, and I have worked on many web map applications for different clients. One problem I keep running into is that AI agents are still not very good at dealing with maps. When I use AI to help with application development, debugging, or QA, everything usually works fine until the agent reaches the map. A web map is often rendered as a WebGL canvas, so the agent cannot easily understand what is actually on the map, which features are being displayed, or what happened after an interaction. Sometimes it simply cannot continue. Other times, it tries to rely on screenshots and visual interactions, but the result is often inaccurate or unreliable. This has always felt like a major limitation to me, especially because maps are not just visual content. Behind the screen, they contain structured geographic data, layers, coordinates, features, spatial relationships, and actions. When I learned about WebMCP, I immediately saw a way to solve this problem. Instead of forcing an agent to understand a map through pixels, the map can directly expose its data and capabilities as tools. That idea became the starting point for GlassMap . My goal was to make a web map that is no longer a black box to AI agents. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project was WebMCP itself. I spent a lot of time thinking beyond the basic question of “how do I expose a function as a WebMCP tool?” The more interesting question for me was: What kinds of experiences become possible when an AI agent can directly interact with a website through structured tools? While building GlassMap, I kept looking for use cases where WebMCP could do more than simply make an existing feature easier to automate. For example, instead of an agent looking at a screenshot and guessing which places are inside an area, it can directly ask the map for features within an exact spatial boundary. Instead of trying to reproduce a sequence of mouse clicks, it can work directly with map objects, coordinates, routes, and geographic queries. That changed how I thought about the project. WebMCP is not only a better way for an agent to operate an existing interface. In some cases, it can enable an entirely different user experience where the human, the application, and the AI agent all work with the same underlying state. That gave me many new ideas for projects I would like to explore in the future. How I built it GlassMap is a web map built with Next.js, MapLibre, OpenStreetMap data, Turf.js, and Zustand . MapLibre handles the map visualization, while Turf.js performs spatial operations directly in the browser. The application exposes map capabilities through 15 WebMCP tools , including operations for searching places, querying nearby features, working with map objects, changing the map view, adding notes, and planning routes. I designed the WebMCP layer separately from the map UI through a common store interface. This makes the tools easier to test and allows both the human interface and the AI agent to operate on the same map state. I also added a development shim so that the WebMCP tools can be tested in browsers that do not yet support the API natively. One thing this project also reminded me of is that, with today's AI coding tools, actually implementing an application is becoming much easier. The harder questions are increasingly: How should the system be designed? and What should the user experience actually be? Those were much more difficult for me than writing the code itself. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was actually deciding how to use WebMCP well . This is a WebMCP hackathon, so it would have been easy to build a normal web application first and then add a few WebMCP tools on top of it just to satisfy the requirement. I did not want to do that. I wanted GlassMap to be a project where WebMCP is fundamental to the experience — where removing WebMCP would remove one of the main reasons the product exists. Because of that, I spent a lot of time thinking about the user experience instead of simply adding more tools. I asked questions like: What should an agent be able to understand about the map? What operations are actually useful as tools? What should happen when both a human and an agent are working on the same map? When should the agent return structured information instead of trying to manipulate the interface? And most importantly, what can WebMCP enable that would be difficult or unreliable with a traditional screenshot-based agent? That design process was probably the hardest part of the project. Building the features was relatively straightforward. Deciding which features should exist, how they should work together, and how WebMCP could genuinely improve the experience took much more thought. For me, that is also the most interesting part of building AI-native applications today. The bottleneck is becoming less about whether we can build something, and more about whether we can design the right system and the right experience around it. title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement
pitch: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it.
about_excerpt: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it. Like Comment Story Updates No existing option works for everyone. Agreement reached with zero raw private context received from the live participant. Agents construct an option that did not exist. Inspiration Group decisions routinely force people to reveal more than they should. A person may have a strict budget, an accessibility need, a caregiving deadline, or another private reason an option will not work. Polls make the group choose among fixed answers. Meetings make people explain themselves. We wanted a third path: let each person’s private agent understand the full context while the shared room learns only what it needs to build agreement. What it does UNSAID is a shared decision canvas. Participants privately brief their own browser agents. The room receives structured ballots rather than raw explanations. When no existing option works for everyone, participants or their agents can publish minimum structured signals and create a bridge proposal by changing known attributes. Candidates move toward a visible common-ground ring as aggregate support improves. A candidate can be nominated only when every participant accepts it, and the live person must ratify the final agreement through the human interface. The judge demo uses one live ChatGPT participant and three clearly labeled deterministic demo agents so the complete multi-party experience can be tested immediately. Why WebMCP UNSAID is not improved by adding generic chat. Its core depends on the webpage exposing a precise coordination protocol. Through WebMCP, a personal agent can read shared room state, submit a private ballot, publish a structured signal, create a bridge candidate, and nominate a viable option. Tool schemas prevent raw private narratives from being sent accidentally. The tools reuse the same state transitions and permissions as the human interface, and their availability changes with the room phase. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape cards, guess form controls, and infer whether a shared state mutation succeeded. With WebMCP, agent actions are typed, reliable, attributable, and visibly reflected in the common canvas. What people and agents can do together now A person can give their own agent the complete private context. The agent can translate that context into the minimum structured contribution, reason across aggregate group signals, and construct a new option that did not previously exist. The group can reach a better agreement without collecting everyone’s raw private explanation. Agents do the translation and option construction; people retain final authority. How it was built UNSAID is a full-stack TypeScript application hosted on ChatGPT Sites with durable room state in D1. The top-level page registers imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read-only and state-changing tools have narrow JSON schemas and compact verifiable results. The room uses server-authoritative versioning, aggregate ballots, a deterministic consensus function, and a fixture evaluator for the three fictional demo agents. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Limitations UNSAID is a prototype for minimum disclosure, not an anonymity or encryption system. Source-hidden signals may be inferable in a small group. The deterministic demo agents are fictional fixtures, clearly labeled in the product and source. The current submission demonstrates an offsite decision rather than a general production platform. video_title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement | WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Group decisions come with a hidden cost. To coordinate, people share budgets, accessibility needs, family obligations, and other private details. Or they stay quiet and settle for a bad outcome. Unsaid offers a third path. Everyone tells their own agent the whole truth. The shared page gets only the structured judgments needed to find common ground. Agents negotiate. People make the final call. Four people are choosing an offsite. Three labeled demo agents already evaluated the options deterministically. I am the live participant. The room has none of my private context. I tell ChatGPT my constraints in private. Through WebMCP, the page gives it two type tools, get room state and submit ballot. ChatGPT evaluates the choices, then shares only preferred, acceptable, or unacceptable. No reason. No private story. None of the original options works for everyone. Now the page changes the tools available to the agent. Bridge tools appear, and the room shares only the minimum attribute signals needed to move forward. ChatGPT combines those public signals with my private context and creates a new option. Lakeside Lab on Thursday, ending by 4:00 for $235. The proposal changes what matters without revealing why it matters. The demo agents evaluate the new proposal. This time, all four participants accept it. The candidate moves into common ground, and Web MCP exposes a new action, nominate it for ratification. The agent can open ratification. It cannot make my final decision. I review the shared outcome and approve it myself. The receipt shows the disclosure boundary, structured ballots, public signals, one bridge proposal, and final approval. My private explanation never entered the room. Each agent action used a phase-specific Web MCP tool tied to the same operations as the human interface. The old web helps one person transact. Unsaid helps many people agree.
