title: Forge
pitch: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project.
about_excerpt: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Forge An agent-native web IDE for humans and AI agents Inspiration AI coding agents can generate impressive amounts of code, but generating code is only one part of software development. A real development workflow also involves creating projects, managing files, installing dependencies, running applications, reading console output, debugging errors, rebuilding, and eventually deploying the result. Most AI coding experiences handle these tasks through a chat interface, while the actual development environment remains separate. Forge asks a different question: what if the development environment itself could be used by an AI agent? Forge is a browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Instead of asking an agent to generate code and then manually moving that code into an IDE, Forge exposes its development capabilities directly through WebMCP. The agent can operate the IDE itself. Why WebMCP? Forge is a particularly strong fit for WebMCP because its core functionality is already organized around meaningful actions that an agent needs to perform. An IDE is not just a page to read. It is an environment to operate. Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with a browser-based IDE would need to rely on indirect mechanisms such as simulated clicks, keyboard input, or copying and pasting code. With WebMCP, Forge can expose its capabilities as structured, semantic tools. The agent can discover what Forge can do and directly invoke those capabilities. This transforms the IDE from a human-only interface into an agent-accessible development environment . What agents can do in Forge Forge exposes meaningful development operations through WebMCP, including: Create and manage projects List project files Read files Write and modify files Run projects Inspect console output Build projects Deploy projects These tools are connected directly to Forge's underlying application logic. The WebMCP layer is therefore not a separate demonstration layer. The agent and the human interface operate on the same project and the same underlying state. For example, an agent can be asked to: "Create a React landing page for a fictional company." It can then: Create the project. Create and modify the required files. Run the development server. Inspect the result. Check the console for errors. Modify the code when necessary. Build the project. Deploy it. The agent is not merely generating a code snippet. It is operating the development environment. Human + Agent collaboration Forge is designed around collaboration rather than replacement. The human developer remains inside the IDE and can see the project, preview the application, inspect the code, and make manual changes at any time. The agent can perform repetitive or complex development operations through WebMCP while the human remains in control. A developer can ask an agent to create a project, modify multiple files, run it, inspect an error, fix the problem, and build the result. The developer can then review the changes, edit the code themselves, and ask the agent to continue. Both human and agent can work on the same project without leaving the development environment. This is the experience that WebMCP makes possible. What was difficult before? Without WebMCP, an AI assistant could generate the code for a project, but the developer would still need to transfer that code into the development environment and manually perform many of the surrounding operations. The workflow becomes: Ask AI → Copy code → Open IDE → Create files → Install dependencies → Run → Find errors → Go back to AI → Copy fixes → Repeat Forge changes this interaction into: Ask agent → Agent operates Forge → Review → Iterate The important difference is not simply that AI can write code. It is that the agent can use the tools of the development environment itself. Built for the browser Forge runs directly in the browser using WebContainers, providing a real development environment without requiring a local installation. The editor is powered by Monaco Editor, giving developers a familiar coding experience while keeping the entire workflow inside the browser. Forge is built with: React TypeScript Vite Monaco Editor WebContainers WebMCP Tailwind CSS WebMCP implementation Forge registers its capabilities using the WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a clear name, description, structured input schema, and execution function. The tools call Forge's actual application logic rather than simulating interaction with the UI. This architecture allows both the human interface and AI agents to work with the same underlying functionality. The result is a genuine WebMCP integration rather than a chatbot placed on top of an existing application. Execution and agent-native design Forge was designed around the idea that WebMCP tools should represent meaningful operations , not low-level interface actions. Instead of exposing tools such as "click button" or "type text", Forge exposes higher-level development operations such as create_project , read_file , write_file , run_project , get_console , build_project , and deploy_project . This makes the interface understandable to an agent while keeping the application usable for humans. The result is an IDE that has two interfaces: A visual interface for humans. A structured tool interface for agents. Both operate on the same environment. Potential impact Forge explores a future where web applications are not only designed for people, but are also designed to be used by AI agents. For developers, this could reduce the friction between AI-generated code and a working application. For AI agents, it provides a structured environment where they can move beyond generating text and actually perform meaningful software development tasks. The same principle could extend beyond IDEs to other professional web applications: design tools, data platforms, project management systems, scientific software, and more. Forge is therefore an experiment in a broader idea: What happens when the tools we use every day become directly accessible to AI agents? Creativity & ambition Forge is not simply an online code editor with AI assistance. It explores the idea of an agent-native IDE : an environment where AI agents are first-class users of the application rather than external assistants sitting beside it. WebMCP provides the bridge between the agent and the application. The goal is not to make AI better at pretending to be a developer. The goal is to give AI agents the tools they need to actually participate in the development process. Open source Forge is open source and designed to be transparent and inspectable. The project demonstrates how a complex browser application can expose useful capabilities to AI agents through an open web standard. Built for the WebMCP Challenge Forge was created for the WebMCP Challenge to explore the future of the open web, where humans and AI agents can interact, collaborate, and create together. The central idea is simple: The future of agentic software may not be an AI sitting beside an application — it may be an AI working inside it. Forge — The IDE that agents can use. title: Ohmni
pitch: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair.
about_excerpt: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair. Like Comment Story Updates the landing page Inspiration I’m learning robotics, and one of the most frustrating parts has been getting an AI to understand what is actually happening on the board in front of me. I was constantly taking screenshots, copying serial logs, and pasting telemetry into ChatGPT just to explain the physical world. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a different idea what if the browser itself could become the bridge between the agent and the hardware? Ohmni came from that. Using WebMCP and Web Serial, the agent can inspect the board through real tools in real time and you see the result of your action in front of you instead of relying on screenshots and copied logs. What it does Ohmni is a browser based hardware debugging workbench where AI agents and humans diagnose physical device problems together. Using WebMCP, Ohmni exposes hardware capabilities as structured tools an agent can call directly. The agent can inspect reset history, measure supply voltage, read telemetry, run controlled diagnostic tests, collect evidence, and build a diagnosis from real measurements instead of guessing from screenshots or pasted logs. For safety, read only tools can run autonomously, while actions that can affect hardware require explicit human approval. When a physical change is needed, such as moving a jumper or reseating a connection, the agent hands that step back to the human and then retests the device to verify whether the fix actually worked. Ohmni also supports real hardware through Web Serial apis , alongside a deterministic virtual ESP32 environment that lets anyone experience the full diagnostic workflow without needing a physical board. How we built it We built Ohmni with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Bun, using WebMCP as the core interface between the AI agent and the hardware workbench. Device capabilities are exposed through document.modelContext as structured tools. Read-only tools can run directly, while actions that may affect hardware pass through a human approval gate before execution. A device adapter handles both the deterministic virtual ESP32 environment and real hardware over Web Serial. Telemetry is streamed into the browser in real time, and each diagnostic action produces evidence that the agent can use to form, test, and verify hypotheses. We also added dynamic tool registration, capability filtering, safe disconnect handling, and an evidence trail so the system stays useful, inspectable, and safe throughout the debugging process. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making agent access to hardware useful without making it unsafe. Some tools only read data, while others can actually change device state, so I had to design a clear safety boundary and pause physical actions for human approval. Another challenge was making the diagnosis trustworthy. The agent should not simply guess the fault, so Ohmni hides the underlying problem, exposes only measurements and test results, and requires the diagnosis to be built from evidence. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built a full debugging loop instead of just a WebMCP demo, An agent can inspect the device, run controlled tests, collect evidence, form a diagnosis, ask the human to make a physical change, and then rerun the test to verify the fix. And the diagnosis is not just a chat response. Ohmni keeps an evidence trail so every conclusion can be traced back to actual measurements and test results. What i learned i learned that giving an AI access to hardware is not just about exposing more tools. The real challenge is deciding what the agent can do autonomously, what requires human approval, and how every conclusion can be grounded in evidence. WebMCP made that separation much clearer. It let us treat the browser as a trusted bridge between the agent and local hardware, while keeping the human in control of physical actions. I also learned that the strongest agent workflows are collaborative: the agent measures and reasons, the browser enforces safety, and the human handles the physical world. What's next for Ohmni I want to grow Ohmni into a broader hardware debugging tool that works across more boards and devices. The next step is expanding the Web Serial layer so more microcontrollers can connect over USB, expose their own diagnostic capabilities, and use the same WebMCP workflow for measurement, testing, human intervention, and verification. title: Curbcut
pitch: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together.
about_excerpt: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Scanned Workspace Mechanical Repair Preview Verified Mechanical Repair Blocked Agent Action Contextual Proposal Responsive Workspace Inspiration Accessibility scanners are good at finding problems, but finding them is only the beginning. A developer still has to find the correct source code, understand the evidence, choose the correct repair, preview its effect, and check the result. We built Curbcut around the question: What if the developer and an external browser agent could work together on the same live accessibility workspace? The agent could handle repetitive technical work, while the developer maintained authority over changes that require meaning, context, or design judgment. What it does Curbcut is a browser-native accessibility repair workbench for static HTML and CSS. The workspace keeps everything together: Editable source A securely isolated live preview Real axe-core accessibility findings Exact source mapping and rendered-element highlighting Proposed code diffs A rendered preview of each proposed repair Human approval for semantic changes Fresh verification scans Exact Undo and clean source export A shared timeline of human and agent actions axe-core scans the actual rendered preview, and the results aren't hard-coded. Selecting an issue focuses its exact source range and highlights the corresponding element in the preview. Every repair begins as a non-mutating proposal. Curbcut shows the exact source diff and proposed visual result before changing the working source. Technical repairs, such as removing a positive tabindex, can be applied and verified in the code directly. Contextual repairs, including form labels, image alternatives, button names, and document text, remain blocked until the developer reviews and approves the exact proposal. If the browser agent attempts to apply a contextual proposal early, Curbcut returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED, visibly records the blocked action, and leaves the source unchanged. Curbcut exposes ten focused WebMCP tools covering the real workflow: workspace inspection, scanning, listing and inspecting issues, previewing, applying, rejecting, undoing, summarizing, and exporting. These tools operate on the same React store and preview used by the visible interface. There is no arbitrary JavaScript tool, arbitrary DOM mutation, or whole-document AI rewrite. How we built it Curbcut is a browser-only React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed as a static site on Vercel. It requires no account, backend, or database, and the developer’s source stays local to the browser. We use parse5 8.0.1 to parse canonical HTML with source locations and assign revision-bound internal node IDs. Mapping metadata is added only to generated preview markup, so it never contaminates the working or exported source. Repairs use validated raw-offset patches that preserve unrelated source text. Imported HTML is treated as untrusted. DOMPurify sanitizes it before it enters an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and no same-origin permission. A nonce-based Content Security Policy blocks network requests, navigation, forms, embeds, and untrusted scripts. axe-core 4.13.0 runs inside that opaque preview realm. A validated postMessage bridge connects scanning and highlighting to the React workspace while checking the channel, request ID, message shape, and source revision. The top-level page registers exactly ten WebMCP tools through document.modelContext. Inputs are runtime-validated, imported source and accessibility snippets are marked as untrusted content, stale revisions are rejected, and read-only tools use the appropriate annotations. Most importantly, the agent cannot manufacture human approval. Contextual approval tokens are created only when the developer approves the exact visible proposal through the interface. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was executing axe inside an opaque sandbox while safely returning useful results to the parent application. We needed enough communication for rendering, scanning, and highlighting without granting the preview same-origin access. The second was reliable source mapping. Existing HTML IDs were not sufficient because imported documents can have missing or duplicate IDs. We instead built parser-backed mappings using exact source ranges and preview-only internal metadata. The third was keeping proposals bound to the correct source revision. Rendering, scanning, agent calls, and human actions are asynchronous, so Curbcut rejects stale issue and proposal IDs and requires the exact proposed preview to report ready before Apply becomes valid. Finally, we had to make the human-agent boundary technically enforceable. A prompt asking the agent to wait was not enough. The application itself had to reject unauthorized contextual changes and preserve the proposal and source unchanged. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real end-to-end WebMCP workflow where external browser-agent actions visibly update the same workspace the developer is reviewing Real axe scans against an isolated live preview rather than stored or fixture-specific results Exact mapping from rendered axe nodes to editable source without relying on user-provided IDs Small deterministic patches instead of whole-document model rewrites A visible, enforceable human-approval boundary for semantic changes Fresh rescan verification, exact Undo, and clean export Five bounded repair families, with color contrast intentionally kept as evidence rather than guessed automatically An unrelated imported profile-form test proving that the scanner and mapping system are not hard-coded to the checkout demo 88 passing unit and integration tests and 30 passing browser tests A 72-trajectory WebMCP evaluation with 69 operationally correct workflows, zero approval-boundary violations, and zero infrastructure failures A production deployment exercised through browser-agent tooling with all ten tools discoverable and no WebMCP console errors Curbcut does not claim automated WCAG compliance. A cleared automated finding proves only that the targeted automated check disappeared after a fresh scan. Manual review, assistive-technology testing, and disabled-user expertise remain essential. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful product actions rather than generic browser control. The browser agent does not replace the application; it gains a structured way to participate in the application’s existing workflow. We also learned that accessibility repair is as much an authority problem as a code-generation problem. Some changes are mechanical. Others require someone to decide what an image, label, or control means. A useful agent should understand and respect that distinction. Finally, source mapping and safe execution boundaries were more challenging than generating the patches themselves. Making every action visible, reversible, revision-bound, and verifiable is what turned the idea into a coherent product. What's next for Curbcut Next, we would test Curbcut with more accessibility practitioners and frontend developers, improve the editing and diff experience, and carefully add more deterministic repair families where automation is defensible. Longer term, the same shared-workspace model could support reviewed accessibility contributions across larger projects. The principle would remain the same: let the agent handle mechanics while the human retains authority over meaning. title: The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had
pitch: Build your dream Board of Directors. Consult living legends on consequential decisions, get feedback, & pressure test your thinking, just like a real-world boardroom. Bring your own agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Build your dream Board of Directors. Consult living legends on consequential decisions, get feedback, & pressure test your thinking, just like a real-world boardroom. Bring your own agents via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had Codex joining & participating in the board meeting Bring-your-own-agent Post-meeting exec summary Inspiration The most consequential decisions are rarely intelligence problems alone; they are perspective problems. Founders and executives rely on boards because no single adviser sees the whole situation. Yet most people cannot convene the particular founders, investors, and operators whose judgment they admire—and even well-connected decision-makers rarely have all of them in the same room. We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Council , which demonstrated the value of collecting independent answers from multiple models before reviewing and synthesising them, and by Zapier CEO Wade Foster’s "War Council" , which uses opinionated advisers to stress-test decisions. We were also inspired by people building personal AI boards of directors for their own work and lives. Our project takes a different step. The members of this board are not merely different base LLMs answering the same prompt. Each seat is occupied by a genuinely separate AI agent with its own source-grounded personality, worldview, expertise, decision heuristics, conversational style, strengths, blindspots, and context. That makes the experience closer to a real board meeting with a group of distinct human experts—and much more useful than general-purpose chatbots politely converging on the same answer. WebMCP supplied the missing interoperability layer. The boardroom does not need to become the user’s only assistant or ingest everything their existing agent knows. Instead, the user’s personal agent can enter the live room, take a seat, contribute relevant context, and participate through the application’s structured meeting actions. What it does The Best Board Meeting You’ve Ever Had lets a user assemble a personal Board of Directors (BoD) and convene it around a high-stakes decision. The MVP is designed with startup founders in mind, but the same interaction works for major career and life questions: Should we change our pricing strategy? Should I accept this job? Should I move to another city? During onboarding, the user chooses up to six board members from a starter library of well-known founders, investors, and domain experts. Each persona is grounded first in that "reference human's" public writing, talks, podcast interviews, and work. Think Deep Research to distill their beliefs, tastes, and wisdom. The user describes the decision by providing a brief (they have talk if they don't want to type) and can include links or any other relevant context. We kick off a boardroom simulation, with every AI board member taking their seat at the table. Before the group discussion begins, each board member privately forms an independent position so that the first speaker does not anchor the entire room. The meeting then unfolds as a free-flowing group conversation rather than a rigid sequence of generated reports. Board members can: "grill" the user and one another; directly address specific people; react, interrupt, disagree, and persuade; revise their position when another member makes a better argument; contribute more or less depending on the relevance of their expertise and the strength of their opinion. The user can call on a member at any time with an @mention. Every board member contributes, but nobody is forced to dominate the conversation simply to fill airtime. When the chair ends the meeting, the app generates an exec briefing-style readout containing the board’s recommendation, the options and tradeoffs it considered, important assumptions, open questions, concrete next actions, and a closing comment from every member. When the board remains divided, the memo notes where they disagreed instead of making up false consensus. WebMCP makes the room open to the user’s own agent. A personal assistant / chief-of-staff agent can join as a board observer or full participant, supply context about the user, make statements, question a board member, request a synthesis, and retrieve the final readout. The boardroom remains the shared "control plane" (excuse my use of an AI word!!) that the human and every agent can see together. How we built it We built the product as a Next.js and TypeScript web application. The frontend presents a skeuomorphic board table, a shared conversation, visible speaker and reaction states, and a lightweight meeting arc without turning the experience into a form-driven workflow. Every board member runs as an independent agent using Vercel’s eve framework and an OpenAI GPT model. Each agent receives its own instructions, persona context, source material, and view of the meeting. A shared orchestration layer manages the private opening positions, the public conversation state, @mentions, reactions, requests for the floor, direct replies, and the decision to invite another member into the discussion. The goal is controlled spontaneity: enough orchestration to keep the room coherent, but enough freedom for it to feel like an actual conversation. We also created a local /init-board-member skill for our coding workflow. Given the name of someone you want to recruit to your board, an agent Deep Researches the person and distills them into an Eve agent package. The output captures the person's worldview, core values, expertise, voice/style, and personality. It also generates evaluation prompts so we can test whether the persona remains recognizable, useful, and meaningfully different from the other board members. At the end of a meeting, a separate synthesis step turns the complete transcript into the exec readout that shows you what decisions were made and why. For WebMCP, the application exposes a small set of structured capabilities over the live meeting, including inspecting the agenda and current state, joining as an observer or participant, contributing context or a statement, addressing a board member, requesting a synthesis, and retrieving the final readout. This lets an outside agent participate through the product’s real meeting logic instead of attempting to operate the UI through brittle browser use. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was keeping the personas genuinely distinct. Because every member uses the same model family, weak persona prompts quickly collapse into the same polished, agreeable "helpful assistant" voice. We had to ground each agent in primary sources, encode not only what the person believes but how they reason and disagree, and test personas against one another rather than evaluating them in isolation. Natural turn-taking was another orchestration problem. Six autonomous agents can easily produce repetitive agreement, simultaneous monologues, or a meeting that feels mechanically round-robin. We had to balance independent thinking, selective participation, interruptions, direct replies, user @mentions, and the requirement that everyone contribute—while keeping latency low enough that the room still feels alive. Finally, WebMCP participation required a clear boundary between the outside agent and the application. The personal agent needed enough structured access to become a real participant, while the boardroom still had to own membership, meeting state, speaker identity, and the final record. What we learned We learned that convincing multi-agent collaboration is equal parts an orchestration and a prompting problem. Separate context and independent opening positions help prevent persona bleed and anchoring. Productive disagreement is often the most valuable output. Finally, concise turns and selective participation improve both realism and latency. Bringing natural, human-like agents to life is an art and a science. What's next for The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had The MVP treats each meeting as a one-time session. Next, we want to add durable agent memory so a user’s board becomes a long-term relationship: members remember the user’s goals, prior discussions, recurring tensions, and past advice. We also plan to add voice conversations, user-created board members, persistent decision journals, follow-up meetings, and outcome reviews that compare what the board thought would happen vs. what actually happened. Over time, the product can become less like a novel demo and more a cornerstone to how everyone will work eventually: a board of directors that knows them, challenges them, and gets better at helping them navigate their work and life. Minimum information. Maximum relevance Imagine what the same storefront can become for each of these people These names make the demonstration easier to follow; they are not stored customer profiles. Each person states their current situation in the conversation, and PRSIM selects the closest merchant-authored scenario. Ana, 27 - junior interior architect. Marketing angle: visual projection for a Barcelona weekend, real locations and color confidence. Bundle or promotion: none. Maya - digital nomad. Marketing angle: laptop access, work/travel separation and protection in a tropical climate. Bundle or promotion: none. Nicolas - travel photographer. Marketing angle: camera organization, weather protection and measured material evidence. Bundle or promotion: optional rain-protection bundle. Graham, 54 - frequent business traveller. Marketing angle: British Airways compatibility, 16-inch laptop access and restrained premium efficiency. Bundle or promotion: none. Chloé - choosing a gift for an urban cyclist. Marketing angle: stability, light-rain protection and simple exchanges. Bundle or promotion: none. Paul, 31 - software engineer and analytical buyer. Marketing angle: measurable specifications, transparent comparisons and test protocols. Bundle or promotion: none. Hugo, 22 - first-time traveller to Japan. Marketing angle: emotional and visual projection through an editorial travel journal. Bundle or promotion: none. Nora - office-to-sport commuter. Marketing angle: one organized bag for a laptop, clothes, towel and shoes. Bundle or promotion: organization bundle only if requested. Camille - long-distance cycle commuter. Marketing angle: stable carry, laptop separation and honest light-rain protection. Bundle or promotion: none. Emma - campus student. Marketing angle: price, weight, laptop protection and measured durability for classes and weekend travel. Bundle or promotion: none. Julien - parent planning a family weekend. Marketing angle: shared organization, common documents and quick access. Bundle or promotion: none by default. Samir - young adult taking a night coach. Marketing angle: under-seat storage and access to essentials during the journey. Bundle or promotion: none. Ax - end-of-month budget comparer. Marketing angle: a clear price ladder with one cheaper choice and two more complete alternatives. Bundle or promotion: optional organization bundle. Thomas - consultant travelling by Eurostar. Marketing angle: material quality, business organization and continuity from train to meeting. Bundle or promotion: none. Ryan, 18 - budget Ryanair traveller. Marketing angle: verified under-seat compatibility and avoided baggage fees. Bundle or promotion: none. Lucia - backpacker travelling through South America. Marketing angle: capacity, resistance, secure access and coach/hostel use. Bundle or promotion: none. Marc, 63 - leisure rail traveller. Marketing angle: low weight, comfortable handling and simple access during train changes. Bundle or promotion: none. Amina - parent travelling with two children. Marketing angle: hands-free travel, one-handed access and under-seat organization. Bundle or promotion: contextual 15% code for a later second bag. Daniel, 68 - cautious long-haul traveller. Marketing angle: returns, warranty, payment, compatibility and comparable customer evidence. Bundle or promotion: none. Kevin - traveller leaving tomorrow. Marketing angle: confirmed stock, pickup and express delivery without artificial urgency. Bundle or promotion: none. Sophie - grandmother choosing a birthday gift. Marketing angle: personalization, delivery timing, hidden pricing and easy exchanges. Bundle or promotion: optional gift bundle when she asks how to make the present more complete. The scenario establishes the first hierarchy, but it does not freeze the page. Follow-up WebMCP tools can add, remove, replace or prioritize a focused block when a new question appears, while preserving the current product, color and purchase context. The project Most ecommerce pages are designed around the complete product story rather than the buyer's current decision. They accumulate features, lifestyle imagery, reviews, guarantees, promotions and repeated calls to action, then leave every shopper to filter the page alone. PRSIM explores a different relationship between shoppers, AI companions and merchants. The shopper expresses an ordinary need: a destination, a deadline, a budget, a concern, a preferred style or the person receiving a gift. Their companion passes only the context that is useful for this purchase to one high-level WebMCP tool. PRSIM then finds the closest merchant-authored scenario and updates the same storefront with the relevant product, layouts, copy, imagery, evidence and call to action. The model never invents the interface. The merchant defines the brand, reusable layouts, blocks, product facts, assets, reviews, assemblies and permissible variants. WebMCP lets the companion operate that bounded system locally in the browser. Once the first experience is ready, the broad preparation tool is removed and smaller tools become available. The shopper can ask whether the bag fits a specific airline, change color, compare formats, request customer evidence, add a bundle, inspect delivery, navigate to a relevant section, reset the experience or proceed to a local checkout. Each follow-up changes only the necessary part of the current page. The prototype uses a fictional cabin-bag brand to show how one product system can support many buying scenarios. This example already includes 21 authored scenario seeds and dozens of contextual variations across four bag formats, four colorways and 198 registered visual assets. They cover low-cost air travel, business rail, gifts, cycling, photography, family travel, study, long-distance coaches, digital nomad work and more. At a glance PRSIM lets a shopper and their own AI companion adapt the storefront already open in the browser. The shopper can mention a destination, budget, deadline, concern, style preference or gift context. PRSIM updates that same page using only merchant-approved product facts, layouts, imagery, customer evidence and purchase controls. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an assistant can describe what the shopper should inspect, return a generic product list or provide a link. With WebMCP, the companion invokes structured capabilities owned by the current website, and the website applies the result directly to its visible storefront. The model does not generate the interface or invent product truth. WebMCP leverage PRSIM begins with one intent-level entry tool, prepare_shopping_experience . Once the closest merchant-authored experience is prepared, that broad entry point is removed and focused tools become available for page refinement, product evidence, variants, bundles, delivery, cart and checkout. Alongside this adaptive layer, PRSIM exposes familiar commerce operations comparable to a Shopify MCP storefront and a local UCP-like checkout lifecycle. WebMCP therefore connects the complete journey from expressed intent to page adaptation, product evaluation and payment review. 60-second test Open https://prsim.yafa.sh/#preview in ChatGPT's in-app browser. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Groundline
pitch: A shared reasoning workspace where humans map claims and evidence while AI agents use WebMCP to evaluate, triage, trace dependencies, and propose revisions - humans keep final control.
about_excerpt: A shared reasoning workspace where humans map claims and evidence while AI agents use WebMCP to evaluate, triage, trace dependencies, and propose revisions - humans keep final control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Groundline visualizes how conclusions rest on claims, evidence, assumptions, and sources. Start from a decision in plain language, then turn it into an inspectable reasoning workspace. Explore the reasoning graph, inspect individual objects, and trace what each conclusion depends on. A WebMCP-aware agent reviews the same live workspace, identifies weaknesses, and proposes safer revisions. Groundline See what your conclusions stand on. Inspiration People rarely make important decisions from perfectly structured arguments. A conclusion usually begins as a paragraph, a conversation, a recommendation, or a confident sentence such as: “We should do this.” But underneath that sentence may be assumptions that were never examined, evidence that only supports part of the claim, missing sources, unresolved counterarguments, or reasoning that works for one narrow case but is being generalized far beyond it. The problem is not always that the conclusion is wrong. The problem is that the reasoning underneath it is difficult to inspect. Generative AI makes this problem more interesting. An AI agent can critique reasoning, identify assumptions, trace dependencies, and propose better alternatives, but giving an agent unrestricted authority over the reasoning creates another problem: Who decides what becomes accepted knowledge? Groundline started from two questions: What does this conclusion actually stand on? and: Can an AI agent help inspect and repair reasoning without silently taking control of the decision? The goal was not to build another chatbot that produces polished advice. The goal was to build a shared human-agent reasoning workspace where arguments become inspectable, weaknesses become reviewable, proposed repairs remain proposals, and the human retains final authority. What it does Groundline is a WebMCP-native human-agent workspace for auditable reasoning . A user represents a decision as explicit reasoning objects such as: QUESTION CLAIM COUNTERCLAIM ASSUMPTION EVIDENCE SOURCE CONCLUSION Those objects can be connected using semantic relations such as: SUPPORTS CHALLENGES DEPENDS_ON QUALIFIES Groundline then exposes the active workspace to a WebMCP-aware external agent through structured tools. The agent can: inspect the workspace; inspect individual reasoning objects; evaluate evidence and assumptions; trace dependencies; identify contradictions; find evidence gaps; focus important reasoning paths; triage what deserves review first; propose semantic relations; and propose safer revisions. Groundline does not treat the agent's answer as canonical truth. Instead, the agent can stage proposals for human review. A semantic relation does not enter the canonical reasoning graph until a human approves it. A revision does not silently overwrite an accepted conclusion. The human can: accept; accept with edits; reject; or defer. Groundline's central interaction contract is: Agent proposes. Human decides. How we built it Groundline uses a hybrid human-agent architecture. The semantic reasoning responsibility belongs to an external WebMCP-aware agent . Groundline itself owns the deterministic parts of the system: reasoning-object contracts; canonical workspace state; relation validation; dependency mechanics; structural analysis; semantic-review freshness; review-priority calculation; revision lifecycle; state invalidation; audit history; and human approval boundaries. There is deliberately no hidden page-local LLM. The external agent supplies semantic interpretation. Groundline supplies the state machine and authority model. Core Reasoning Flow The reasoning lifecycle begins with human-authored decision context. Groundline turns that input into typed reasoning objects and stores them as canonical workspace state. Deterministic structural analysis identifies represented dependencies and review targets. A WebMCP-aware agent can then inspect the same canonical reasoning state, perform semantic review, trace weak assumptions or evidence gaps, and propose repairs. Any canonical change crosses a human review boundary. When reasoning changes, stale semantic review is invalidated and the new state must be inspected again. System Flowchart The operational flowchart shows the complete reasoning-review cycle from input and validation through agent inspection, semantic evaluation, deterministic triage, repair proposals, human review, canonical state transitions, audit recording, and fresh review after changes. Architecture Groundline separates four responsibilities: The human defines the reasoning and controls canonical acceptance. Groundline's deterministic domain layer manages structure, state, review priority, revision semantics, and audit history. The WebMCP tool surface exposes structured reasoning operations. The external agent performs semantic interpretation and proposes changes. The implementation uses: React 19; TypeScript; Vite; Zustand; Zod; @xyflow/react ; Vitest; Testing Library; jsdom; and WebMCP. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, the reasoning workspace is primarily something a human can inspect visually. With WebMCP, the website becomes an agent-operable reasoning environment . The agent does not need the user to manually copy every claim, assumption, and evidence item into a chat message. Instead, it can discover structured operations directly from the active Groundline workspace. This means the agent can reason over canonical application state rather than relying only on conversational descriptions of that state. This distinction became especially important during testing. In one revision-lifecycle scenario, the conversation claimed that a revision had already been accepted. The agent re-inspected Groundline and found that the canonical state had not actually changed. It trusted the workspace instead of the conversational claim. That is exactly the behavior Groundline is designed to support: canonical application state outranks conversational assumptions. Semantic review without pretending to measure truth Groundline uses three review-priority states: CRITICAL REVIEW STABLE These labels do not mean: false; uncertain; or true. They answer a narrower question: What deserves review first? Groundline separates semantic assessment from deterministic prioritization. The current priority mechanic is based on: priority = weakness × downstream impact with: priority >= 7 -> CRITICAL priority 3..6 -> REVIEW priority <= 2 -> STABLE This distinction matters because missing evidence is not the same thing as contradiction, and contradiction is not automatically proof that something is false. Likewise, a weakness can exist without being decision-changing. The system is designed to preserve those distinctions rather than collapse everything into one confidence score. Human authority is part of the architecture One of Groundline's most important design decisions is that human control is not just explanatory text. It is implemented as part of the application workflow. Agent-generated revisions remain PROPOSED . Agent-generated semantic relations remain pending. Groundline explicitly tells browser agents to stop at the human review boundary. Human decision controls use a deliberate press-and-hold interaction before canonical state can change. This includes: accepting a revision; accepting an edited revision; rejecting a revision; deferring a revision; approving semantic relations; and rejecting proposed relations. The interaction is intentionally asymmetric: Agent: inspect evaluate trace triage focus propose Human: accept edit reject defer Explicit conversational permission does not automatically convert the external agent into the canonical human reviewer. Revision history instead of silent rewriting Groundline does not overwrite accepted reasoning when a revision is approved. Instead: old accepted item ↓ SUPERSEDED new replacement item ↓ ACCEPTED ↓ UNASSESSED The previous reasoning remains part of the audit lineage. The replacement becomes the current accepted item. Previous semantic evaluations and triage are not silently inherited. Semantic relations are also not automatically copied simply because the new item replaces the old one. Groundline therefore treats SUPERSEDES as revision provenance, not as semantic support. Meaning must be reviewed again against the new reasoning state. Challenges we ran into WebMCP changes the interaction model One of the first architectural assumptions we had to abandon was the idea that a page button could simply “call the agent again.” Baseline WebMCP does not make a connected external agent behave like a callback function owned by the page. This is a live reasoning workspace where a human and an AI agent can examine the same claims, assumptions, evidence, and conclusions together. When we make an important decision, the problem is rarely just the final answer. The real problem is hidden underneath it. Which assumptions are weak? What evidence actually supports them? And if one part fails, what else in the conclusion breaks with it? Normally, an AI explains this in text. Ground Line turns that reasoning into shared inspectable state. The human does not need to learn a reasoning ontology. I describe my decision in ordinary language, and Ground Line maps it into explicit reasoning objects. The graph is not decoration. title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: West Sparta Agent-Ready Chamber
pitch: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates West Sparta Chamber homepage with current events and member discovery. Visible Agent Activity panel showing structured member results. Sponsorship opportunities with agent-ready comparison and inquiry tools. Inspiration Chamber of commerce websites are full of useful local information, but most of it is packaged for visual browsing: directory cards, event listings, sponsorship tables, and forms. An AI agent can try to scrape and interpret those pages, but the process is brittle, expensive, and disconnected from what the person sees. West Sparta asks a simple question: what if an existing chamber website could become directly usable by an agent without becoming less useful to people? What it does West Sparta is a fictional Chamber of Commerce website enhanced with five browser-native WebMCP Site tools: search_members searches fictional chamber members by service, category, name, or town. find_events finds current events by date, audience, type, or keyword. find_sponsorships compares annual and event opportunities by budget and goal. register_for_event completes a clearly labeled fictional registration. start_sponsorship_inquiry completes a clearly labeled fictional sponsorship inquiry. A visitor can make a natural-language request that crosses several parts of the site—for example, find a commercial electrician, identify the next networking event, and register a fictional attendee. The agent receives structured results instead of reconstructing page layouts. Every tool invocation is also reflected in a visible Agent Activity panel. The person and the agent stay grounded in the same interface and can inspect what was found or completed. How we built it The project adds a focused WordPress plugin to an existing chamber demonstration site. PHP extracts and normalizes member and event information from the site's current content. Vanilla JavaScript registers the five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , supplies narrow JSON schemas, and reuses the site's existing interface logic. The two action tools are intentionally safe simulations. They accept only fictional example-domain email addresses, create no payment, send no message, and store confirmations only in the current browser session. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the normal website through progressive enhancement. Challenges The hardest design problem was not registering a tool; it was choosing the right boundaries. A useful chamber workflow crosses discovery, comparison, and action, but each tool still needs a narrow purpose, predictable schema, and clear safety contract. We also had to keep dynamic event data consistent between the human homepage and the agent-facing tools, make tool activity visible without overwhelming the design, and preserve the behavior of the existing WordPress site for ordinary visitors. Accomplishments Five working Site tools on a live WordPress website. One request can move from member discovery to event discovery to a simulated registration. Structured results and human-visible feedback remain synchronized. The repository contains a reproducible plugin, sample content, architecture notes, testing instructions, and an open-source license. The project demonstrates a reusable pattern for associations, destinations, universities, and local governments—not only chambers. What we learned WebMCP is more than a new form of search optimization. Search helps an agent find a site; structured content helps it understand the site; WebMCP lets it use the site. When the website exposes the right narrow tools, the agent can spend less effort interpreting layouts and more effort helping the person complete a real task. What's next The next step is to adapt the pattern to real chamber-management systems so directory, event, and sponsorship tools can use authenticated member data and real transaction APIs with explicit confirmation and permission controls. West Sparta remains deliberately fictional so the interaction model can be tested safely. Try it Open the live site in a WebMCP-compatible browser and ask: I'm looking for a commercial electrician in West Sparta. Find three chamber members who could help. Then find the next networking event and register Jordan Demo from Demo Business using jordan.demo@example.com . title: RelayLab
pitch: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control.
about_excerpt: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control. Like Comment Story Updates What RelayLab is RelayLab is a focused B-roll overlay editor built around human-agent collaboration. A creator keeps control of the visual timeline while an external AI agent works through WebMCP to understand the transcript, inspect indexed B-roll moments, propose ghost edits, respond to human changes, and commit only after explicit approval. The base talking-head video stays locked and remains the master audio source. B-roll is always visual-only and muted. The agent can propose, revise, remove, search, and replan, but it cannot approve its own plan, change human locks, or trigger paid video generation. Why RelayLab is a strong fit for WebMCP Traditional browser automation gives an agent pixels, DOM controls, approximate coordinates, and brittle click sequences. RelayLab instead exposes the actual editing concepts the agent needs: transcript ranges, source moments, timeline positions, pacing opportunities, ghost overlays, human locks, approval state, and the exact tools currently allowed. This makes the agent state-aware rather than screen-aware. It can reason about the same structured timeline the human is editing and safely adapt when the human changes something. Better user experience Instead of asking a creator to manually hunt through long B-roll reels and place every clip from scratch, RelayLab lets the agent do the repetitive search and planning work while preserving human editorial judgment. The collaboration loop is: The agent reads the transcript, timeline, pacing opportunities, and indexed source moments. It proposes ghost B-roll edits on the same timeline the human sees. The human can move, swap, resize, remove, or lock any edit. The agent rereads the updated timeline and replans only unlocked sections. The human approves the plan. Only then does commit_approved_plan become available through WebMCP. The agent commits the approved plan without overwriting human timing, locks, or source choices. For moments where uploaded B-roll is a weak match, the agent can suggest an AI-generation prompt. Actual generation remains a separate human-clicked action, so the agent cannot spend credits on its own. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before RelayLab turns a video editor into a shared stateful workspace between a human and an AI agent. The agent can inspect the real editorial state, understand source-time versus timeline-time, preserve locked human decisions, avoid re-proposing explicitly rejected moments, and replan around live human edits. That is difficult to do safely with normal browser automation because the agent would need to infer editorial state from the UI and could easily overwrite user decisions. With WebMCP, the collaboration contract is explicit and bounded. How WebMCP is implemented RelayLab registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in a centralized WebMCP layer. The tool surface changes with project state. Always-available read tools include project summary, transcript, timeline, edit plan, overlay opportunities, and B-roll search. During planning, additional tools allow proposing, updating, removing, and replanning unlocked ghost edits. After the human approves in the UI, those planning tools are removed and commit_approved_plan becomes available. After commit, only the read surface remains. RelayLab also tracks a monotonically increasing timelineRevision . Mutating tools can reject stale agent writes with STALE_TIMELINE instead of silently overwriting a timeline the human has already changed. Locked overlays reject agent mutation with HUMAN_LOCKED . The project includes a deterministic /demo route with a pre-indexed transcript and B-roll moments so judges can test the WebMCP collaboration loop without API keys. Additional capabilities RelayLab supports local B-roll source reels, timestamped transcript segments, manual and automatic captions, uploaded-footage-first search, optional human-triggered fal.ai B-roll generation, edit JSON export, SRT export, and reproducible ffmpeg export commands. The base video's audio remains the only audio source. Built for the WebMCP Challenge RelayLab was created during the challenge period as a focused experiment in how a human and an external AI agent can safely co-edit the same creative artifact without handing full control to either side. title: AgentGate
pitch: A human approval gate for AI agents, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A human approval gate for AI agents, built on WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Theme fit 

 AgentGate directly uses the WebMCP API — document.modelContext.registerTool() , getTools() , and executeTool() — to register three real WebMCP tools ( propose_action , check_approval , list_pending ) that any WebMCP-aware AI agent can discover and call on this page. It solves a real, open problem in the WebMCP spec itself: there is currently no built-in way for a page to require human confirmation before an agent's tool call takes effect (see webmachinelearning/webmcp#165 and #50 ). AgentGate is a working, application-level answer to that gap. 

 Inspiration 

 WebMCP lets a website expose real, callable functions to AI agents — a huge step up from agents having to fake being a human clicking through a UI. But that power cuts both ways: the moment an agent calls a tool, it runs, instantly, with nothing built into WebMCP to pause and ask a human first. The spec's own maintainers have this flagged as unresolved. We wanted to build the missing piece rather than just another demo of the happy path. 

 What it does 

 AgentGate gives a site a safe way to expose sensitive actions to agents. Instead of wiring a tool directly to something real (delete a file, send a message, spend money), the site registers propose_action . Calling it doesn't do the real thing — it queues a request and shows it in a live approval inbox for a human to review. A human approves or rejects, optionally with a note. The agent calls check_approval with the proposal id to find out what happened, and only proceeds with the actual action once it sees "approved" . 

 How we built it 

 React + Vite front end. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers the three tools directly against the real WebMCP API — no framework or SDK wrapping it, just the native browser API as documented. State (proposals, their status, notes) lives in a small observable store backed by localStorage , so the approval history survives a reload. No backend — the whole mechanism works client-side, which is enough to prove the pattern end-to-end. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely experimental — getting a real document.modelContext in an unmodified browser required registering for Chrome's WebMCP Origin Trial and embedding a token scoped to our exact origin. Once we had a real API to test against (not a mock), we also found the actual behavior differs from a naive reading of the docs — getTools() and registerTool() are both asynchronous (return Promises), and executeTool() takes the tool object itself plus a JSON-string of arguments, not a tool name and a plain object. We also hit a real bug this way: React's StrictMode double-invokes effects in development, and since the real API has no unregisterTool , that caused duplicate-registration errors — fixed with an idempotency guard. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 Getting this working against the actual WebMCP implementation, not a simulated one — calling propose_action through the real document.modelContext , approving it as a human in the UI, and watching check_approval reflect that back correctly. 

 What we learned 

 That an open spec with unresolved design questions is fertile ground for a real contribution, not just a demo — and that testing against the real API (even a gated, experimental one) surfaces mismatches with the documentation that no amount of reading catches. 

 What's next 

 A cancellation path using AbortSignal (the spec supports it for in-flight tool calls), and richer proposal types (e.g. structured diffs for code-change proposals) so a human reviewer has more context before approving.

title: Concierge
pitch: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Concierge Concierge The web has APIs. Most businesses still have phone numbers. Concierge lets ChatGPT prepare an inquiry call, while the webpage keeps the consequential action with the person. Why we built it A surprising amount of ordinary life still requires a phone call: asking a hotel about late arrival, checking accessibility, clarifying a bill, confirming a delivery window, or speaking to a business in another language. A chat assistant can write a script, but the person still has to place the call, take notes, and translate the answer. Giving an agent unlimited authority would be worse. A call can create a booking, accept a fee, change a reservation, or commit the user to terms. We wanted the useful part of delegation without hiding those actions. What Concierge does The user describes the inquiry in ChatGPT. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT creates or revises a structured call plan on the signed-in Concierge page. The page shows the destination, exact questions, shareable context, call language, authority limits, price ceiling, and revision. Then the workflow stops. Only the person can press Confirm one call . Confirmation is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool list. After confirmation, the voice worker places one disclosed information-only call. It cannot book, pay, cancel, accept a fee, accept terms, or make a commitment. The result records each requested question as answered, uncertain, or unanswered, with a short evidence excerpt. It also returns duration, cost state, disclosure state, terminal reason, and a one-attempt receipt. ChatGPT can read that result through WebMCP and explain it in the conversation where the request started. The user never sees Twilio settings, calling-country permissions, provider credentials, or API keys. Concierge owns that infrastructure. Every call still needs a fresh quote and a visible confirmation. Why WebMCP is the point Without WebMCP, ChatGPT can suggest a call plan but cannot safely manipulate the authenticated task the user is reviewing. With WebMCP, the chat and the page share the same revisioned object: ChatGPT creates, updates, reads, and monitors the task. The webpage shows the exact plan and owns confirmation. Convex enforces identity, revisions, idempotency, credits, and one-attempt dispatch. The Cloudflare worker handles temporary live audio. Twilio connects the call to OpenAI Realtime. This is not a chatbot pasted next to a form. WebMCP is what lets the agent do the preparation and retrieval work while the page preserves the trust boundary. A repeatable judge demo Calling a real hotel for every judge would be rude and hard to debug. We built Aurora Demo Hotel, a clearly fictional automated recipient reached through the real phone network. Judges can write their own information-only questions. The recipient answers from a versioned server-owned fact sheet, says when it does not know, and cannot book or take payment. The same inquiry contract also accepts arbitrary real services and destinations. The hotel is a controlled test path, not the product boundary. How we built it The browser app is React and TypeScript. It registers six page tools with document.modelContext: create a general draft, create a controlled demo draft, update a draft, read a draft, read status, and read the result. Convex owns the task state machine. Confirmation is bound to the exact execution revision; any material edit invalidates it. Provider uncertainty never creates an automatic retry. Signed worker events become a deterministic public activity log and result. The phone worker runs on Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects. Twilio Media Streams carry bidirectional PCMU audio to OpenAI Realtime gpt-realtime-2.1-mini. Audio is not stored. A separate extraction step turns bounded call evidence into candidate facts; the model cannot publish its own receipt or grant itself more authority. Authentication supports Continue with ChatGPT and WorkOS AuthKit. The ChatGPT bridge exchanges identity for a short-lived, audience-bound Convex token. What was hard The difficult work was not dialing a number. It was keeping authority exact across several asynchronous systems. We tested stale confirmations, duplicate dispatches, interrupted disclosure, repeated questions, corrections, barge-in, provider uncertainty, signed callbacks, expired quotes, and failed calls. The public UI reports failure as failure; it does not polish an incomplete call into a successful result. Concierge started before the challenge as a mobile call-avoidance prototype. During the submission period we rebuilt the product around the web and WebMCP: authenticated page tools, the general inquiry contract, exact-revision confirmation, evidence-linked results, ChatGPT sign-in, the controlled recipient, responsive judge onboarding, and production release gates. Those changes are separated in the public repository history and documentation. Ask whether I can arrive after midnight, when breakfast is served, and whether on-site parking is available. Do not book anything or accept a fee. Review the plan on the page.
