title: ClassSignal
pitch: ClassSignal turns student mistakes into testable hypotheses that teachers and AI agents investigate together.
about_excerpt: ClassSignal turns student mistakes into testable hypotheses that teachers and AI agents investigate together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Teachers often know which questions students answered incorrectly, but not why. The same wrong answer can come from several different misconceptions, and choosing an intervention too early can reinforce the wrong idea. We wanted to explore a more useful role for AI in education: not automatically diagnosing students or giving them answers, but helping teachers turn uncertainty into a small, testable experiment. What it does ClassSignal is a shared Misconception Lab where teachers and AI agents investigate student reasoning together. ChatGPT can use WebMCP to inspect structured classroom evidence, compare competing explanations, and create a 60-second diagnostic probe directly inside the teacher’s workspace. The teacher can edit that probe, and the agent can inspect and reason about the exact revision. After explicit teacher approval, the probe appears in the student workspace. The student answers and explains their reasoning, producing new evidence that updates the hypothesis ranking and unlocks a targeted intervention for teacher review. ClassSignal also includes six-question guided practice, Socratic hints that do not reveal assessed answers, saved student reasoning, intervention approval controls, and an activity feed that attributes teacher, student, and agent actions. How I built it ClassSignal is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Mantine’s default theme, Mantine Charts, and Recharts. We implemented WebMCP using @mcp-b/global and @mcp-b/react-webmcp . The application exposes 12 structured tools for: Inspecting classroom and student evidence Analyzing competing misconceptions Creating and inspecting diagnostic probes Publishing teacher-approved probes Analyzing new student evidence Previewing and applying interventions Providing answer-safe guided support Measuring learning outcomes The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same React state. This means an agent-created probe appears in the open page without a refresh, teacher edits become visible to the agent on its next call, and student responses change what the teacher and agent can do next. The demonstration uses deterministic fictional data stored in localStorage , allowing the complete experience to be reset and reproduced reliably without collecting real student information. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the project feel genuinely native to WebMCP rather than like a conventional dashboard with a chatbot attached. Our first version focused too heavily on analytics and tool count. Although the tools worked, the experience was not memorable. We redesigned the product around one collaborative loop: competing hypotheses, an agent-created experiment, a teacher revision, controlled publication, new student evidence, and an unlocked intervention. We also had to carefully separate preview operations from consequential actions. Publishing student-facing content and applying interventions require explicit confirmation, while student-support tools enforce answer safety inside their execution logic. Other challenges included keeping browser-local state consistent across teacher and student routes, preventing duplicate actions, handling rapid React form updates, making six questions navigable and reviewable, and maintaining responsive layouts without introducing a custom design system. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that the agent creates something meaningful inside the teacher’s existing workflow instead of only summarizing data. The teacher can improve the agent-created probe, and that human contribution becomes new context the agent can inspect. The student then contributes evidence that changes the shared state and determines which action becomes available. We are also proud of the trust boundaries built into the experience: Findings are presented as hypotheses rather than diagnoses. Evidence strength is not presented as statistical confidence. The sample size remains visible. Student-facing publication requires teacher approval. Intervention application requires separate approval. Guided-help tools do not reveal assessed answers. Every consequential action is attributed in the activity feed. All classroom information is fictional. What we learned We learned that exposing many tools does not automatically create a compelling agent experience. The important question is whether people and agents can contribute different capabilities to the same workflow. WebMCP became most valuable when the website remained the trusted owner of state, the agent contributed structured reasoning and creation, and the teacher controlled consequential decisions. We also learned that uncertainty can be a product feature. Instead of making the AI appear certain, ClassSignal shows competing explanations and gives the teacher a practical way to collect better evidence. Finally, we learned that a strong WebMCP demonstration needs visible state transitions. A judge should be able to see that an agent action changed the application, a human edit changed what the agent knew, and a student response changed the next available decision. What's next for ClassSignal Next, we would test the workflow with professional teachers and learning-science experts before making stronger educational claims. We would replace the demonstration heuristic with a validated evidence model that aggregates multiple student responses over time. We would also add secure authentication, server-enforced roles, a production database, separate teacher and student sessions, classroom-management integrations, and longitudinal intervention measurement. The long-term goal is not to automate teacher judgment. It is to give teachers and their agents a shared laboratory for asking better questions before acting on student data. about_excerpt:
A secure, agent-ready learning experience where people and AI use WebMCP to find training, build learning paths, track progress, and take permitted actions together.

 Inspiration 

 LearnLogos has a large collection of instructional videos, captions, and sentence-level timestamps. Learners often Blackjack remember what John taught but cannot remember the course, video, or terminology
 needed to find it. We wanted agents to retrieve LearnLogos teaching directly instead of generating a generic answer or guessing how to navigate the website. 

 ## What it does 

 The LearnLogos WebMCP Learning Assistant turns a natural-language question into the most relevant approved teaching excerpt. 

 A supported browser agent can discover and invoke learnlogos.search_training.v1 . The result includes: 

 
 The relevant lesson title and summary 
 Exact source timestamps 
 An SBL-style citation 
 An explanation of why it matched 
 Controlled video playback with captions 
 

 The visible demonstration provides eight alternative questions across two topics. Different ways of asking about program scaling find “Set Exact Program Scaling,” while reading-plan questions find “Jump to Your
 Next Reading.” 

 This demonstrates how people and agents can find the same authoritative instruction without knowing its essentially compression reti Bots exact title or location. 

 ## How we built it 

 The application uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, and Zod. The page registers a structured tool through document.modelContext.registerTool , while both the human interface and browser agent use the same
 validated search service. 

 The contest deployment is separate from the production LearnLogos website. It uses: 

 
 A hard server-side content allowlist 
 Two exact, rights-approved demonstration excerpts 
 Synthetic session state with no customer information 
 Dedicated Upstash Redis rate limiting 
 Short-lived, session-bound media grants 
 Exact media and caption digest verification 
 Same-origin restrictions and a strict content security policy 
 Automated tests covering tool registration, retrieval, authorization, media access, and browser behavior 
 

 ## Challenges 

 The largest challenge was combining a useful demonstration with strict security and intellectual-property boundaries. We needed to show real question-to-video retrieval without exposing production Nz content,
 customer data, full transcripts, or unrestricted media URLs. 

 Natural-language ranking also required care. Common words such as “the” initially created ties between unrelated lessons. We corrected this by excluding conversational filler words from ranking and added
 regression tests for every demonstration question. 

 ## What we learned 

 WebMCP works best as an interface over reusable application services—not as a separate business-logic layer. Structured tools give agents reliable inputs, validated outputs, and clear authorization boundaries
 while preserving an accessible experience for people. 

 We also learned that retrieval quality depends on preserving provenance. A useful answer should remain traceable to the exact lesson, source recording, timestamp range, and access decision. 

 ## What's next 

 The contest entry is a secure vertical slice of a larger LearnLogos vision. Future work includes searching customer-owned training first, coherent transcript segmentation, hybrid semantic retrieval,
 personalized learning paths, progress-aware recommendations, and secure previews of additional approved lessons. 

 LearnLogos is an independent training provider. It is not owned, operated, sponsored, or endorsed by Logos.

title: Koshara
pitch: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI
about_excerpt: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard update charts using AI Statement import review and approve Add update categories Add update transactions Landing page Inspiration Managing household finances still involves repetitive work: reviewing statements, categorizing transactions, finding duplicates, and configuring dashboards. We wanted to explore a model where users keep the familiar financial interface while their chosen AI handles tedious preparation through structured WebMCP tools—not fragile browser automation. What it does Koshara is a household finance application for managing accounts, transactions, categories, statements, and cash-flow insights. Using WebMCP, an AI agent can: Configure dashboard charts from a natural-language request. Parse an unstructured bank statement. Send the extracted transactions to Koshara as a temporary import batch. Koshara then validates and groups transactions into Ready, Needs Review, Possible Duplicates, and Suggested Merges. The user reviews everything in the normal UI and clicks Approve Import before any transaction enters the main history. How we built it We built Koshara with Next.js and TypeScript, using Astryx for the interface and Recharts for financial visualizations. Koshara registers structured WebMCP tools directly in the browser. The dashboard tool updates chart presentation and insights, while the statement tool accepts parsed transactions and stages them for review. The prototype stores its data locally in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should end and human control should begin. Financial statements may contain ambiguous categories, duplicates, refunds, or related transactions. To handle this safely, we separated staging from committing. The AI prepares the data, Koshara validates it, and the user approves the final changes. We also had to ensure WebMCP actions updated the same application state and UI used by the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created an end-to-end workflow where an external AI can interpret an unstructured statement and transfer the result into a structured, human-controlled review experience. We are also proud that Koshara does not require an embedded chatbot. The application supplies the data, rules, tools, and interface, while users can bring their preferred AI. What we learned We learned that an agent-native application does not need to replace its visual interface. WebMCP works best as an almost invisible capability layer behind a useful product. AI is effective at interpreting messy information and preparing work. Applications are better at validation and business rules, while humans should remain responsible for ambiguous or consequential decisions. What's next for Koshara Next, we plan to support more statement formats, improve duplicate and merge detection, add authenticated persistent storage, and provide a clearer audit trail for agent-prepared actions. We also want to expand the WebMCP tools so users can ask richer financial questions and generate more personalized dashboard views. title: Hearth. Design a home with your agent.
pitch: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout.
about_excerpt: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Agent placing furniture, arranging, comparing layouts Living room at golden hour with catalog, inspector and activity log The Tools panel listing the WebMCP tools and schemas A home built from an uploaded floor plan, furnished The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results Ghost preview of a Shopify product plus the cart Door-swing and clearance conflict diagrams with a fix Accessibility mode with turning circles and paths Exported design board Whole-home framing The seven floor-plan templates plus "Import your own plan" Orbit camera view Inspiration I was thinking of buying a home, and one question that kept coming was how will I furnish it. The hard question was not the price. It was: will the furniture fit, and will the door still open? Where should I place the furniture, will it look good as per my home layout, and what will be the total cost I might need. An AI agent should be able to help with this, but it can't. A chat model can't see the room. A screen-scraping agent can guess at pixels, but it can't measure a wall, and it certainly can't be trusted to drag a sofa. Room planners exist (IKEA Kreativ, Planner 5D); none of them let an agent in. Browser agents exist; none of them can measure a wall. When I read the WebMCP proposal the idea clicked: instead of making the agent reverse-engineer my page, I could hand it the same verbs I use. Interior design felt like the perfect test. It's spatial, iterative, visual, and it ends with a real purchase. So I built Hearth: a 3D home studio where a person and an agent work on the same rooms, and the agent gets forty real tools instead of a screenshot. What it does Hearth is a shared interior-design studio. You get a dollhouse-style 3D home you can drag furniture around in, with magnetic snapping and live dimension lines. Your agent gets the same home through tools registered on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . It reads the space as data: rooms, walls and their free spans, door swings, every item in centimetres, and a conflict report (clearances, traffic paths, blocked doors) with a one-line fix for each. It designs with semantic anchors, so "put the sofa against the north wall facing the window" becomes move_furniture {anchor:{wall:"north", facing:"window:…"}} and no coordinates cross the conversation. It can arrange a room for a purpose, change the time of day, and turn on accessibility mode (90 cm paths, 150 cm turning circles) and then fix what that flags. It can also build the home. Pick one of seven floor plans, or drop a photo of your own and call import_floor_plan : a vision model reads room names, printed dimensions, doors and windows, and Hearth's layout engine turns that into a to-scale scene with shared walls snapped, doors paired across them, and starter furniture that arrives conflict-free. Every placed item has an exact size, resize_furniture changes it, and search_catalog ranks real Shopify products by closeness to that size and says whether each match is exact, close or off, with the centimetre delta. The shop is a live Shopify store with 71 products. The agent can filter by what fits a wall, ghost-preview a product in the room in a colourway, add it to the cart and hand you the checkout link. The purchase click stays yours, which is the only version of agent shopping I would actually use. A typical session: drop a photo of the flat and get a furnished home to scale; ask for a sofa that fits the north wall under $800 and watch it ghost into the room; confirm it, add it to the cart, take the checkout link. Nothing in that chain needs a coordinate or a product id from me. Everything is visible and reversible. Save layouts and compare two with a slider, undo anything, clear the home and restore it, export a design board. When the agent acts, an orb flies to the spot, a receipt lands in the activity log with the exact tool input and result, and an Undo chip appears. Destructive tools open a confirmation dialog in the page, and if I decline, the agent gets {error:"cancelled", detail:"The human declined…"} back, so it knows why, not just that it failed. How I built it I wrote the contracts before the code. TOOLS.md specifies every tool's name, description, parameters, result shape, group and gate; SCENE_SCHEMA.md pins the scene graph, units and coordinate frame. Everything else was judged against those two files. The stack is Next.js 16 and React 19 with React-Three-Fiber for the scene. A zustand store tags every mutation human or agent , and a pure TypeScript geometry engine (walls, clearances, traffic paths, floor-plan layout) has no React or three.js in it and is covered by a few hundred unit tests. The shop is the Shopify Storefront API; the floor-plan reader and the fallback assistant use the OpenAI Responses API through server-only route handlers. It runs in ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser, in Chrome with WebMCP enabled (the production origin ships an origin-trial token), and where a browser has no WebMCP yet, an in-page assistant drives the same tools through Chrome's polyfill. The WebMCP layer is one registry, src/tools/registry.ts . The surface I use: registerTool with an AbortSignal per group, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, the toolchange event and getTools() mirrored into a Tools panel so a judge can inspect the surface without an agent, executeTool through the polyfill for the fallback assistant, and Chrome's published budgets as CI assertions. Each tool is defined once with a zod schema and converted to JSON Schema. The registry asserts the budgets at definition time (names ≤ 30 chars, descriptions ≤ 500, parameter descriptions ≤ 150) and the test suite asserts every result stays under 1,500 characters across three scene fixtures. 29 tools register synchronously on load so DevTools and Lighthouse see them cold. 11 more live in four state-gated groups (build, preview, variants, checkout), each behind its own AbortController . When the scene changes the registry diffs the desired groups and registers or aborts, and any tool whose result changes the gate set ( set_mode , but also update_cart opening checkout or preview_in_room opening preview) waits for the registry to settle and returns tools_ready . Results are plain JSON envelopes. Success carries the room, the conflicts and a hint. Failure carries an error code, a detail and a suggestion; a blocked placement adds the free wall spans, an unknown id adds the three closest candidates, so the model can self-correct instead of retrying blindly. Every room , item or product parameter accepts an id or a name, item accepts selected , and room_id -style keys are rewritten to the documented ones before validation, because models send them anyway and a good call shouldn't die as invalid . A webmcp-evals suite of 32 prompts checks that the right tool is called with the right arguments in the right order. Challenges I ran into Chrome (before 153) cancels in-flight executions on abort. My first gating implementation aborted a group the moment the scene said it should go away, which killed the very tool call that had changed the scene. The fix was a deferral rule: never abort while a tool is executing, queue the sync, flush it on a macrotask afterwards, and have the tool that caused the change release its own executing count before waiting for the registry to settle. That one rule took longer to get right than most features. Describing a room to something with no eyes. Early tool descriptions were long and situational, and models made worse calls with them. What worked was static, short descriptions, all live context in get_scene_summary , semantic anchors instead of coordinates, and putting the "what to do next" hint inside the result rather than the description. Floor plans are messy. Vision models return bounding boxes drawn backwards, width and depth swapped depending on the image's aspect ratio, and room names in ALL CAPS. Getting from that to a scene where shared walls line up, doors are paired on both sides of a wall, every room is reachable and the starter furniture has zero conflicts took a per-axis scale from the printed dimensions, edge clustering, overlap resolution and a connectivity pass. I tested it on the three sample plans and a dozen more I pulled off the web; five recorded reader outputs now run as fixtures. Making agent actions legible without being noisy. Silent state changes feel like a haunted house. The orb, receipts, pulses and the eight-second Undo chip were as much design work as engineering, and stepper-driven resizes had to be coalesced so a human dragging a value didn't generate forty receipts. title: Watch with Codex
pitch: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback. Like 1 Comment Story Updates how it works Watch with Codex The same conversation, now present in the moment. Inspiration The difference between watching something with another person and merely discussing it later is timing. It is the laugh at the exact frame, the quiet “wait, what did that mean?”, or the look you exchange when something unexpected happens. AI can already summarize a video, answer questions about a transcript, or analyze a screenshot. But most of those experiences begin after the moment has passed. The model may understand the content, yet it does not share the timing, the interruption, or the viewer’s reaction. I wanted to build the opposite: not another video summarizer and not a second chatbot embedded beside a player, but a way for the Codex conversation you already have to become present inside the same live experience. What it does Watch with Codex turns a video page into a shared timeline between a person and Codex. The viewer pastes a YouTube link, direct video file, or embeddable player and asks Codex to watch along. The existing conversation remains the memory and response surface. There is no duplicate chat, separate account, or artificial companion persona. While the video is playing, Codex keeps a WebMCP observation open. The viewer can choose a cadence of 5, 10, or 15 seconds of media time. Codex stays quiet by default and decides whether the current moment deserves a reaction, a short comment, an explanation, or no interruption at all. Speech-heavy videos are already supported. For YouTube videos with captions, the active captions are captured together with the rendered player. At the five-second cadence, successive observations provide a rolling, time-aligned language context, while the existing conversation preserves what came before. This lets Codex follow what is being said as well as what is visible. Lectures, tutorials, interviews, historical speeches, and captioned films are practical use cases today—not only videos with visually obvious action. The viewer can also react with an emoji. That reaction is not a canned command. It immediately wakes the pending observation and arrives with the exact playback time and the current visible frame. A 😂 might mean “this chart is ridiculous.” A ❓ might mean “what is the historical context of that sentence?” The meaning comes from the frame, the captions, the conversation, and the viewer’s intent—not from a hard-coded emoji-to-answer mapping. Codex can answer inside the same conversation, publish one to five lightweight visual reactions directly over the player, or pause and resume supported videos when a longer explanation would compete with playback. Why it matters The core value is not constant AI commentary. It is reducing the distance between noticing something and getting useful help. A student can tap ❓ in the middle of a difficult proof, let Codex pause the video, receive an explanation of that exact step, and continue without losing the place. A language learner can ask about a phrase while the caption, speaker, and visual context are still connected. Someone watching a historical speech can receive context at the sentence where it becomes relevant instead of searching for an explanation afterward. The same interaction can also reduce physical and cognitive friction. A viewer who finds repeated pausing, scrubbing, switching tabs, or typing difficult can communicate with a single reaction while Codex handles the timing and playback. That can be useful for people with motor limitations, pain, fatigue, temporary injuries, or anyone who benefits from a lower-interaction interface. In a conversation guided by a parent or teacher, younger learners can receive simpler explanations and deliberate pause points without navigating away from the lesson. Because the existing Codex conversation owns the memory, the experience can adapt to the viewer’s actual goal: exam preparation, language learning, historical context, simplified explanations, accessibility support, or simply quiet companionship. Voice will make that interaction even more natural, but the current one-tap workflow already removes much of the mechanical overhead between the viewer and the assistant. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a person and Codex can discuss the same video, but they cannot reliably inhabit the same moment. A link has no live state. A screenshot is detached from playback. A transcript may contain the words, but it does not tell Codex where the viewer is now, whether they paused, rewound, changed playback speed, or reacted to a particular moment. WebMCP is load-bearing in this project. The page exposes five tools: watch_get_session , watch_observe_next_moment , watch_play , watch_pause , and watch_react . The central tool, watch_observe_next_moment , acts as both a clock and an event channel. It resolves at the next scheduled media-time checkpoint or immediately when the viewer reacts. Its cadence follows video playback time rather than wall-clock time, so pauses, playback-speed changes, and time spent reasoning do not silently move Codex farther away from the shared moment. A persistent cursor preserves the schedule between observations, reports missed checkpoints, and resets cleanly after the viewer seeks to another part of the video. WebMCP gives Codex the structured moment: the media identity, player state, exact timecode, viewer signal, and available actions. Browser observation then captures the rendered player immediately before reasoning, including cross-origin video, active captions, and visible overlays. Together, these two layers let Codex know where the viewer is, see what the viewer sees, follow what is being said, and act inside the same experience. Remove WebMCP, and Watch with Codex becomes an ordinary video player with chat beside it. How I built it Watch with Codex is a deliberately small Next.js and React application deployed on OpenAI Sites. One page owns the live session: the selected source, normalized playback state, observation cadence, media-time cursor, pending viewer signals, and on-screen reactions. The existing Codex conversation owns memory, language, and interpretation. The project needs no database and no independent assistant backend. YouTube playback uses the IFrame Player API, while title and author metadata are resolved through oEmbed. Direct video files use the browser’s native video element. Generic embeds remain viewable, but timing and playback tools fail explicitly when the page cannot access those capabilities. One architectural boundary was especially important. A host page cannot read pixels from a cross-origin YouTube iframe. Instead of pretending otherwise or returning meaningless image data inside JSON, each WebMCP observation provides the exact checkpoint and a capture contract targeting .player-frame . The browser captures the rendered frame immediately before Codex reasons about it. This also means that YouTube captions remain attached to the speaker, slide, chart, or scene they belong to rather than becoming a detached block of transcript text. The observation loop has been tested across pauses, resumes, seeks, playback-speed changes, model latency, missed checkpoints, and viewer-triggered interruptions. The persistent media-time cursor keeps the session synchronized instead of restarting the clock after every model response or gradually drifting behind the video. Deterministic code owns timing, validation, rate limits, and failure states. Codex owns the meaning of the moment. Challenges The hardest problem was not embedding a video or registering tools. It was making the interaction feel like company rather than surveillance or narration. A companion that comments every five seconds quickly becomes unbearable. A companion that reacts several seconds too late no longer feels present. The observation loop therefore had to be quiet, event-driven, and anchored to media time. Speech-heavy content created another important design requirement: the model needed linguistic context without turning the experience into a detached, post-video transcript workflow. For captioned YouTube videos, successive five-second observations preserve a rolling view of the spoken content inside the same live timeline. In testing, this has been enough for Codex to follow lectures and other dialogue-heavy material while remaining synchronized with the current visual moment. Viewer reactions also needed to interrupt the pending observation immediately without stopping the watch-along. At the same time, model latency could not be allowed to restart the clock after every response and gradually move Codex behind the viewer. The final challenge was respecting browser security boundaries. WebMCP can expose structured page state, but the page cannot directly inspect every rendered pixel inside a third-party player. about_excerpt: A human-governed game design workspace where WebMCP agents inspect, propose, validate, and playtest while creators keep final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Designing a tabletop game means coordinating rules, card costs, timing, win conditions, play length, and balance. An agent that relies on pixels has to guess how those parts relate, while unrestricted mutation can remove the designer from the decision that matters most. Ruleloom explores a better agentic-web pattern: the page exposes semantic operations, and the person keeps authorship and final approval. What it does Ruleloom is a visual game-design studio where a person and a WebMCP agent work on the same versioned specification. An agent can inspect, validate, run deterministic seeded playtests, and stage a bounded patch. Staging is inert: Ruleloom shows every operation, path, and value while the game remains unchanged. Only a direct human click creates a short-lived, proposal-bound, version-bound, one-use approval. That action dynamically registers apply_approved_patch . The agent can apply once; Ruleloom advances the version, consumes approval, removes the tool, and shows post-change evidence in the same workspace. In the captured public flow, Lunar Orchard advanced from v1 to v2. Replay was unavailable because the dynamic tool disappeared. Validation returned 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 1 informational finding. A 200-game deterministic run with seed 42017 produced 78 Player 1 wins, 89 Player 2 wins, and 33 draws, averaging 15.835 turns. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the product architecture, not an add-on. Five stable native tools expose inspection, draft creation, proposal staging, validation, and seeded playtesting. A sixth tool exists only while a current direct human approval is valid. The React UI and every WebMCP call share one versioned store. Tool mutations update the visual workspace, and human actions change which tools exist. Human authority and replay protection Approve, Reject, Reset, and Undo are UI-only. The approval value stays in a private store closure and never appears in tool input, output, persistence, or the activity trace. Approval expires and is tied to one proposal and base version. Stale or mismatched work is rejected without partial mutation; one successful apply consumes and unregisters the capability. How we built it Ruleloom is a static React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Zod app on Vercel. src/domain contains the strict schema, versioned store, allowlisted patch engine, validator, and seeded simulator. src/webmcp owns native document.modelContext registration, JSON Schemas, validation, bounded results, and registration lifetimes. src/App.tsx renders the human workspace from the same store. There is no login, server, remote database, production API, private package, or required secret. The complete MIT-licensed source, tests, threat model, evaluation definition, judge guide, and reproducible video materials are public. OpenAI Codex helped scope, implement, test, verify, and prepare this new standalone project. The runtime does not call an LLM API. Challenges The hardest problem was useful agent mutation without a reusable bearer token. We solved it with a private approval closure and a dynamic tool bound to proposal, version, expiry, and one successful use. Native WebMCP support also varies by client, so Ruleloom feature-detects support and names only tested clients. Seeded simulation stays reproducible through strict schemas, workload limits, recorded seeds, and versioned reports. Accomplishments Five stable WebMCP tools plus one state-dependent tool Direct human approval without agent-visible approval material Observed one-use apply and replay prevention 45 passing unit tests and 6 passing browser tests Public no-login deployment and MIT repository 2:44 public narrated demo with authored English captions Honest live-agent subset reporting without a fabricated full-suite rate What we learned Dynamic tool registration can express authority directly: if the person has not approved, the mutation capability does not exist. Strong human-agent interfaces need clear state, constrained mutations, version binding, and visible evidence. What's next We want to support more bounded tabletop systems, richer simulation distributions, side-by-side scenarios, opt-in collaboration, and the full frozen 27-task evaluation across more WebMCP clients. Testing Open https://ruleloom-nu.vercel.app in the Codex in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm five tools, use the Judge Quickstart prompt, review the staged proposal, click Approve for agent , ask the agent to apply, then validate and run 200 playtests with seed 42017. Confirm v2 and that the apply tool disappears. No credentials are required. pitch: Play Minecraft using WebMCP
about_excerpt:

 Minecraft 3D — Agentic Voxel World via WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore what happens when an AI agent stops being a chatbot bolted onto the side of a game and instead becomes a real co-player inside it. Most "AI plays Minecraft" projects (Voyager, MineDojo, etc.) rely on native Java installs, Python backend daemons, Docker containers, and modding frameworks like Forge or Fabric just to get an agent to see the world and press a key. That's a huge amount of friction for something that should feel as simple as talking to a friend while you build together. 

 Around the same time, the W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) draft and Chrome's WebMCP origin trial started gaining traction as a way to expose structured, agent-callable tools directly from a web page. That felt like the missing piece: a 3D voxel sandbox running entirely in the browser, with an AI agent that could see exact coordinates, block IDs, and inventory state natively — no screen-scraping, no guessing pixels, no external bridge processes. We wanted to build the voxel-game equivalent of giving an agent hands and eyes instead of just a text console. 

 What it does 

 Minecraft 3D (WebMCP Edition) is a procedural 3D voxel sandbox built from scratch with Three.js and React, featuring 14 biomes, dynamic day/night cycles, weather (clear, rain, snow), hostile and passive mob AI, procedural audio synthesis, physics, survival/creative modes, and crafting. 

 On top of that game, we embed WebMCP directly into the browser client, exposing 23 standard-compliant tools on document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext , plus a standard MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 postMessage bridge. This lets an AI agent: 

 
 Inspect voxel terrain and query exact player state (position, orientation, health, hunger, biome, held item) 
 Architect complex structures — castles, cottages, watchtowers, pyramids, fountains, portals — with progressive, block-by-block animated construction 
 Manage inventories, hotbar selection, and item granting 
 Terraform landscapes, clear areas, and build 15 procedural geometric primitives (domes, spheres, cylinders, pyramids, etc.) 
 Mine blocks, spawn and attack mobs, control weather and time of day 
 Respond to natural-language commands in real time ("build a stone castle in front of me and make it daytime") 
 

 A player can literally say "clear this hill and give me a diamond pickaxe" and watch the agent do it live in the same browser session, block by block. 

 How we built it 

 
 Game engine : Three.js for rendering and voxel chunk management, React for UI/state, with custom physics, procedural terrain generation across 14 biomes, procedural audio synthesis, and a survival/creative mode system. 
 WebMCP polyfill & bridge ( WebMCPPolyfill.js ): A spec-compliant implementation of the W3C WebMCP draft that installs the ModelContext interface on document.modelContext , navigator.modelContext , and window.modelContext . It implements registerTool , unregisterTool , getTools , executeTool , fires toolchange events, and exposes a JSON-RPC 2.0 postMessage bridge ( tools/list , tools/call ) so external extensions, iframes, or agent runtimes can drive the game without any custom protocol of their own. It also keeps an in-memory execution history for diagnostics. 
 23 core tools ( MinecraftWebMCPTools.js ) organized into five functional categories: Navigation & Exploration, Environment & World Settings, Inventory & Block Inspection, Mining & Entities, and Architectural Building & Geometry. 
 Zero-hallucination design : every tool uses structured JSON Schemas with typed inputs, coordinate bounds, and annotations like readOnlyHint , so the agent never has to guess where a block is — the engine validates every action, loads chunks on demand, and returns structured feedback. 
 Safety net for building : a 20-step undo buffer ( undo_last_build ) so any agent (or human) mistake in a large build is trivially reversible. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The single biggest challenge was integrating WebMCP into an actual game rather than a static web page. Most WebMCP examples in the wild are forms, calculators, or simple content sites — a 3D game with continuous physics, chunk loading, mob AI, and real-time state is a completely different beast. We had to design and build a lot of tools, and think hard about the underlying game mechanics behind each one, so that an AI agent could actually play Minecraft without getting stuck: things like clamping movement to terrain, exposing raycasting ( get_target_block ) so the agent knows what it's aiming at, batching block placement so an agent doesn't have to place 1,000 individual blocks one tool call at a time, and building an undo stack so mistakes aren't catastrophic. Every tool we added exposed a new edge case in the underlying voxel engine (chunk boundaries, out-of-range coordinates, invalid block IDs, physics collisions) that we had to handle gracefully so the agent's experience stayed smooth. 

 The second major challenge was that AI-powered IDEs and coding assistants simply aren't aware of WebMCP yet. Because it's such a new, emerging standard, tools like Copilot and other AI coding assistants couldn't reliably generate correct WebMCP registration code, tool schemas, or bridge logic — they'd only produce useful results once we explicitly spelled out the spec, the interfaces, and the exact patterns ourselves. More amusingly, several times the assistants misunderstood the goal entirely and tried to build an MCP server instead of registering WebMCP tools in the browser client — a funny but telling sign of just how early and undocumented WebMCP still is in training data and tooling. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that we were able to provide enough tools within WebMCP — 23 in total, spanning navigation, environment control, inventory, mining/entities, and architectural building — that an AI agent can play the game without any real friction, essentially like a normal human player. The agent can check its surroundings, manage its inventory, build complex multi-block structures, fight or spawn mobs, and change the world around it, all through the same structured interface, with no external bots, no screen scraping, and no modding. Watching a single natural-language prompt ("check my inventory, set it to creative, clear this area, and build a castle") turn into a fully coherent, multi-step, correctly-sequenced sequence of tool calls that plays out live in the 3D world felt like a genuine proof that WebMCP can support something as complex and dynamic as a voxel game. 

 We're also proud of the zero-setup story: no Java, no Docker, no Forge/Fabric mods, no Python daemon — just open a browser tab and an agent is ready to co-play. 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is genuinely capable of supporting high-dimensionality, real-time environments — not just flat DOM-based tools — as long as you design tool schemas around grounded, structured state (exact coordinates, block IDs, bounding boxes) rather than relying on visual guesswork. 
 Good tool design for an agent is really game design: things like batching, animation delays, undo buffers, and clamped movement aren't just nice-to-haves, they're what make an agent's actions feel safe and legible to a human watching alongside it. 
 The current AI tooling ecosystem (IDEs, coding assistants) lags behind emerging web standards like WebMCP, so early adopters need to be ready to write very explicit, spec-referencing prompts and expect some confused detours (like an assistant trying to spin up an MCP server when what's needed is browser-side tool registration). 
 Exposing a standard postMessage JSON-RPC bridge alongside the native ModelContext interface paid off — it means any MCP-aware client, not just ones that know about our specific game, can plug in immediately. 
 

 What's next for Minecraft WebMCP player 

 
 Expand the tool catalog further — crafting recipes, farming/automation tools, redstone-like logic, and multiplayer-aware tools so multiple agents and players can coordinate in the same world. 
 Improve agent "situational awareness" tools (e.g., pathfinding queries, structural stability checks) so agents can plan more ambitious builds autonomously. 
 Work with browser vendors and the WebMCP community to help shape the spec based on real lessons learned from a complex, real-time 3D use case.

title: Domain Tools for WebMCP
pitch: The layer Shopify can't ship: domain tools + a knowledge playbook that let AI agents get expert advice on two real stores — live on tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com.
about_excerpt: The layer Shopify can't ship: domain tools + a knowledge playbook that let AI agents get expert advice on two real stores — live on tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration On Aug 5, Shopify made a million storefronts agent-ready overnight — identical catalog/cart/checkout WebMCP tools everywhere. The question that interested us: what does an agent still fail at on a real store? Answer: everything a human clerk knows. "Which tape for plantar fasciitis if I sweat a lot?" returned nothing useful. What it does On tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com, document.modelContext.getTools() returns 15 tools each: Shopify's 10 defaults + 5 domain tools that encode merchant expertise — injury-to-product recommendation with taping-guide URLs, kids nasal-strip sizing with medical guardrails, hat sizing by head circumference, duties/shipping by country, wholesale tiers. Read-only, data-driven, with an on-page results panel so the human sees what their agent did, and GA4 telemetry (webmcp_tool_call) because server analytics can't see WebMCP. We also rebuilt the knowledge layer Shopify's own FAQ tool reads: 7 to 77 answers (TapeGeeks) and 0 to 45 (GearTOP), mined from the query log, our blogs' FAQPage schema, Google People-Also-Ask, and Reddit. Two doors, one brain TapeGeeks also runs "Tappy," a human-facing AI chat concierge (a Storefront MCP client — proprietary, not part of this submission's code). The WebMCP tools are the second door into the same knowledge: Tappy serves humans conversationally, the WebMCP tools serve the visitor's own agent instantly at $0 per call — and both read the same data file. Update webmcp-data.json once (a price, a sizing rule, a shipping fact) and the human door and the agent door stay in sync. How we built it Vanilla JS registered via registerTool(tool, {signal}) with one AbortController per group; decision tables in a JSON asset (edit data, not code); tight schemas (enum, required, additionalProperties:false); descriptions written as instructions with explicit negative cases ("Do NOT use for cart — Shopify's update_cart does that") so a model picks correctly among 15 tools. Shipped as Shopify theme assets via the Admin API. A Node harness stubs modelContext and tests every tool. Challenges The old navigator.modelContext.provideContext draft is everywhere in tutorials and dead since March; argument shapes changed mid-build with Shopify's UCP migration; and the live theme turned out to hard-code its widgets, so app-extension deploys silently did nothing — we ship straight into the theme. Accomplishments Live on two real revenue-producing stores, verified end-to-end in Chrome; a store "mystery-shopper" journey eval that went 3-stalled-of-5 to 5-of-5 completed; a reusable MIT-licensed pattern any Shopify merchant can adapt in a day. What we learned The moat isn't tool plumbing — it's encoded domain knowledge and description quality. And the knowledge layer (the FAQ tool's data) matters as much as custom tools: it's what every agent quotes. What's next Description tuning against real agent traffic via the GA4 events; a generator that builds a store's domain tools from its own blog FAQPage schema automatically. Try it: open tapegeeks.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser and ask: "I have plantar fasciitis and sweat a lot — which tape should I buy, and how do I apply it?" title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Tangible Coding Studio: Mission Builder
pitch: A WebMCP-powered studio where primary teachers and AI agents co-create, adapt, validate and review screen-light tangible coding missions on one shared visual lesson canvas.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered studio where primary teachers and AI agents co-create, adapt, validate and review screen-light tangible coding missions on one shared visual lesson canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Teachers set the class context: stage, class size, lesson duration and computational-thinking focus. Available robots, tiles, mats and instruction packs determine grouping and rotation. The shared canvas turns accepted context into a structured mission across all four learning-cycle stages. Learner supports and extension challenges are reviewed separately from the core mission. WebMCP proposals stay pending until the teacher accepts, edits or rejects each operation. Deterministic validation reports 13 checks. Ready for teacher review is not approval. Accepted lesson content becomes a printable Teacher Guide preview. The printable Observation Checklist supports observation without inventing evidence. Inspiration Primary teachers who want to teach computational thinking through physical, screen-light activities face a complicated planning task. A usable lesson has to connect the curriculum goal, class size, lesson duration, available robots and tiles, learner differences, group participation and observable assessment evidence. A conventional AI chatbot can generate a lesson plan, but it normally works outside the teacher’s planning interface. It does not automatically share the application’s accepted class context, may rewrite too much when only one section needs changing, can overlook physical equipment limits, or present generated text without a clear human review boundary. We created Tangible Coding Studio: Mission Builder to explore a different relationship: a primary teacher and an AI agent working on the same structured lesson canvas through WebMCP. The agent can understand the available actions and propose precise changes, while the teacher remains the authority over every accepted lesson decision. What it does Mission Builder supports a seven-step teacher workflow covering: Class context Tangible resources and grouping Mission design Learner support and extension The tangible learning cycle Proposal review Deterministic validation The production application registers exactly five WebMCP tools: set_class_context select_tangible_resources build_tangible_mission adapt_for_learners validate_and_prepare_lesson The first four tools do not directly overwrite accepted lesson content. They create section-scoped pending proposals. The teacher can inspect each operation and then accept it, edit and accept it, or reject it. The fifth tool runs the same deterministic validator available in the visible interface. Validation can mark a lesson Ready for teacher review , but it cannot approve the lesson. Teacher approval and prepared-file generation are intentionally not implemented in this challenge prototype. The Preview workspace derives three browser views from currently accepted content only: Teacher Guide Pupil Mission Card Observation Checklist Pending and rejected proposal content is excluded. Native printing can print the currently selected browser preview, but no PDF-generation or prepared-output service is claimed. Why WebMCP fits this use case WebMCP changes the collaboration from “copy text out of a chatbot” into structured work on a live web application. The key shift is that the agent moves from outside the teacher’s workflow to operating through typed tools against the same structured lesson state. The browser exposes a small, purpose-built set of tools with typed schemas and meaningful descriptions. The agent can select the correct action, return a portable structured proposal and operate against the lesson’s current accepted context. The teacher can see exactly what is proposed inside the product before anything becomes authoritative. This makes several things possible together that are difficult in an ordinary chatbot workflow: The agent works with the application’s real class, equipment and lesson structure. Changes are section-scoped rather than uncontrolled full-document rewrites. Accepted content and proposed content remain separate. Context fingerprints detect stale downstream proposals. Every accepted contribution retains teacher/AI provenance. Validation checks the accepted lesson rather than the agent’s unreviewed draft. The manual workflow remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on chat box. It is the collaboration boundary between a browser agent and a teacher-controlled lesson state. Demonstration scenario For our public demonstration, we use The Lost Story Path, a fictional P4 literacy lesson designed for 24 pupils and a 45-minute session. The class has three robots, nine tile sets, three activity mats, three instruction-card packs and 24 role cards. Working in groups, pupils plan a route through a story, arrange the instructions in sequence and test their route using either a robot or a tile-only walkthrough. When they find the mixed-up instruction, they explain what went wrong and how their change repairs the story. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can suggest learner supports and extension activities using the lesson’s actual class context and resources. These suggestions never enter the lesson automatically: the teacher reviews each proposed change and decides whether to accept, edit or reject it. Once the accepted lesson is complete, it passes all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings. Its status becomes Ready for teacher review, and the teacher can preview a Teacher Guide, Pupil Mission Card and Observation Checklist based only on accepted content. How we built it The application is a browser-local Vite, React and TypeScript prototype. Zod validates WebMCP inputs and portable proposal packages. The accepted lesson, proposal history, validation result and provenance are stored in browser localStorage for the exact origin. The proposal model supports operation-level review and atomic acceptance. Downstream proposal packages can bind to a SHA-256 fingerprint of copied accepted context so stale packages are rejected instead of silently applied to a changed lesson. The same domain validation logic is used by both the visible Validate workspace and the WebMCP validation tool. The Preview workspace reads accepted lesson state only and does not create a second output state. The public application is deployed on Vercel and the complete challenge source is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. Tangible Coding Ltd’s trademarks, commercial curriculum, hardware designs and other excluded commercial materials are outside the challenge repository’s licence scope. Challenges we faced Preserving human authority The hardest design decision was ensuring that a successful agent call never meant that lesson content had already been accepted. Tool execution may create pending proposal state, but only an explicit teacher action can move a proposed operation into accepted lesson content. Moving context safely between agent and teacher browsers Browser-local storage is intentionally origin- and profile-specific. We created portable proposal packages and accepted-context packages so the teacher controls what moves between contexts. Versioned packages, structural “before” values and context fingerprints protect against stale imports. Recovering a lesson without bypassing review During testing we restored a lesson from portable proposal evidence. The mission operations and learner adaptations were imported as pending changes and accepted individually. This demonstrated that recovery could preserve the teacher-review boundary instead of importing an authoritative lesson snapshot. Keeping readiness separate from approval The validator can determine that required planning information is present, durations match and resource/grouping conditions are feasible. It still reports Ready for teacher review rather than “approved.” This distinction is visible across Validate, Preview and the WebMCP result. Verified production result On 31 August 2026, we tested the complete workflow in production using a WebMCP-capable browser agent. The agent discovered and successfully used all five registered WebMCP tools. Across the session, the teacher reviewed and individually accepted 13 proposed changes. The completed lesson then passed all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings, and all three accepted-content previews rendered correctly. We also refreshed the application to confirm that the lesson, resources, proposal history, authorship information and validation result were retained. The lesson remained Ready for teacher review, not approved. This is an important part of the design: the agent can help create and improve the lesson, but the teacher remains responsible for every accepted decision. title: Merchant Stock Rescue
pitch: An agent finds the stock. A merchant keeps the authority.
about_excerpt: An agent finds the stock. A merchant keeps the authority. Like Comment Story Updates Story / problem Independent merchants lose sales when a nearby shop has the item but their own shelf is empty. Finding a source, checking details, and coordinating a transfer is repetitive operational work, but silently moving stock is a consequential action that should remain under merchant control. Solution Merchant Stock Rescue exposes five WebMCP tools for discovery, source inspection, transfer preparation, commit, and status verification. The agent can do the research and prepare a proposal in the visible console. The proposal remains pending until a merchant explicitly approves it in the UI; only then can the agent commit it. Every transition appears in an audit timeline and the commit returns a transaction receipt. How it was built Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. A deterministic browser-local external store is shared by the UI and WebMCP handlers. Candidate ranking uses price, distance, pickup time, and reliability. The tests cover tool contracts and the pending → approved/rejected → committed state machine. The project includes a real-browser registration harness; Chrome Inspector/WebMCP manual testing is not claimed. Challenges The central challenge was designing a useful agent workflow without allowing an agent to bypass human authorization. The approval bit is recorded by the UI in shared state, and commit rejects every proposal that is not both approved and in the approved state. Repeatable seed data and structured error codes make the safety boundary easy to demonstrate. Accomplishments Exactly five narrowly scoped WebMCP tools. A visible, deterministic approval gate that blocks pre-approval commit. Idempotency and stale-stock protections for commit. An auditable activity timeline and receipt after commit. A polished, repeatable demo with unit coverage. What we learned Tool descriptions and schemas are part of the product contract, not incidental glue. Separating preparation from authorization makes an agent useful while keeping high-impact authority legible to a human. A shared state model also makes UI behavior and tool behavior testable together. What’s next Connect authenticated merchant inventory APIs, add durable transfer records and multi-merchant permissions, and integrate fulfillment/payment workflows while preserving explicit approval and auditability. Testing instructions npm install npm test npm run build For the demo, run npm run dev , use a compatible Chrome WebMCP flag in a secure context, prepare a proposal, attempt commit before approval (expect HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED ), approve in the UI, then commit and verify the receipt. title: Sift
pitch: Decision infrastructure where people and AI agents co-drive one live case, with evidence, uncertainty, and final approval kept human.
about_excerpt: Decision infrastructure where people and AI agents co-drive one live case, with evidence, uncertainty, and final approval kept human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A chat window is great for conversation. It is a poor place to hold a living decision. As a decision gets more complicated, the options, priorities, evidence, tradeoffs, and unanswered questions get buried in an increasingly long conversation. Every new concern produces another answer, but nothing reorganizes around what changed. The person sees messages, the model sees context, and neither has a shared surface where the decision itself can take shape. We wanted to explore what becomes possible when ChatGPT and a web application can do more than exchange text. What if ChatGPT could turn a conversation into a live, visual workspace, and then keep reshaping that workspace as the person's thinking evolves? That idea became Sift. Sift creates a dedicated, adaptive workspace for each decision — something closer to an interactive chalkboard than a form or a chatbot. Options become objects that both the person and the model can manipulate, priorities become weighted criteria, evidence attaches to the claims it supports, unknowns stay visible, and comparisons reorganize as the question changes. WebMCP is what makes the interaction genuinely two-way. Sift exposes the current workspace, evidence, ranking, and available actions to ChatGPT through typed capabilities, and ChatGPT can change the workspace in return: focusing attention, configuring views, adding information, introducing new decision dimensions, and initiating deeper investigation. Those changes flow back into Sift's deterministic analysis and become immediately visible to both sides. The result is not a chatbot bolted onto an application — it is an interaction model where conversation and interface continuously shape one another. What it does Sift is a shared decision workspace for people and AI agents. Our demonstration follows a family comparing vehicles, but the system is domain-generic: each case begins with a versioned Decision Pack supplying the initial vocabulary, criteria, evidence requirements, and investigation capabilities, and from there the workspace adapts to the person rather than forcing the person into a fixed form. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can: Inspect the exact case, options, criteria, evidence, selection, ranking, and workspace state the person is currently looking at. Add or update options and populate their structured attributes. Add, remove, or reweight the criteria driving the decision. Select and focus options, evidence, or unanswered questions. Switch between purpose-built views and configure which options and fields appear in a comparison. Add notes, submit sources, evaluate evidence, and request deeper investigation. Read Sift's own deterministic ranking and criterion-level explanation instead of inventing a separate analysis. Define entirely new case-specific attributes that neither the application nor the Decision Pack ever anticipated. That last capability is the one we most wanted to demonstrate, so the demo turns on it twice. Our buyer has an 18-month-old and a second child due in three months, and partway through the conversation he raises a concern the pack has no field for: whether a rear-facing child seat fits behind the driver without pushing the driver's seat forward. No manufacturer publishes that number, and the interface was never designed to hold it. ChatGPT turns that sentence into structure. It defines a typed custom attribute, declares which options it applies to, specifies the allowed values, and — critically — supplies an explicit worst-to-best ordering, because Sift will not assume that ["does not fit", "fits", "fits with room to spare"] is ordered simply because it arrived as an array. It then populates the attribute across all four vehicles, and every applicable option must receive either a real value or an explicit unknown . The model cannot leave an empty cell or invent a value to make the comparison look complete. In the demo the Outback comes back "fits with room to spare," the RAV4 "fits with driver seat back," the CX-5 "driver seat must move forward" — and the CR-V comes back explicitly unknown rather than guessed. That unknown then survives into the ranking as reduced evidence coverage instead of being quietly scored as zero. ChatGPT then adds the new attribute as a weighted criterion and configures the workspace to display it. The decision has gained a dimension while it is already in progress, without a developer changing the application — and Sift's scoring engine incorporates it and recalculates immediately, with no further model call. In the recording the buyer's current pick drops from second of four at 67% to third at 64%, and the Subaru Outback takes the lead. Later in the same session the model repeats the whole pattern for a second concern, in-car software platform, and reconfigures the comparison view to show it. The ranking is computed deterministically from the criteria and evidence stored in the case, under rules that hold regardless of what the model does: Missing information reduces evidence coverage; it is never scored as zero. Conflicting evidence stays visibly disputed. A hard-constraint violation flags an option but never silently removes it. Mixed currencies, incompatible units, free text, and unordered qualitative values are refused rather than coerced into a misleading number. Every score can be explained criterion by criterion, and Sift can name the single criterion that actually causes one option to outrank another. The ranking the person sees is the same ranking ChatGPT reads and the same one used to validate the recommendation. Together this forms a continuous loop: the person raises a concern in conversation, ChatGPT turns it into a structured part of the workspace, Sift recomputes the ranking and exposes what changed, ChatGPT reads that new state and decides what still needs investigation, the workspace updates as evidence arrives — and the person keeps the final decision. Behind the workspace, a Strands Graph coordinates six specialist agents across three stages. Four analysts investigate in parallel, a source challenger examines weak or conflicting evidence, and a decision synthesizer proposes a recommendation, with skills and context activating only when the work requires them. The model can reshape the workspace and start investigations, but it cannot approve the decision. There is no hidden approval endpoint and no disabled approval tool in the WebMCP catalog — the capability does not exist for ChatGPT at all. The demo shows this directly: asked to approve the purchase, the model reaches for a review tool and the host answers that no such tool is registered. Only the person can close the case. How we built it Sift is a TypeScript monorepo: a React and Vite web application, an Express service, a deterministic domain core, SQLite persistence, and a multi-agent runtime built on the Strands Agents SDK. The web application registers 26 bounded, schema-validated tools through document.modelContext . Those tools are not a parallel automation layer. Actions taken through WebMCP and actions taken through the visible interface run the same command implementation against the same case and produce the same domain events, so a change made in chat appears in the workspace and a change made in the workspace is immediately available to ChatGPT. We organized the capabilities into complementary forms of control: Shared awareness — read the active case, options, criteria, ranking, evidence, research, notes, and interaction state. Shared attention — focus an option, evidence item, or question so the person and the model are looking at the same thing. Workspace configuration — change views and configure comparisons without changing the underlying criteria. Structured mutation — add options, attributes, notes, sources, evidence dispositions, and weighted criteria. Dynamic schema extension — define and populate new case-specific attributes at runtime. Bounded delegation — request investigation or revision through the supervised Strands runtime. Every canonical mutation is recorded as an append-only domain event and committed transactionally alongside the latest case snapshot, with server-sent events updating the browser as case state and investigation results change. Mutating tools carry an expectedSequence , so a stale write is rejected rather than silently overwriting newer state — the recorded demo contains a real conflict, where the model's write is refused, it re-reads the case, and retries successfully. The architecture deliberately gives each part of the system one job. WebMCP gives ChatGPT structured access to the live workspace; ChatGPT interprets intent and decides how to adapt it; Sift's deterministic core owns case state, ranking, evidence rules, and readiness; the Strands runtime performs bounded multi-agent investigation; and
