title: Cartwright — WebMCP-native storefronts
pitch: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's.
about_excerpt: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is, and why WebMCP (the use case) In-browser AI agents act on websites by guessing at the DOM — brittle selectors, scraping, silent failures, no way to verify what happened. WebMCP fixes that at the platform level: the page declares tools, the agent calls them. But it only matters if sites actually implement it, and hand-wiring agent tools for every page of every site does not scale. Cartwright is an open-source (MIT) engine that scaffolds complete stores — design system, database, cart, checkout, admin, i18n — with one command. During the challenge window we made the engine WebMCP-native : webshop templates now scaffold with the surface ON ( npx create-cartwright my-shop --template coffee → a store whose every page registers typed, page-contextual tools via document.modelContext the moment an agent-capable browser opens it). Not one agent-ready site — a generator of them. Shopify has shown storefront-scale WebMCP for its hosted platform; this is the same idea for the self-hosted, open-source world: the whole engine is MIT, and every scaffold owns its stack. WebMCP leverage — the depth of the surface 13 tools on the demo shop, three registration styles, one shared core: Site-wide (imperative): search_products (reduced, bounded rows — no checkout endpoints or internal fields ever enter the browser surface), get_cart (verification-rich returns: line handles, stock ceilings, structured money), same-origin navigate . Contextual, per route — progressive disclosure (the shape proposed in the tool-collections discussion, webmcp#255): an agent only ever sees the collection that makes sense on the page it is on. The product page registers add_current_product_to_cart with the page's live variants as natural-language enum values ("Whole beans, 250 g" — not internal ids), prices and stock in the descriptor. The cart page registers update_cart_item_quantity / remove_cart_item (line ids enumerated in the schema) / go_to_checkout . The catalogue page registers list_visible_products (exactly what the human sees, zero network) and filter_products (schema server-derived from the live categories). Declarative forms: search, contact and newsletter carry toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes — the form itself is the tool, answered via SubmitEvent.respondWith (preventDefault-first). toolautosubmit only on read-only search; the human confirms communication. Agent activity is visible : :tool-form-active styling highlights the form the agent is filling. Design-pack tools: the homepage brew calculator is also calculate_brew_ratio — the same math module serves the human's widget and the agent's tool, so the two can never disagree. Any design pack can ship tools ( DesignPack.webMcpToolBindings ); the safety tests aggregate them all. The engine also answers the frameworks meta-issue (webmcp#199) in shipped, test-pinned code: execute() reads state freshly at execution time (never captured props); effect dependencies are serialized props, so re-renders never thrash the registry; every mount owns an AbortSignal and cleanup runs before the next route's registrations (abort-then-register, the current-spec-safe order — our e2e fake rejects duplicate names, and a soft-navigation spec proves the swap inside one document); one rejecting registration cannot drop the tools after it. One governed tool registry, two transports: the same operations back the in-page WebMCP tools for browsing agents and a server-side MCP endpoint ( /api/mcp ) for headless agents — same session, same state in the browser; same scopes and audit trail on the server. Beneath the callable layer sits the readable and discoverable one: llms.txt with capability truth, JSON-LD on every citable page, content negotiation (the homepage serves markdown to agents that ask), an ARD catalog, OpenAPI — and on the payable side the engine carries protocol-pluralistic commerce rails (ACP endpoints and UCP identity-linking on the same engine), so the merchant doesn't have to bet. Readable, discoverable, callable, payable — one engine. Execution — a complete product, tested like one This is a production Next.js 16 App Router application deployed on Vercel: a real store with a live database, working cart and checkout, an admin, and i18n — not a mock. The WebMCP layer is held to the same bar: ~100 unit tests across the registrar, the per-route mounts, the declarative forms, the pack tool, and the safety moat (below). A Playwright e2e suite installs a faithful fake document.modelContext (current spec semantics: duplicate-name rejection, pre-aborted-signal rejection) and walks home → catalogue → product → cart → checkout, including one real add-to-cart round-trip against the database and a soft-navigation leg that proves route teardown inside one document. Evaluation-driven, with the Chrome team's own harness: we ran GoogleChromeLabs/webmcp-tools' webmcp-evals (smoke mode) against the live demo — 12/12 steps green across brew-ratio, cart reads, catalogue listing/filtering, search, a real add-to-cart and the checkout handoff (runner webmcp-evals@0.0.3 , repo commit d39eae4 , 2026-08-27). The run's three genuine findings (a prefetch loop on the empty-cart page, non-canonical URLs in two tool returns, Danish parameter names on an English store) were fixed the same day — the eval harness caught real bugs, which is the point of running it. Byte-identity discipline: with the flag off, no registrar mounts, no tool* attribute renders, the HTML is byte-identical — pinned by tests. The live surface is smoke-monitored : the store's deployment gate asserts /en/webmcp-check and the pack tool on every run. Potential impact — who this is for Every small store that will never hand-write agent tools. The economics only work at the engine level: implement WebMCP once, correctly, with tests — and every scaffolded site inherits it. The demo is a real storefront a judge can buy from (demo checkout), running the exact code a scaffold produces. And the scaffold proves it in a first minute: npx create-cartwright myshop --template coffee && cd myshop && npm run dev seeds the demo's own nine-product catalogue — images, stock, attributes, and real variants on one product (an agent must handle both shapes) — so the tools have something true to act on with no config and no API keys. The same engine runs a second live vertical (eyewear, different design pack, Danish locale) — the surface is engine-level, not bespoke to one demo. Creativity & ambition — the line we drew The collaboration model is explicit: the agent gets the errands, the human keeps the decisions. Every cart mutation returns the fresh cart, so the agent verifies instead of assumes; an ambiguous mid-request failure says so and routes the agent through get_cart before any retry. Communication forms never autosubmit — the agent fills, the human sees the copper glow on the form, the human confirms. The purchase is deliberately out of the agent's hands: a test-enforced safety moat holds the entire browser surface — across the layout, every per-route mount, and every registered design pack — to the cart/catalogue tool families. No order-placing tool exists in the browser. go_to_checkout opens the page; the checkout form is annotated for no one. Graceful handoff, in the commerce-protocol sense: the agent escorts the human to the door it cannot open. /en/webmcp-check documents the shop's own agent surface — generated from the same constants the moat test verifies, so the page structurally cannot lie — with an intent-first explorer ("I want to… → the tool + a copyable example") and the Chrome team's polyfill as fallback so it demonstrates in any browser. And the agent-experience layer is measured, not asserted: every change to the store's agent surface (WebMCP, MCP, llms.txt, discovery files) ships through tests + live smoke, and the store publishes machine-readable pricing, auth and capability truth alongside the tools. Prior work vs. this submission (per the rules) The engine — storefront, cart, checkout, admin, server-side MCP/REST APIs — pre-exists the challenge, as does a four-tool WebMCP experiment from June 2026 (v0.25.0: global search/add/get-cart/navigate behind a flag). The entire WebMCP surface submitted here was designed and built inside the submission window (Aug 27 – Sep 3, 2026): the shared registration core, contextual per-route tools, declarative form annotations, catalogue tools with server-derived schemas, design-pack tools with registry-aggregated safety tests, the moat, the e2e suite, the eval run, /webmcp-check , and the WebMCP-native scaffold default. title: MetaWebMCP
pitch: WebMCP builds WebMCP. Turn observable website workflows into bounded, reusable WebMCP tools. Then activate, test, and export them.
about_excerpt: WebMCP builds WebMCP. Turn observable website workflows into bounded, reusable WebMCP tools. Then activate, test, and export them. Like Comment Story Updates Small test in ChatGPT ChatGPT using MetaWebMCP to find games on steam ChatGPT using the tool to find properties in Finca Raiz Inspiration As new standards and protocols come, adoption is key. WebMCP gives agents a clean, semantic way to interact with websites, but most of the web will not add native integrations overnight. We wanted to see whether compatibility could grow from the other direction: let an agent observe an existing workflow, give it a narrow WebMCP interface, use it immediately, and export it as a native integration later. What it does MetaWebMCP is WebMCP that builds WebMCP. It turns the useful, observable parts of a website into bounded, reusable tools. An agent can inspect a site, define tools grounded in its interface, activate them on the current page, test them, and export the same contracts as a standalone WebMCP repository. How we built it We built MetaWebMCP through a lot of small iterations. We intentionally kept the architecture lightweight so we could focus on the hard problem of creating a useful compatibility layer between existing websites and WebMCP. The core runs on Node.js without runtime package dependencies. A permanent set of seven meta-tools handles analysis, contract creation, activation, testing, export, state inspection, and reset. Activating a project dynamically registers a second set of domain tools on the same top-level page. One of our most important decisions was to use the same ToolSpec objects for live activation, execution, testing, and export. The exported integration is not a separate code-generation demo. It is another representation of the exact contracts the agent reviewed and used. For public websites, MetaWebMCP uses an isolated browser session to capture the rendered page and its accessibility model. For owned sites, it exports a standalone repository containing direct document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. It also includes a fallback registry so the complete workflow remains usable in ordinary browsers without native WebMCP support. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was, of course, not generating code. It was finding the right boundary between brittle browser automation and a useful semantic tool. Real websites are messy. Controls may be ambiguous, inaccessible, repeated, dynamically rendered, or changed without warning. We had to ground every generated tool in observed evidence while refusing to expose arbitrary JavaScript or unrestricted browser operations. The recursive lifecycle was another challenge. MetaWebMCP needs to keep its permanent tools active while safely adding, replacing, and removing generated tools. It also needs the live implementation and exported implementation to behave consistently. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of The main accomplishment is that MetaWebMCP is legitimately useful. It is not only a recursive gimmick built for a hackathon. In our native test, the page exposed seven permanent WebMCP tools, dynamically expanded to eleven, passed all four generated-tool checks, and exported a standalone repository whose tools continued to work without MetaWebMCP as the runtime. Our limited benchmarks also produced a concrete result. Across the matched tests, MetaWebMCP reduced model-facing tool text by 4.11× to 57.31× and non-cached token usage by 1.28× to 6.81×. It was also 1.39× to 2.18× faster on the larger, multi-page workloads. It was slower on one shorter, single-page task because the initial analysis and tool-authoring cost did not have time to amortize. That counterexample matters. The strongest result is not that MetaWebMCP always makes an agent faster, but that a small semantic interface can keep large amounts of repetitive browser output out of the agent’s context. What we learned Agents have come a long way. They can now inspect an unfamiliar interface, reason about its useful capabilities, shape those capabilities into typed contracts, and use the resulting tools without requiring a separate model API inside the application. A weaker version of this was already possible some years ago, with a lot of issues, but now the agents seem to get it consistently, enough for tools like this to exist. What's next for MetaWebMCP The next step is to develop MetaWebMCP into a robust platform with fully managed services, so agents can connect to the existing web reliably through WebMCP. That means persistent and versioned integrations, stronger evaluations, monitoring for interface drift, managed browser execution, better owner-installation workflows, and production-grade controls for authentication, authorization, auditing, and confirmation. The goal remains the same: make WebMCP adoption incremental, practical, and useful across the web. title: Wishlist Concierge
pitch: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists
about_excerpt: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a gift for someone means opening a dozen browser tabs, clicking filters that never quite match your intent, mentally adding up prices, then abandoning the cart when you realize the total blew past your budget. We asked ourselves: what if the storefront could understand "birthday for my nephew" and do the search, curation, and budget math for you while still giving you, the human, full control over what gets added to your cart? What it does Wishlist Concierge exposes 12 imperative WebMCP tools on a Sylius 2.0 storefront, covering the full gift-planning lifecycle: Find products by theme (tags); hard match on tags first, then soft match on product name, then fallback to all channel products Build & curate themed wishlists, add or swap products, reorganize at will Apply a budget constraint using a knapsack algorithm over quantity × ChannelPricing, with active catalog promotions discounts factored in; Return a human-readable explanation of what was chosen and why Move selected items into the Sylius cart and hand you the token to proceed How we built it The entire project is a Sylius 2.0 plugin with the Sylius Wishlist plugin providing the persistence layer. The key architectural choice was single-source-of-truth tool definition: Each tool is declared once via a #[ModelContextTool] attribute on its shop controller action with a name, description, input DTO class, path params, confirm/destructive hints, all in one place. A ModelContextToolCollector service introspects these attributes at compile time, resolves each tool's route via the Symfony router, and produces a JSON manifest. The frontend registry.js fetches that manifest and calls document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, {signal}) for each — so adding a tool means writing a controller method and a DTO, not touching JavaScript at all. Server-side, a ToolContractValidator kernel.request listener deserializes every incoming payload against the DTO's #[Assert] constraints and returns deterministic 422 envelopes on failure. As a bnous, the schema the agent sees is the schema the server enforces. The frontend uses two Stimulus controllers. A toolbox modal that dynamically renders a run form for every registered tool, and a toast controller for live feedback via webmcp:* custom events. Accomplishments that we're proud of The single-source-of-truth tool definition. A tool lives once as a #[ModelContextTool] attribute and that single declaration drives the manifest, the frontend registration, the server-side validation, and the toolbox UI. No duplicate schema, no drift, no manual sync. What we learned WebMCP changes the agent & web relationship. Instead of agents screen-scraping your UI, you hand them structured tools with typed schemas. That means better agents (clear contracts) and safer apps (no ambiguous click paths). Single source of truth is everything for developer experience. When a tool is defined in one place and everything else is derived, adding a new tool is a 5-minute task. Structured error shapes make agents better. Once the server returns {"error":"Validation failed", "message":"...", "violations":[{field,message}]}, the agent can reason about what went wrong and fix its next call - the feedback loop closes. What's next for Wishlist Concierge Real-world testing Extend the knapsack algorithm to consider stock levels and quantity discounts, not just unit price × quantity. title: webclerk
pitch: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates webclerk uses WebMCP to prepare evidence-backed forms while preserving conflicts, uncertainty, and human control. webclerk exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools over live browser state: 7 read & 2 write, with evidence-backed actions & no submit capability. Inspiration AI agents are getting very good at filling forms, navigating websites, and taking actions on behalf of users. But consequential forms create a harder problem: What happens when the agent sounds confident about something the evidence never actually proved? For scholarship applications, insurance claims, benefits, compliance workflows, and similar processes, a plausible answer is not necessarily a supported answer. That led to the core idea behind webclerk : Evidence > confidence. The agent prepares. The human commits. webclerk explores what happens when a website does not merely expose capabilities to an AI agent, but also defines the boundaries of the agent's authority. What it does webclerk is a WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms . Instead of giving an agent unrestricted access to form fields, the website exposes semantic tools backed by deterministic trust rules. Every field can remain in one of several meaningful states: Verified — supported by current, accepted evidence Needs confirmation — plausible, but requires the applicant Conflict — the form and evidence disagree Human-only — the agent is not authorized to decide or attest it The agent can safely prepare the application while uncertainty stays visible. In the scholarship workflow, the agent can: inspect the current application state read supporting evidence find evidence-backed values explain why a field is unresolved check consistency run preflight checks request approval before making supported edits The site exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools: 7 read tools and 2 write tools . There is deliberately no submission tool . Truthfulness declarations and final submission stay with the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is not an add-on to webclerk. It is the interaction model. The browser page exposes semantic capabilities such as: get_application_state fill_verified_fields_from_evidence inspect_field list_evidence suggest_field_value set_field_value find_missing_information check_consistency run_preflight These tools operate over the same live browser state the user sees . That means the agent does not need brittle DOM scraping or coordinate-based automation to understand the application. More importantly, the website itself controls what the agent is allowed to do. Writes pass through deterministic authorization rules before the visible form state can change. Live scholarship proof The scholarship demo begins at approximately 70% completion . When prompted: Fill everything you can verify from my documents. Don't guess anything. the agent identifies six evidence-backed fields and requests approval before writing. After approval: completion moves from 70% to 96% verified fields increase from 3 to 9 6 evidence-backed agent edits are made 0 unsupported guesses are made 0 consequential agent actions are performed Every agent mutation is visibly attributed to WebMCP. But the more important behavior is what webclerk refuses to do. For example, the enrollment certificate proves that the applicant is enrolled, but it does not establish whether the mode of study is full-time, part-time, or something else. webclerk leaves that field unresolved instead of inferring it. Conflicts stay conflicts The scholarship form intentionally contains an income conflict: application value: ₹3,50,000 supporting evidence: ₹3,20,000 webclerk does not silently choose one. The field remains blocked and preflight surfaces the conflict for human review. The system also detects stale evidence and preserves applicant-confirmation fields instead of promoting them into verified facts. The principle is simple: Blocked, not guessed. Human authority Some actions should not be delegated simply because an agent is technically capable of interacting with the page. webclerk therefore treats actions such as truthfulness declarations as human-only. If the agent attempts to perform a protected action, the trust layer rejects it. Final submission is even more explicit: there is no submit_application capability exposed through WebMCP. The absence of that capability is intentional. Proving the architecture generalizes I did not want webclerk to be a scholarship-specific automation script. So I built a second live workflow: a motor insurance claim . It uses the same trust engine and the same WebMCP tool factory, but with insurance-specific domain rules and evidence. The agent safely prepares: claimant name policy number vehicle registration incident date while preserving a deliberate repair-estimate conflict: form: ₹85,000 evidence: ₹78,500 Fault admission, incident narrative, and truthfulness remain under human authority. This demonstrates the underlying idea: Same engine. Same WebMCP layer. Different consequential workflow. How I built it webclerk is a browser-first TypeScript application with a reusable deterministic trust engine. The implementation separates: workflow data and evidence deterministic trust rules agent authority policy WebMCP semantic tools shared browser state human-facing provenance and preflight UI The WebMCP tool factory is reusable across both the scholarship and insurance workflows. The project also includes automated tests for: safe evidence-backed writes stale evidence conflicting evidence human-confirmation fields human-only actions tool metadata WebMCP read/write classification machine-readable authority rules adversarial agent behavior cross-domain generalization Challenges The hardest part was not getting an agent to fill a form. The hard part was defining when it must not fill one. That required treating uncertainty, stale evidence, conflict, provenance, and human authority as first-class states rather than edge cases. Another challenge was making those constraints useful without making the agent useless. The goal was not to block automation. The goal was to maximize safe preparation while preserving the decisions that genuinely belong to a person. What I learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when websites expose more than actions. A semantic tool can communicate: what the agent can do what evidence supports an action whether approval is required why an action is blocked and what authority the agent does not possess That changes the relationship between websites and agents. Instead of an agent trying to infer what a page permits from its DOM, the website can participate directly in defining the collaboration model. What's next The current project demonstrates scholarship and motor-insurance workflows, but the trust model can extend to other consequential processes such as: financial aid government benefits visa applications compliance forms healthcare administration regulated onboarding The long-term idea is a reusable trust layer where AI agents can do substantial preparatory work while evidence, uncertainty, provenance, and human authority remain explicit. Autofill is easy. Authority is hard. webclerk is an experiment in making that authority programmable. title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: Previz
pitch: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame.
about_excerpt: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame. Like Comment Story Updates Project Story About the project Previz is a browser-based 3D blocking and camera previsualization tool built for human–agent collaboration. Directors can stage characters, animate cameras, mark important positions, and describe creative goals in natural language. A WebMCP-enabled agent can then inspect the complete scene, propose a shot plan, calculate precise trajectories, validate them, and update the visible project. Inspiration Film previsualization tools are powerful, but turning an idea like “follow the character, hide the second performer, then reveal both in one continuous shot” into animation often requires manually editing hundreds of positions, rotations, and keyframes. We wanted to explore a more natural workflow: the human directs while the agent handles calculation. Instead of controlling the interface through fragile mouse coordinates, the agent receives structured access to the same scene the director sees. WebMCP made that relationship possible. What it does Previz provides a browser-based workspace for: Adding and positioning characters and cameras in a 3D scene Creating character and camera keyframes on a timeline Previewing the selected camera in real time Adding world-space and camera-space annotations Importing scene geometry and changing its visualization style Saving, importing, and autosaving project data Exporting camera previews as video Exposing the project to agents through WebMCP The accompanying previz-director Codex skill turns directorial intent into validated character blocking and camera motion. It reads the scene, discusses a creative plan with the user, calculates trajectories, checks continuity and safety, and writes the approved result back into the editor. How we built it The interactive editor uses Three.js and WebGL for the scene, characters, camera frustums, lighting, imported geometry, transform controls, and real-time camera previews. The timeline and editing interface are implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The application is packaged with React, Vinext, Vite, and Cloudflare’s runtime tooling so it can run locally or as a hosted web application. WebMCP is implemented through two tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : read_state returns the complete project and its current revision. write_state accepts a complete project and an expected revision, validates the data, updates the editor, creates an undo snapshot, and autosaves the result. Both tools use JSON Schema. Revision checking prevents an agent from overwriting newer human edits. We also created the previz-director skill, which defines a two-stage workflow: Read the scene and agree on the directorial plan. Calculate, validate, and execute the approved character and camera trajectories. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was connecting creative language to exact 3D motion. A request can be visually clear to a director while leaving many mathematical details unspecified: timing, path shape, camera distance, target transitions, angle continuity, and collision clearance. Camera movement introduced additional problems. Smooth positions do not guarantee smooth framing, and direct look-at calculations can cause sudden rotations during close passes or near-vertical shots. We needed to consider speed, acceleration, angular motion, occlusion, and composition together. Another challenge was safe human–agent collaboration. The agent may spend time calculating a scene while the user continues editing it. Revision-based writes ensure that stale calculations cannot silently replace newer work. Finally, we had to keep the visual editor responsive while rendering multiple views, imported geometry, shadows, annotations, playback, and video exports. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Previz does not treat WebMCP as a remote-control layer. The agent works with meaningful project concepts—characters, cameras, annotations, frames, and trajectories—instead of imitating clicks and drags. Other accomplishments include: Transactional, revision-protected project updates Immediate synchronization between agent writes and the visible editor Per-frame trajectory support for precisely calculated movement A reusable directing skill that separates creative approval from execution World-space and camera-space annotation workflows Browser-based video preview and export Automated coverage across 62 application tests A completely browser-based workflow with no traditional 3D application required What we learned We learned that the strongest agent experiences divide responsibility clearly. Humans are best at narrative intent, taste, rhythm, and deciding what an audience should feel. Agents are valuable when a creative decision expands into hundreds of dependent calculations and consistency checks. We also learned that structured state is much more reliable than visual automation. Giving the agent a small, well-described tool surface produced safer and more understandable behavior than exposing every interface control individually. Most importantly, planning and execution need a clear boundary. Having the agent present its interpretation before writing the scene keeps the user in control and prevents technically valid motion from becoming the wrong creative choice. What's next for Previz Next, we want to add: Adjustable focal length and camera sensor controls Look-at and subject-tracking constraints Editable easing and motion curves Motion paths and onion-skin visualization Keyframe copy and paste More detailed collision and occlusion diagnostics glTF and USD camera export Multi-user and multi-agent collaboration Additional WebMCP tools for targeted, incremental scene operations A reusable library of blocking and cinematography patterns Our long-term goal is to make Previz a shared creative surface where people direct ideas and agents turn those ideas into precise, editable cinematic motion. title: Jibe
pitch: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. Toggle between dev and prod like switching themes: agents use your app in prod and build it in dev. Local-first design keeps your data on your machine.
about_excerpt: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. Toggle between dev and prod like switching themes: agents use your app in prod and build it in dev. Local-first design keeps your data on your machine. Like Comment Story Updates Home origin tracks local installs About DOOM Editor preview Jibe Shell MCP Inspector Inspiration The first thing I thought when I saw the WebMCP spec was: that would be perfect for integrating dev tools into a frontend framework I'm building. Then I started thinking about putting the agentic coding environment itself in the browser. That unlocks a few extremely compelling qualities: The browser is an excellent sandbox. URLs are the easiest sharing mechanism on earth. The browser runtime eliminates an entire class of environment mismatches and runtime failures—things like process.env , missing binaries, incompatible runtimes, and "works on my machine" problems. The bigger idea behind Jibe is that an application doesn't have to be just its built dist/ . A mutable source tree, a runtime, and the capabilities needed to operate on them can travel together as one disposable software environment. WebMCP was the missing piece: Jibe can use WebMCP to build software that itself exposes WebMCP tools. In production, an agent can use the tools built into the application. Flip into development, and that agent can instead get the capabilities it needs to change the application itself. What it does Jibe wraps a web application with a small but pluggable framework that adds the concept of an environment to the browser. It allows for all kinds of interesting designs, but here's what happens in jibe.run when you switch a jibe from PROD to DEV : The service worker switches from serving built dist/ files to rendering the application's src/ . The root layout changes, moving the application from the root surface into a live preview panel inside an IDE environment. Development capabilities become available: a file explorer, editor, hot reload, shell, git, and MCP tools that allow an agent to inspect and modify the application live. The important part is that these are modes of the same environment. Switching between PROD and DEV should feel more like switching a theme than provisioning a new machine. Jibe is "batteries included" and built for people developing local-first applications with agents. You can build an agentic application that exposes WebMCP tools, then flip into development mode and your agent goes from using the tools you just built to building the feature that adds them. Jibe runs local-first using browser storage and can connect with WebMCP-compatible agents or local coding agents using the excellent @mcp-b/webmcp-local-relay package. A jibe hits the jibe.run server on first load to clone and bootstrap a project. After that, it can remain fully functional offline for as long as you want. Navigating to my-custom-app.jibe.run creates a local-first web application and its development environment in seconds. Point your agents at the URL and have fun. How we built it Jibe is structured as a core open-source project and a deployed Solid 2.0 application that consumes it. The core framework uses a plugin and capability model to support many different use cases. Most users will want to consume core plugins for things like: Git Transpiling and building source Local MCP Frontend frameworks Filesystems and storage An application manifest declares which capabilities are available to an environment, following a principle of least privilege. For example, agents can be given a virtual filesystem containing only files that are safe for them to edit rather than direct access to everything. One of my favorite agentic features is the Jibe Shell . Agents get a bash tool that parses shell expressions for viewing and editing files as an ergonomic alternative to a collection of bespoke tools like read_file and edit_file . This also doubles as a terminal surface inside the IDE for users. The shell supports commands that require additional capabilities—effectively sudo commands—which are gated rather than ambient. The result is something I'm pretty excited about: Bash ergonomics without ambient authority. I built this project on my own using Muse Spark 1.X and GLM 5.3 Flash with my trusty OMP and OpenCode harnesses. Lots of back and forth in web chat with Claude and ChatGPT as well. Coding with agents is the best thing ever.* When I needed to pick a bundler, I did a little research and then handed the problem to a subagent to stress-test and benchmark half a dozen different options. The approach I took with this project was to treat the entire project like a harness and make clear distinctions between intent and scratch. An early win was sketching the shape of the system in a messy repository, then treating that prototype as a library for seeding a new repository. Challenges we ran into Iteration. Agent speed is exhausting because, to keep the speed up, you have to keep entropy down. A particularly bad failure mode is agents placing shims and legacy compatibility code all over the place. Agents will hardcode a "fallback" until the fallback becomes the primary mechanism. Agent-written TypeScript is often effectively just verbose JavaScript. These are all antipatterns done in the name of preserving a green test suite, so it's a real challenge to see through the act. Identifying and preventing these failure modes is the primary implementation job. You have to distinguish between code that represents the intended architecture and code that exists because an agent needed to make the next step work. The faster the agents go, the more aggressively you need to manage that distinction. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Jibe Shell and workflows pattern are awesome. I'll be pushing both of these ideas much further. Bash ergonomics minus ambient authority is incredible. Agents already understand the shell as a general-purpose interface for operating on software. Giving them that ergonomics while constraining the capabilities underneath it feels like a very useful primitive. I'm also happy that the core interaction works as a proof of concept: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. An application can expose useful tools to an agent in production. Flip into development mode and the agent gets a different environment with the capabilities required to change the source and build new tools. Flip back to production and those tools become part of the application. What we learned I learned how far the browser has come as a capable operating system. The tradeoffs compared with local development using a non-browser JavaScript runtime are worth seriously considering. The biggest feature in favor of the browser is that it sandboxes the agent extremely well. The big unlock with coding agents locally was allowing them to interface with software in the same way users do. WebMCP promises a similar unlock, with a very important distinction. Operating system evolution has generally assumed the terminal is safe. Browsers, meanwhile, have spent decades evolving under the assumption that users cannot be trusted. That distinction matters when the user is an agent. A browser-native development environment gives us a mature security model for software agents while still exposing the capabilities they need to operate on real software. What's next for Jibe I think Jibe has incredible promise for a wide variety of uses. It is effectively an executable git worktree that provisions from a URL and has better isolation. Fan out jibes for evals or bakeoffs, then visually inspect the results. Make vibe coding social and collaborative. Give Molty $20 and a jibe and see what happens. The roadmap includes: Agents inside of Jibe Secrets Full-stack framework support Jibe registries More plugins and capabilities Contributions and feedback are very welcome. video_transcript_excerpt: Jive.run manages local first applications inside a web browser. Connect an AI assistant to code new features or interact with your production apps. This homepage lists and manages any applications that you created on this browser. Start by forking a starter project and provisioning a unique subdomain. Your agent can connect via WebMCP and supported browsers or by enabling the relay feature and installing the corresponding MCP server on your local agent harness. title: Wornpage Projects
pitch: A human-first work tracker with agentic improvement. Every work item carries a next action. A small extension of a larger paid SaaS work tracker.

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to make an app for project management teams. The app has a next action field; work items could drive an agentic memory ledger, But really, and simply, WebMCP drives the app here. The work tracker can give work (and meaning) to the agent who then drafts tasks and goes through review and human approval. This human-in-the-loop demonstration that I have here was not novel, now, there are a lot of tools out there. I chose the name Wornpage because I wanted the pages to feel well-worn, through simple, repeatable steps. 

 What it does 

 The web interface has pages for work items, review, computed next action. It is a generalists toolkit for deciding what to work on next. The seed data is an every-day occurence, cleaning the house, fixing a toilet (hiring a plumber), etc. 

 Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? 

 What was started as MCPv2 in a private repo was extended here with WebMCP. What this afforded was a new way of looking at the website. Instead of static work item creation, editing and closing, in traditional way (as a CRUD app), we can utilize tools in the browser with WebMCP that offer a unique approach. Working with an agent, building on projects and developing business plans require a workflow that is dependent on human review. WebMCP allows this. 

 How does it create a better user experience? 

 Web creates an experience of open source javascript accessible to people with varying uses, abilities and needs. MCP brings the agentic self improvement to a project workspace. Together, web users and webMCP protocol handlers can work together to harmonize on work and to make the app more accessible. Every step produces a receipt of what was done. Buttons are able to be run by the person, and the person can decide what to do next. AI can also suggest a recommended action, but the person decides what to do next. 

 What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? 

 Self learn from recent decisions, decide on new business ideas. A backend exists at Projects , but it is closed source, and WebMCP was added concurrently to the challenge.). This is a team/enterprise human-in-the loop workspace. 

 How it was built 

 The entry uses SvelteKit and Wornpage design system components I build. It was made using long agent runs to modernize and align with a North Star: the user should be able to open the app and see what to do next. The design system and tools leverage javascript where updating parts of a page based on something else is efficient. What started as vanilla JS was organized into the Svelte routes I have today. The production effort is hosted on Cloudflare workers and leverages digital objects, R2, and many other features in the platform. I wanted this extension to be a publically identifiable extension to it. When I saw that WebMCP existed and this challenge, I immediately knew I could extend the app into this space. 

 How did you implement WebMCP? 

 I used codex on high or max reasoning to implement WebMCP. I had already implemented MCPv2 recently, so the memory of that was useful in designing an extension to my current project with the new protocol. I know that the app is a little bit of a showcase of WebMCP, but I tried my best to make it actually useful. I design components and can hopefully spot areas where the AI used too much meta-commentary, or limit it first through that design. Eventually, this might be moved into a whole other product vertical. I hope the app and the webMCP contracts allow easy rewriting.

 Over the last two days, I substantially rebuilt Wornpage Projects’ WebMCP experience around visible, reproducible human–agent collaboration. 

 The app now exposes nine page-scoped tools across Guide, Priority, Work, Review, and Next: 

 
 Guide derives real workspace scopes and gives the agent an editable, bounded brief. 
 Priority exposes one current recommendation without navigating or changing data. 
 Work lets an agent inspect the rendered workspace, apply a reversible search, or atomically create up to three Draft items. Drafts are never started automatically. 
 Review exposes exact queue evidence and reversible filtering with explicit denominators. 
 Next lets an agent prepare an evidence-backed proposal, but it remains unsaved until a person chooses Save or Discard. 
 

 I also added a global WebMCP status pill and accessible tool-catalog dialog. It shows whether native WebMCP is actually ready, which tools are registered on the current page, and what authority each tool has. 

 Agent actions now appear in a branch-aware Verified action trail. Read, scope, and preparation receipts are recorded, while the final human decision remains visibly pending rather than being falsely marked complete. 

 Beyond the WebMCP layer, I split large Work, Review, and Next route implementations into smaller focused components, consolidated shared state and evidence logic, removed obsolete CSS and unused code paths, and strengthened keyboard, focus, responsive, and accessibility behavior. 

 Finally, I added a deterministic browser preflight that reproduces the complete demonstration, verifies exact tool catalogs and workspace counts, checks keyboard destinations and action-trail states, and fails on browser errors, unexpected writes, or horizontal overflow. 

 The result is no longer just a scripted agent demo: a judge can open the live app, give an agent the brief shown on the page, and reproduce the same bounded workflow while retaining control of every consequential action.

title: Ticketnauta Seat Concierge
pitch: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Select your seat with AI Inspiration Buying tickets looks simple until real-world constraints appear: a group needs seats together, the budget is total rather than per seat, someone prefers a specific zone, accessibility matters, and availability may change while options are being compared. Traditional interfaces leave the user repeatedly adjusting filters and visually scanning a large map. We built Ticketnauta Seat Concierge to explore a better model: let an AI agent handle the combinatorial search while the person keeps visual context, judgment, and control. Seat selection is an ideal WebMCP use case because it combines structured data, live page state, visual comparison, and consequential actions such as temporary holds. The project is a completely isolated demonstration. It does not connect to real Ticketnauta inventory, customers, sessions, payments, or production APIs. What it does Ticketnauta Seat Concierge lets people and browser agents collaborate on the same interactive seat map. A user can ask: Find four contiguous seats under MX$7,000, prioritize centered seats, show me alternatives, and ask before holding the best option. A compatible browser agent can then use nine purpose-built WebMCP tools to: Search fictional events. Inspect event details, zones, prices, and availability. Find contiguous seat combinations by quantity, total budget, zone, and priority. Highlight recommended seats on the visible map. Select an option. Create or release a temporary hold. Read the cart and hold expiration. Complete an explicitly confirmed simulated checkout. The interface shows ranked alternatives, accessible-seat markers, selected seats, unavailable seats, prices by zone, a cart summary, and a live hold countdown. Every agent action is reflected immediately on the page. The conversation timeline distinguishes built-in guided interactions from actual browser-agent calls using separate GUIDED and WEBMCP labels. This makes the experience transparent and avoids presenting a local command parser as an external AI agent. Every event, venue, seat, price, hold, and checkout result in the demo is fictional. No payment is collected and no ticket is issued. How we built it The WebMCP tools are registered directly from the main document—without an iframe—using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, rejects undeclared properties, and reuses the same application functions as the visible interface. This keeps manual interactions, guided requests, and browser-agent calls synchronized. We deliberately separated tool responsibilities: Read-only tools handle event search, details, seat recommendations, and cart state. Visual page actions handle highlighting and selection. Consequential actions handle holds, release, and simulated checkout. Checkout requires the explicit confirmation value SIMULATE_CHECKOUT . The frontend uses dependency-free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and an interactive SVG seat map. The backend is a .NET 10 ASP.NET Core Minimal API using Npgsql and PostgreSQL . An idempotent bootstrap creates and seeds only the isolated webmcp_demo PostgreSQL schema. Temporary holds use transactional availability checks and event-level locking to prevent conflicting reservations. Expired holds become available again, and the reset operation deletes only runtime demo records. The application is packaged with a multi-stage Dockerfile and Docker Compose. It includes health checks, Windows/WSL/Linux instructions, an optional self-contained PostgreSQL profile, and a Cloudflare Tunnel profile. The public demonstration runs through HTTPS without opening router ports. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was designing tools at the correct level. A single tool that “buys the best seats” would hide too many decisions, while extremely small tools would force the agent to reproduce ordinary UI automation. We designed a focused middle layer where discovery, recommendation, visual feedback, selection, holds, and checkout remain separate. Another challenge was keeping three interaction paths synchronized: manual controls, the guided concierge, and external WebMCP calls. Every path had to update the same map, recommendations, cart, and activity timeline without creating contradictory state. Seat recommendations also required more than sorting by price. The algorithm must preserve contiguity, enforce a total budget, consider zones and accessibility, rank proximity or center position, and still return useful alternatives. Temporary holds introduced concurrency and expiration concerns. We addressed these with PostgreSQL transactions, availability checks, advisory locking, explicit release, and automatic expiration. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and requires a compatible browser agent and a secure HTTPS context. We built a deterministic guided experience so visitors can understand the product even without WebMCP support, while clearly identifying which calls come from a real browser agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that this is a complete, working journey rather than a static interface or isolated tool demonstration. The project includes: Nine discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas. A responsive and accessible interactive seat map. Multi-constraint contiguous-seat recommendations. Visible alternatives and map highlighting. PostgreSQL-backed temporary holds and expiration. Explicit release and simulated checkout flows. A transparent activity timeline for human and agent actions. A fully isolated fictional dataset. A reproducible .NET 10, PostgreSQL, Docker, and Cloudflare deployment. Most importantly, the agent does not replace the interface. It collaborates through it, and the person can see and evaluate every meaningful action. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is not simply a way to add a chatbot to a website. Its real value is giving an agent a structured, browser-mediated contract for what the page can safely do. Tool design is product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, result shapes, and action boundaries directly influence whether an agent behaves predictably. We also learned that visual transparency remains essential. Even when an agent can find the mathematically best option, people still want to compare alternatives, understand tradeoffs, inspect the map, and approve consequential actions. Finally, separating read-only operations from state-changing actions makes both the implementation and the user experience easier to reason about. What's next for Ticketnauta Seat Concierge Next, we would expand the fictional demo with richer venue layouts, additional accessibility preferences, multilingual requests, more detailed explanations for recommendation scores, and automated WebMCP regression tests. We would also explore configurable approval policies so users can decide which actions an agent may perform automatically and which always require confirmation. The larger vision is an open web where agents do not need to guess how interfaces work from pixels. Websites can expose safe, narrow, purpose-built capabilities while people retain context, visibility, and final control. title: Cutoff
pitch: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP
about_excerpt: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP Like 2 Comment Story Updates Rosa’s absence triggers two releases and Nadia’s proposed 4-hour prep cover. Cancelled derby and private booking produce a 910-cover order preview before adoption. The agent records chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring. Manager actions and agent tool calls appear in one filterable service-day record. One desk connects Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log through shared browser state. Inspiration Restaurant orders often lock at a supplier cutoff. The forecast may have been correct yesterday, but the shift changes in real time. A nearby event gets cancelled, a private booking arrives, a shelf count changes, or a staff member calls out. Those facts affect the order and roster together, yet they often live in separate notes or in the manager's head. I built Cutoff so a manager can state a change once and work through its effects with a browser agent on the same page. What it does Cutoff is a shift operations desk for a fictional restaurant. Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log share one revisioned state inside the browser. The Saturday scenario starts with 1,140 covers, 95 required labor hours, and a 3,629-unit supplier order. An 80-person booking and a cancelled derby produce a preview of 910 covers, 76 hours, and a 2,767-unit order. Every changed line explains its reason before the manager adopts anything. Once the manager adopts the order, Labor reads the approved 910-cover plan. The agent can record an absence and propose releases or on-call cover without changing the roster until the manager approves it. A corrected stock count feeds the same state. Recording chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring changes the recommendation from 15 to 16 cases and raises the proposed order cost to 2,835 units. The agent can also save a bounded handoff for the next manager. Shift log joins the manager's actions and the agent's tool calls into one filterable record that can be downloaded as JSON. Why WebMCP The state that matters is not fully visible in the page. It includes local signals, shelf counts, quantity pins, roster absences, preview identifiers, and the current shared revision. An agent cannot recover that state reliably by reading pixels. Cutoff exposes this information through WebMCP. The manager gives the agent the task in plain language. The agent discovers the tools available on the current page, reads the latest revision, and uses the tools it needs. The manager never has to name a tool or copy values between systems. The result appears in the same interface the manager is already using. Proposed changes stay visible and reversible, while final approval remains with the manager. How I built it Cutoff is a static React and TypeScript application with no backend, account system, or application keys. It registers 16 hand-built tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each page exposes only the tools relevant to that section. Order has 6 tools at rest and 7 while a preview can be adopted. Labor follows the same pattern with 4 and 5 tools. Stock exposes 4 tools, and Shift log exposes 3. The two adoption tools exist only while their preview is current. Route changes replace the previous page's tools before navigation finishes. Every write requires expectedRevision . If another action has changed the state, the tool returns a structured stale-write error with the current revision instead of overwriting newer work. Human-entered text is marked as untrusted when it appears in tool results. Small deterministic engines calculate order quantities, labor demand, waste, and roster proposals. The visible controls and WebMCP tools call the same store methods, so the manager and agent cannot drift into separate versions of the plan. Challenges The hardest part was keeping previews, adoption, invalidation, undo, navigation, and tool registration consistent under one revision. A stock count must make an old order preview stale without invalidating an unrelated labor preview. Adopting an order must update labor demand. Changing pages must remove the previous tools before the agent continues. Undo must restore the saved plan without printing a breakdown that no longer matches it. The interface also had to remain readable as the product expanded from one order page into a four-section desk. I tested the final layouts on laptop and mobile widths and added direct links from agent-change notifications to the affected row or receipt. What I learned WebMCP works best when the page and its tools share the same product model. The tools should expose state and calculations that an agent cannot obtain reliably from the rendered interface. The page should still show every result and keep consequential decisions under human control. Tool availability can also communicate state. An adoption tool appearing only when a valid preview exists is clearer and safer than exposing an action that may fail or apply to an old proposal. Accomplishments 16 contextual WebMCP tools across 4 decision pages Dynamic preview and adoption tool lifecycles One shared revision with structured stale-write recovery Reversible local order and labor adoption Agent-driven navigation between sections Local handoff and Shift-log JSON exports 111 deterministic tests and a clean production build Direct production testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled Nothing sends an order, updates a rota, contacts a supplier, or writes restaurant data to a server. All names, events, inventory, quantities, and costs are fictional. title: Relay
pitch: One plan for you and your agents.
about_excerpt: One plan for you and your agents. Like Comment Story Updates Relay command center with shared task board and live workspace metrics. Human Inbox for deliverable review and clarification decisions. Activity History records the full human, agent, and system handoff. Human approval completes RP-104 and unlocks dependent task RP-106. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Relay Inspiration People increasingly ask separate AI agents to research, build, write, test, and review, but conventional task boards were designed only for humans. They rarely expose whether a task has enough context for an agent, whether dependencies are actually complete, which agent has capacity, or which result still needs a human decision. We wanted a control center that makes delegation legible without handing away authority. What it does Relay combines a command center, six-column task board, Human Inbox, agent coordination roster, structured task packets, and complete activity history. It shows human-owned, agent-owned, unassigned, locked, blocked, review, and completed work. Agents can read the same workspace, find eligible Ready tasks, claim work, post progress and blockers, ask questions, and submit evidence-backed deliverables. Deliverables stop at Human Review; only the visible human interface can approve or reject them. Approval completes the task, records the handoff, and automatically unlocks eligible dependencies. How we built it Relay uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and ChatGPT Sites. A page-side WebMCP provider feature-detects the Model Context API and registers six schema-constrained tools exactly once. Both the interface and tools call the same /api/workspace service and pure domain-rule engine. A Cloudflare D1 table stores a versioned workspace aggregate; optimistic writes prevent silent lost updates. Runtime validators reject unknown fields and enforce input limits. The UI reacts to successful tool mutations through a shared browser event and remains fully usable without WebMCP. How WebMCP is used Relay registers get_workspace_context , list_ready_tasks , claim_task , update_task_progress , submit_deliverable , and request_human_input in the top-level page through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read tools are annotated read-only. Write tools explain their side effects, validate narrow closed schemas, mutate durable visible state, return verifiable transition metadata, and append activity events. Approval, rejection, clarification answers, deletion, and project finalization are deliberately not exposed as agent tools. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent must infer a project from pixels or copied text and cannot safely act on it. Relay turns the website's own semantics into a structured, in-context capability layer. The agent can ask the page what is Ready, receive the exact task packet, perform a rules-checked mutation, and immediately show the person the same updated board. That removes brittle screen automation while preserving visible human oversight. What humans and agents can do together Humans set goals, own sensitive tasks, answer ambiguities, inspect evidence, request revisions, and make final decisions. Agents discover structured work, claim it within capacity, report progress and blockers, request missing context, and submit deliverables. Relay coordinates the handoff: dependency rules decide what becomes Ready next, the Human Inbox concentrates decisions, and Activity History makes every transition interpretable. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was making the page genuinely agent-operable without letting agent tools bypass human authority. We centralized every transition in one domain-rule layer, constrained schemas and ownership checks, and made deliverable submission terminate at Human Review. We also needed production state to be the same state judges see, so we used durable D1 persistence and optimistic workspace versions rather than a disconnected WebMCP mock or per-tab local storage. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six real page-side WebMCP tools sharing visible durable state Human-only approval and rejection enforced at the tool boundary and rule layer Structured task packets with dependency, capacity, and completeness checks Immediate visible updates plus a full before/after activity history Responsive, keyboard-friendly planner that still works when WebMCP is absent Deterministic demonstration reset, JSON export, D1 persistence, runtime validation, tests, green CI, deployment documentation, and a public MIT-licensed repository What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to domain actions instead of generic clicks. Read tools should reveal enough context for good decisions; write tools should be small, auditable, and return proof of the exact state transition. Human control is strongest when it is structural—missing from the agent surface—rather than a warning agents are expected to obey. What's next for Relay Next we would add user-created projects, validated JSON import, role-based accounts, signed agent identity, scoped permissions, notifications, richer revision threads, project templates, and multi-workspace search. We would add real-time collaboration only after implementing and validating appropriate conflict resolution and authorization. Try the WebMCP flow Open the live app in a WebMCP-capable ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome evaluation environment. Confirm the lower-left activity dock reports six registered WebMCP tools. Ask: "Read this Relay project and give me a brief summary. Do not modify anything." Ask: "Show me the Ready tasks that the Research Agent can claim." Claim RP-104 , post progress, then submit a deliverable with evidence and a known limitation. Confirm the task stops at Human Review and appears in the Human Inbox. Approve it through the visible UI; confirm RP-104 becomes Completed, dependent RP-106 becomes Ready, and Activity History records the handoff. Refresh to verify the mutation persisted, then use Reset demo to restore the starting state.
