title: Sizel
pitch: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage WebMCP Tools Product Catalog Product detail Inspiration What inspired Sizel was mostly my own experience while building my current PC. I barely knew what to look for or which specifications actually mattered. I had 30 tabs open just to research and compare the parts, yet i still felt lost when i found out that my graphic card doesn't fit in my desired case. It's not like the informations were hidden, but they were buried inside a long spec list, and for someone not very technical at that time it was a really hard task. Because the real challenge is understanding how each component affects the other. The experience made me wonder how many people encounter same problem, how many people buy wrong component because they lack the knowledge? I made Sizel expose WebMCP tools so that agents can connect details and explain compatibility. What it does? Sizel is a fictional Electronics e-shop. Internally, you may encounter another name - Rigsmith - that's no longer used internal project name. Shoppers can browse and filter products, inspect individual product pages, select multiple variations of the product, or assemble a PC from a floating build summary. Each build slot opens its own category catalog. The repo implements and registers 15 WebMCP tool descriptors. The tools do not automatically choose a winner or place a real order. For example the create_watchdog asks user before calling it. All products, brands, logos, reviews, prices, stock values and performance data are made up just for this demo. The important part for me is that the agent actually operates in the same tab in which you are. The shopper can watch what is happening, inspect the same products, and keep control over decisions like adding something to the cart or creating a watchdog. The agent helps with the difficult reasoning, but it does not silently take over. How I built it? I built Sizel using agentic development. The languages used are: Typescript, Vite and CSS. The project contains a self contained local catalog of 135 products, with color and storage variations. The JSON catalog is source for the front end, but there is a SQLite copy included for inspection. The application therefore does not depend on external api for its products. The UI and WebMCP tools share one central App.tsx . picks stores parts, while chosen tracks explicit selections. Centralized mutations and validation keep compatibility, totals, build summary, cart, and checkout aligned. Checkout field and progressions remains shopper-controlled. The tools are intentionally scoped as specific shopping capabilities. Searching and comparing listings, finding compatible components, and validating it. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was making the flow snappy. In the A/B runs from the video, the WebMCP flow took 2 minutes 35 seconds. Though this timing isn't an average across more runs, it usually stays around that 2:30 -3 minute mark. Initially, the process was a lot slower, the breakthrough came when i simplified the tools themselves, and let the agent use its own reasoning. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should not claim. The product reviews, stock and performance values are synthetic, so I had to make the tools say that clearly. League of Legends, for example, has no simulated benchmark in the catalog, and the tool reports that instead of inventing a number. Accomplishments that I'm proud of To be honest, I'm mostly proud of how the UI turned out. I wanted the store to feel like a real e-shop, so i took care with it. I am also proud that the agent does not just return a hidden answer. It can show products and categories in the storefront while it works, so the shopper can follow the process instead of only receiving a final block of text. What I learned I learned that agentic tools work best when they are as dumb as possible, because the agent's own reasoning is powerful enough, and when there is not that much of them. A large tool repertoire just makes agent slower, and occasionally makes his reasoning more complex because he has to figure out which of there 40 tools to use now, especially when they are all so similar. title: Evidence Desk
pitch: Evidence Desk lets agents investigate disputed evidence through four bounded WebMCP tools while humans keep the verdict—and preserves the investigation and human decision in a tamper-evident receipt.
about_excerpt: Evidence Desk lets agents investigate disputed evidence through four bounded WebMCP tools while humans keep the verdict—and preserves the investigation and human decision in a tamper-evident receipt. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can read a packet in seconds. The hard part is showing a person exactly what it used—without quietly turning the agent into the decision-maker. Evidence-heavy procurement, compliance, audit, and dispute decisions need agent speed, but they also need human accountability and a reviewable chain of evidence. What it does Evidence Desk gives an agent four bounded WebMCP tools over a signed synthetic packet: search_evidence , inspect_exhibit , evaluate_claim , and update_caseboard . The agent searches thirteen exhibits, inspects hash-linked source spans, evaluates a contested claim, and proposes evidence to a shared caseboard. The demo makes one contradiction visible: the packet records acceptance on March 14, while the signed inspection report says inspection occurred March 19. The evaluator returns CONTRADICTED with two reasons tied to exact spans. Then the agent stops. It cannot pin or remove evidence, reject a proposal, approve the verdict, or seal the receipt. Those decisions remain human-only. How we built it The TypeScript and Vite app registers four tools with awaited document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. Inputs are validated at runtime, outputs are bounded JSON strings, and corpus text is treated as untrusted. Real tool executions emit visible started and completed lifecycle events in the provenance rail. An Ed25519-signed manifest and per-span SHA-256 checks quarantine altered evidence before evaluation. After human adjudication, Evidence Desk creates a readable, locally signed receipt binding the tool trail, evidence, final human decision, and signed build manifest. The app runs entirely client-side on synthetic data, and its runtime application logic makes no network requests. Challenges we ran into The central engineering challenge was separating capability from authority. Registration is not execution, simulation is not live provenance, a proposal is not approval, and a structurally valid receipt is not meaningful if it seals zero accepted evidence. We hardened those boundaries: simulation-only sessions stay labeled SIM ; untrusted receipt entries fail verification instead of throwing; the evaluator accepts common date-and-event word orders while rejecting unrelated or impossible dates; long reason lists disclose their full meaning; and sealing refuses an empty evidence anchor. Accomplishments that we're proud of All four production tools executed live on the deployed page. Every call showed its started and completed lifecycle events. The evaluator produced a span-tied CONTRADICTED verdict, while the agent remained unable to perform the human-only actions. The Forgery Bench makes the trust boundary testable: change one signed date byte and the manifest check quarantines the exhibit, withdraws the verdict, and refuses sealing. The implementation closes with 189 passing tests, typecheck, and a production build. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable here not as UI automation, but as a semantic contract between a person, an agent, and shared evidence. The agent becomes faster and more precise without inheriting the person's authority. Visible provenance and negative controls matter as much as the happy path. What's next for Evidence Desk The next step is moving from the synthetic packet to user-supplied signed evidence bundles, durable organizational signing keys, trusted timestamps, and configurable reviewer roles—while preserving the same human-only adjudication boundary. The current local receipt is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof. It does not prove identity or trusted time and is not a legal signature. Agent proposes. Human decides. Evidence preserves what happened. title: Booksy reloaded
pitch: Booksy Reloaded lets an AI compare Tampa professionals, securely use a customer's history, book exact matches within preset limits, and ask only when a substitution needs a decision.
about_excerpt: Booksy Reloaded lets an AI compare Tampa professionals, securely use a customer's history, book exact matches within preset limits, and ask only when a substitution needs a decision. Like Comment Story Updates About the project Booksy Reloaded is our answer to a simple question: if a customer already knows who they like, what they normally book, how they pay, and how much they are comfortable spending, why should booking the next appointment still take so many steps? We built an original two-sided marketplace where a customer can ask an AI to find or rebook an appointment through WebMCP. The customer can set practical limits once, such as using the usual provider and service, paying in person, and staying at or below $50. If the appointment fits those rules, the AI can complete the repetitive work. If the provider is unavailable, the service changes, the requested time changes, or the price goes above the limit, the system comes back and asks the customer what to do. The project also shows the provider side. Once an appointment is created, the exact same appointment appears in the provider's calendar and activity feed. That makes this more than an AI filling out a booking form. It demonstrates how a customer, an agent, and a provider can share one visible workflow. Inspiration I am an avid Booksy user, especially when I want to get a haircut. That made it a good starting point for thinking about WebMCP because it is a real consumer habit I already understand. Even when I know the barber I want, I still have to open the app, find the provider, check availability, and repeat a decision I have made before. I wanted to see what this experience could look like if I could simply ask AI to handle it. The goal was not just to make booking faster. It was to let the website give the AI structured, reliable information while the customer stays in control of the rules that actually matter. What we built Booksy Reloaded is an original bilingual marketplace for six fictional beauty and wellness professionals in Tampa, Florida. Three customer profiles see the same provider pool ranked differently. Returning customers can ask for their usual service in natural language without starting over. An AI agent can use fifteen WebMCP tools to inspect authenticated relationship history, find rebooking options, weigh goals, specialties, proximity, budget, review themes, language, accessibility, promotions, and availability, explain every score and tradeoff, and prepare an appointment. The customer sets a practical policy: use the usual provider and service, pay in person, and stay at or below $50. Exact matches can be booked when the customer asks. A different provider, service, requested window, or higher price returns a structured exception and requires a new customer choice. The final tool creates one idempotent sandbox appointment. Switching to the provider account shows that same appointment on the professional's calendar and activity feed. Why WebMCP The website owns provider facts, services, prices, availability, and booking policy. The person owns intent, preset limits, and exception choices. The agent handles the tedious comparison across those constraints. WebMCP lets all three responsibilities meet in one shared visible state without making the agent rediscover cards, buttons, and calendars through visual browser automation. This is not a generic booking form. It is a two-sided marketplace demonstration. The agent's completed action becomes visible to both the customer and the fictional provider, while any material change invalidates stale availability, review, approval, and booking state. How we built it Booksy Reloaded registers fifteen top-level imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Human controls and agent tools call the same deterministic marketplace engine. The recommendation score is inspectable and has no paid placement. A new med spa can compete through price, specialty fit, and availability while its shorter review history remains visible. Returning-customer history is explicit site data, not invisible model memory. Closed JSON schemas limit every input. Read-only actions are annotated, customer history is unavailable before the site-owned demo session is established, and the final booking tool requires confirmed: true plus either an exact policy match or explicit exception approval. The English and Spanish interface uses the same provider and appointment state. All marketplace records and generated portraits are original fictional demo assets. A small browser-local database keeps the public project credentialless and lets a booking created in the customer account appear in the provider calendar without exposing a public production backend. Challenges The first challenge was getting the entire project up to spec while still making it visually appealing and easy to understand. It needed to feel like a real consumer marketplace, not a technical screen built only to show tool calls. We also needed to show what happens after the booking, so we built the customer account, the provider workspace, the provider calendar, and the activity feed around the same appointment state. The biggest design challenge was security. While building this second project, the AI kept returning to security and confirmation. That was useful, but asking the customer to approve every familiar appointment would defeat much of the reason for using an agent. We wanted something secure but also smart. Our answer was parameter locking. The customer can approve a reusable policy for an exact match and change the price ceiling from the account. The workflow fails closed if a provider, service, time window, or price changes. We considered building a real passkey server for exception approval, but this public demo is hosted as a static site. A real passkey requires server-generated challenges and server-side signature verification, so we decided not to fake that security step. Instead, the demo clearly shows the secure boundary we could connect to a production authentication service later. What we learned We learned that security does not have to mean asking the same question every single time. A customer can define clear limits in advance, and the agent can act inside those limits while still pausing for the decisions that are actually different. That is a much more useful version of customer control. We also learned that WebMCP is strongest when tools describe the customer's goal instead of browser mechanics. search_providers , compare_providers , find_rebooking_options , and request_booking are more reliable and understandable than asking an agent to repeatedly scan cards and click through calendars. Finally, we learned that the provider side matters. The agent should not stop after making a recommendation in chat. The completed action should become visible to both sides of the marketplace. Seeing the same confirmed appointment in the customer account and provider calendar made the project feel much closer to a real-world workflow. Results The current policy-aware benchmark uses ten engine calls through final booking status. Across 25 reproducible runs, all 25 completed successfully. The latest artifact measured approximately 84 input plus 1,968 output JSON I/O tokens, for an estimated serialized payload footprint of 2,052 tokens. These are transparent JSON-size estimates, not provider-billed model tokens, and the benchmark excludes rendering, networking, native WebMCP transport, and model inference. Booksy Reloaded is a sandbox. It contacts no real provider, collects no payment, sends no notification, and consumes no production inventory. What was built during the challenge The Booksy Reloaded application, original interface, fictional marketplace data, generated provider portraits, bilingual experience, personalized and returning-customer flows, customer and provider views, browser-local persistence, fifteen WebMCP tools, tests, native browser verifier, benchmark, and submission materials were created during the challenge. title: Research-Devices WebMCP
pitch: Faster, traceable instrument comparison through four read-only WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Faster, traceable instrument comparison through four read-only WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Researchers can spend substantial time choosing equipment because specifications, pricing conditions, source context, and limitations are spread across different pages and formats. Research-Devices organizes information for more than 1,500 instruments in its separate production service. This challenge build explores how a WebMCP-capable browser can retrieve decision material as structured evidence instead of piecing it together from page text. Research-Devices already offered a human-facing research-equipment information service before the challenge. For the challenge, I built a separate interaction model: the page gives a browser AI four read-only functions it can discover and call directly. What it does Research-Devices WebMCP exposes four read-only tools: search_devices searches eight fictional demonstration records. compare_devices compares two to four instruments in the same category using the same field names and units. get_price_range returns fictional price records without mixing currencies, pricing conditions, or configurations. get_literature_signal returns device-name mention counts from twelve fictional research records created for this demo, with explicit interpretation limits. Every response includes a concise summary, stable demo-record URLs, source references, a dataset version, and limitations. Missing values remain missing. Fictional price records with different conditions are not combined. Device-name mention counts are not described as papers, citations, verified use, or proof of performance. The tools expose evidence and trade-offs; the researcher makes the decision. The public challenge build uses only purpose-built fictional records such as RD-SYN qPCR A and RD-SYN qPCR B . They demonstrate the workflow and data contracts; they are not claims about real commercial products. The build contains no production catalog, member data, user submissions, account information, or confidential material. Why WebMCP improves the experience A conventional browser agent must inspect page layout, infer which controls matter, move through several interface states, and extract facts from visual results. WebMCP replaces that guesswork with discoverable functions, constrained JSON inputs, predictable outputs, and read-only annotations. The agent can retrieve structured evidence while the researcher can inspect the inputs, sources, dataset version, and limitations. The interface distinguishes three activities: ordinary human interactions; a deterministic on-page preview using the same processing logic; and tool executions that reach the page through WebMCP. The preview is never presented as an AI-agent call. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Without structured WebMCP tools, an agent helping with instrument selection must reconstruct a comparison from rendered pages. It can lose a pricing condition, misread what a mention count represents, or silently fill a missing specification. Here, a compatible client calls structured functions and receives values together with currency, pricing condition, configuration, dataset version, source URL, and limitations. The page records each WebMCP tool execution with its exact input and result, while making the same source URLs clickable for the researcher. It shows which tools reached the page without claiming to identify the calling AI feature. That combination — structured page-provided capabilities plus a human-readable activity record in an ordinary static web page — is the core WebMCP benefit. Why WebMCP rather than a server-side MCP server The same four functions could be served by a remote MCP server. Three properties appear when the page itself is the tool provider: No site-specific connector step. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the capability travels with the URL; no separate connector or site-specific API key is required. One shared surface. WebMCP tool activity appears in the same document the researcher is reading. Sources the human can open. Every product and source URL handed to the agent points to a page within this demo site, so the agent's source and the researcher's next click resolve to the same document. How judges can test it Native WebMCP is exposed only by a supporting browser. In the latest ChatGPT desktop app , open the built-in browser and enable Settings > Browser > Permissions > Enable site tools ; current availability is listed in the OpenAI Site tools guide . For local Chrome testing, enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and restart Chrome; Chrome documents its origin trial separately in the official WebMCP guide . To confirm the API is ready, evaluate typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool ; it should return function . Then open the live demo and give the agent this request: Compare fictional RD-SYN qPCR A and B for a 96-well workflow that needs 6 detection channels, up to 6 multiplex targets, an audit-trail capability, and a ¥6,000,000 ceiling. Use all four Research-Devices WebMCP tools. Compare specifications using the same field names and units, check the fictional JPY price records without mixing currencies or pricing conditions, and report device-name mention counts in 12 fictional research records created for this demo. Include record URLs, all source links, and every limitation, and explain the trade-off without choosing a universal winner. All four tools should run, and the on-page WebMCP activity panel should show four tool executions. In a browser without WebMCP, the site still works and the inspector buttons run the same processing logic, but the WebMCP activity panel correctly remains empty. A deterministic local equivalent is npm run verify , followed by npm run dev and npm run eval:webmcp:smoke ; see docs/TESTING.md . Representative workflow The main workflow compares RD-SYN qPCR A and RD-SYN qPCR B. The client first locates the two demonstration records. It then compares specifications using the same field names and units, retrieves separately identified fictional price records, and checks device-name mention counts across twelve fictional research records. Neither record meets every constraint. B has six detection channels, supports six targets, and has an audit-trail capability, but its single fictional price record is ¥6,900,000. A is within the ¥6,000,000 ceiling based on two fictional price records, but has four channels, supports four targets, and has no audit-trail capability. WebMCP makes the conflict, sources, and limitations visible; the researcher decides. How I built it The application is a static bilingual site built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, and checked-in JSON data. The English and Japanese interfaces share the same four tool definitions, JSON Schemas, processing logic, runtime guards, and fictional dataset. The page registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Inputs have explicit limits, outputs and URLs are validated at runtime, and compact responses stay within the browser-agent response budget. The application has no backend, authentication, cookies, analytics, persistence, arbitrary remote fetching, or write operations. Automated tests cover domain behavior, input and output validation, localization, static-build safety, and Native WebMCP discovery and execution. The production Research-Devices application, hosting, DNS, authentication, databases, full catalog, and member functions are neither included nor modified. title: Host Whisperer
pitch: When your cloud host fails, your customers’ agents can fix it.
about_excerpt: When your cloud host fails, your customers’ agents can fix it. Like Comment Story Updates Why I built it A checkout error is a dead end for a customer. They do not know whether to refresh, wait, or contact support. The website often knows what failed, but that context never reaches the customer's agent. I built Host Whisperer to make that moment useful instead of frustrating. What it does A developer connects their host and downloads one JavaScript file for their website. That file contains a small WebMCP runtime and the exact recovery actions the developer has allowed. In the demo, Big Pink's checkout returns a 503 because its checkout service is unhealthy. Host Whisperer offers help beside the error. The customer asks ChatGPT to fix checkout, and ChatGPT makes one WebMCP tool call. Host Whisperer checks the incident privately, applies the approved recovery, and verifies checkout before reporting success. The customer sees simple progress instead of infrastructure logs. Their cart is preserved, and ChatGPT never places the order for them. If the problem is unsupported or verification fails, the tool escalates it instead of pretending it worked. The hosting operation is simulated so the demo is repeatable. The WebMCP handoff, state changes, recovery flow, and verification all run in the browser. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an assistant has to guess from the page or from whatever the customer can describe. Here, the website exposes one purpose-built support handoff tied to its current state. The customer supplies the intent, ChatGPT carries it through a structured tool call, and Host Whisperer uses the website's private diagnostics and developer-approved recovery. No one part can safely do the whole job alone. How I built it The setup experience is React and TypeScript. It generates a self-contained, origin-bound plugin. The host token is never stored in the browser or included in the downloaded file. The runtime registers one tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). It includes a small incident state machine, a Shadow DOM support panel, context sanitization, single-use recovery, replay protection, progress updates, and post-recovery verification. WebMCP is registered only on the customer website. What I learned The hardest part was deciding what the agent should actually do. Giving a customer's assistant raw logs or general infrastructure access would be unsafe and confusing. I ended up with one high-level delegation tool and kept the technical work behind Host Whisperer. My main takeaway is that WebMCP can let a website define a narrow support contract: what evidence is safe, what action is allowed, and what must be verified before success is returned. title: Agrivision AI
pitch: Where AI agents and farmers grow smarter, together.
about_excerpt:
Where AI agents and farmers grow smarter, together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Project Story — AgriVision AI 

 Farming decisions shouldn't require farmers to become experts in complicated software. 

 A farmer sees something wrong with a crop. They take a picture, but then they have to figure out what the problem is, check the weather, research treatments, calculate costs, and decide what to do next. 

 We built AgriVision AI to bring all of those decisions together. 

 But for the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to go one step further. 

 Instead of making the farmer learn how to navigate every feature, AgriVision can now work with an AI agent. 

 A farmer can simply say: 

 “Analyze my tomato crop and create the cheapest recovery plan under ₹500 per acre.” 

 The agent can use AgriVision's WebMCP tools to analyze the crop, check relevant weather conditions, find treatment options, calculate costs, and build a recovery plan. 

 The farmer stays in control throughout the process. They can change constraints, ask the agent to optimize the plan, review the recommendation, and approve it before it is saved. 

 For example, if the first plan costs ₹700, the farmer can simply say: 

 “I can only spend ₹300.” 

 The agent can then use AgriVision again to find a better option. 

 That's what WebMCP changes for us: AgriVision isn't just a website that a farmer operates. It's a set of useful capabilities that an AI agent can operate with the farmer. 

 We designed AgriVision around a simple principle: 

 The farmer sets the goal. The agent handles the complexity. The farmer makes the final decision. 

 Our goal is to make agricultural technology feel less like another complicated tool to learn and more like an intelligent assistant that works alongside the people who need it. 

 AgriVision AI — AI-powered agricultural intelligence, built for humans and agents.

Daily execution still depends on tacit judgment that rarely fits inside those systems: which weak signal means stop, which exception justifies a detour, how to recover, and when a handoff is actually safe. title: AccessBridge
pitch: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations.
about_excerpt: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. Like 2 Comment Story Updates AccessBridge combines a private access plan with verified venue facts and browser-agent coordination. Every requirement is evaluated separately, preserving matches, evidence, unknowns, and decisions. Compatible accessible and companion seats are filtered against the person’s active access plan. A reversible 10-minute hold protects the selected seats while the agent prepares the next step. The person reviews exactly what will and will not be shared before enabling submission. Only the approved disclosure is submitted; the full access plan and agent conversation remain private. The shared audit trail records human and agent actions without storing personal prompt text. Inspiration Planning an accessible outing should not require opening multiple venue pages, interpreting vague labels, calling a box office, and repeatedly explaining personal circumstances. Most event platforms answer a generic question: “Is this venue accessible?” People need an individual answer: “Will this specific event work for me, with my requirements, on this date?” The necessary information is often fragmented across venue descriptions, accessibility FAQs, seating inventory, and accommodation forms. Browser agents can help coordinate this work, but conventional UI automation introduces another risk: the agent may misinterpret ambiguous language, overlook an unknown fact, or disclose more personal information than necessary. AccessBridge was created to provide a reliable coordination layer between people, browser agents, venues, and ticketing workflows. What it does AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. A person creates a private access plan using functional requirements rather than diagnoses. For example: A step-free route A maximum walking distance Live captions Accessible and adjacent companion seating A lower-stimulation place for a break AccessBridge compares those requirements with a structured, venue-provided Access Contract. Instead of producing a generic accessibility score, it evaluates every requirement independently and preserves: Verified matches Conditions Blockers Unknown information Evidence sources and verification dates Venue-declared alternatives When a venue offers an alternative, AccessBridge does not decide whether it is acceptable. The person makes that decision, and the agent can record and coordinate the next steps. Once the plan is workable, the agent can find compatible seating, place a reversible hold, and prepare a minimum-disclosure accommodation request. Submission remains structurally unavailable until the person reviews and approves the exact version of the information that will be shared. Every human and agent action updates the same visible interface and appears in a shared activity record. AccessBridge is not a separate chatbot layered over a website—the website remains the source of truth, and WebMCP gives agents a reliable way to work with its live state. How we built it AccessBridge is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and the browser-native WebMCP API. The application registers tools directly through: document.modelContext.registerTool() Its WebMCP surface is state-aware. Only search_events and assess_event_access are available initially. Additional tools appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied: accept_access_alternative find_compatible_seats hold_seats release_seat_hold draft_accommodation submit_accommodation Abort-signal lifecycle cleanup removes tools as soon as they are no longer valid. For example, assessment tools disappear during an active transaction, and the submission tool exists only while the currently displayed disclosure has exact human approval. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema and additional runtime validation. Human controls and WebMCP tools invoke the same application logic, so agent activity always changes the interface the person can see. The compatibility engine is deterministic and preserves unknowns rather than allowing an AI model to infer missing facts. Plans are versioned to reject stale operations, seat holds are reversible, and editing a request automatically invalidates prior approval. The public application is deployed on Vercel with restrictive security headers, responsive semantic UI, keyboard-accessible dialogs, ARIA live announcements, reduced-motion support, automated tests, and WCAG A/AA scanning. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was defining the boundary between coordination and authority. An agent should be able to perform repetitive work, but it should not silently relax a hard requirement, decide whether an alternative is acceptable, or submit personal information without informed approval. We addressed this by making consent part of the tool lifecycle rather than relying on prompt instructions alone. State synchronization was another major challenge. A WebMCP tool must always represent what is currently valid on the page. We introduced versioned plans, transaction guards, abortable tool registration, stale-state rejection, and exact-version approval to prevent outdated actions. We also had to design accessibility information without reducing people to a universal score. Access is individual and contextual, so the product preserves evidence, conditions, unknowns, and alternatives at the requirement level. Finally, an accessibility product must itself be accessible. We tested keyboard behavior, dialog focus, screen-reader announcements, color contrast, responsive layouts, and populated workflow states—not only the initial landing page. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete native WebMCP journey runs successfully in Chromium and ChatGPT-compatible browser contexts. Tools appear and disappear dynamically based on real workflow state. Missing venue facts remain unknown instead of becoming AI-generated assumptions. Hard blockers prevent incompatible seat and accommodation workflows. Seat holds are reversible and protected against stale plan versions. Personal disclosure cannot be submitted before exact human approval. Editing an approved request immediately revokes submission permission. Duplicate submission attempts are idempotent. Human and agent actions remain visible in one shared activity record. The production experience passes automated tests and WCAG A/AA scans with no violations. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it acts as progressive enhancement for a strong product—not as a replacement for the interface. A small, precise, state-aware tool surface is safer and more reliable than exposing every possible action at once. We also learned that important consent boundaries should be enforced structurally through application state and tool availability, not delegated to model behavior. For accessibility workflows, provenance matters as much as the fact itself. People need to know what was verified, when it was verified, what remains unknown, and whether an alternative is genuinely equivalent or simply another option. The strongest human-agent experiences give agents responsibility for coordination while preserving human authority over personal decisions. What's next for AccessBridge The next phase is turning the Access Contract into shared infrastructure for venues, event platforms, and accessibility communities. Planned work includes: Authenticated venue publishing and versioned Access Contracts Independent verification and community review workflows Integrations with real ticketing and seating inventory providers Secure, reusable personal access plans Signed consent and disclosure receipts Notifications when venue facts change after a plan is created Organization dashboards for identifying recurring information gaps Open adapters that let more event platforms expose compatible WebMCP tools The current public experience uses fictional venues, inventory, holds, and submissions so the complete workflow remains safe and repeatable. The product architecture is designed for real venue and ticketing integrations. title: Constraint Canvas
pitch: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again
about_excerpt: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again Like Comment Story Updates Rejecting a table opens rule capture. The app turns that correction into a rule and applies it to future proposals. The agent replans around the new rule and finds 16 seats elsewhere. The layout reaches 144 seats with zero violations. Asked for 40 more seats, the agent proposes five tables through WebMCP. Nothing changes yet because proposals are previews until approved. Willowmere Hall on load. 96 seats, eight built-in rules, and three locked objects the agent cannot move. What it is ConstraintCanvas is a venue floor planner where a human and an agent work on the same canvas at the same time. You place the stage, lock anything that cannot move, and decide which sponsor gets the front booth. The agent handles the tedious parts, like fitting more seats without breaking egress, finding clearance violations, and explaining exactly which rule blocked a placement. The floor planner is only the demo. The real idea is what happens when the human says no. Inspiration Agent corrections are usually temporary. You tell the model not to do something, that instruction lives in context, and a few turns later you may have to repeat it. That felt like the wrong place to store human judgment. If I say seating must never block a door, that should not just be prompt context. It should become application state that is visible, editable, and enforced. In ConstraintCanvas, rejecting an agent proposal can create a named rule with provenance. That rule is added to a visible rulebook and enforced against every future proposal. The agent does not need to remember better. The application enforces the correction. Why this use case fits WebMCP The site owns the semantics. The application knows what counts as blocking an exit in metres. An agent using DOM automation would have to infer geometry from pixels. With WebMCP, the floor state and rules are exposed directly as structured data. State is shared. The human and agent both modify the same floor plan during the same session. Read, preview, and write are separated. Six of the nine tools use readOnlyHint . Tools that can affect the floor only generate previews, and the user approves changes before they are applied. That separation lives in the tool contract rather than in prompt instructions. Refusals are structured. A blocked proposal returns the rule ID, rule statement, offending item, and numeric shortfall. The agent can replan using actual constraint data instead of guessing why a call failed. What people and agents can do together The core use case is constrained spatial planning. The human defines the boundaries and important decisions. The agent optimises inside them. The application guarantees that those boundaries are respected. Without that enforcement, the human either does the optimisation manually or delegates it and rechecks every result. WebMCP enables a third model: delegate the arithmetic, keep the judgment, and turn corrections into persistent constraints. How WebMCP was implemented ConstraintCanvas registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , grouped into inspection, proposal, explanation, and constraint authoring. Two headers are required before document.modelContext is exposed: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) Tools are defined as descriptors and registered through a shared bridge that wraps every execute call. This keeps logging and refusal handling at the tool boundary instead of duplicating it inside each implementation. Each tool has its own abort controller so the surface can be withdrawn and republished cleanly. Results are returned as JSON. The most interesting part is that the tool contract changes at runtime . When a user ratifies a new rule, the proposal tools are re-registered with the active constraints included in their description , then the surface emits toolchange . That means a correction changes what the agent is told it can do before the next call is created, not only what the application rejects afterwards. Validation runs in three passes: Check locks as hard boundaries. Compare rule violations before and after the proposal. Convert valid proposals into a preview for human approval. The differential check is important because an existing violation should not block a proposal that actually improves the layout. How I built it The app uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, SVG, and IBM Carbon design tokens. It is deployed on Vercel. There is no state library and no canvas library. The constraint engine is intentionally simple. Placement uses a greedy search with scoring rather than a general solver. The priority is not algorithmic complexity. It is producing layouts that remain valid and explainable. Eight built-in rules use the same evaluation engine as user-created rules. For egress, the app runs a flood fill outward from doors across the floor grid. Straight-line distance is not enough because an object can be physically close to an exit while still being blocked by surrounding furniture. Circulation also enforces a minimum free-area ratio: $$ \frac{A_{\text{floor}} - \sum_i w_i h_i}{A_{\text{floor}}} \ge 0.70 $$ This gives seat maximisation a hard upper bound. The app also includes a small agent panel that calls getTools and executeTool against the same surface, so the full interaction can be demonstrated without a separate agent browser. Challenges Different WebMCP implementations exposed different APIs. The spec describes ModelContext as an EventTarget , so I initially used addEventListener for toolchange . That worked in Chrome but failed in ChatGPT's implementation, causing React to unmount and render a blank page. Native calls are now feature detected against a minimum surface of registerTool , with regression tests for reduced implementations. Bad refusals waste agent turns. An early optimise_layout refusal only returned: Unknown objective. The agent had no way to discover valid inputs and spent several calls guessing. Refusals now require a next_step , and invalid values return the accepted alternatives. Thinking models preserve metadata across tool calls. Gemini 3 attaches a thought signature to function call parts. I initially rebuilt the response from extracted tool calls and dropped that metadata. The server route now forwards the original model turn unchanged. Valid layouts can still look wrong. Early plans passed every rule but broke the visual rhythm of existing seating. The optimiser now detects repeated furniture spacing and includes alignment in its scoring function. Model calls needed caching. One planning task could use five or six requests because the agent repeatedly inspected unchanged state. Inspection results are now cached per conversation and invalidated when a proposal changes the floor. What I learned A tool contract should be written as if it is the agent's only source of truth. A refusal should explain what failed and what the agent can do next. Otherwise it becomes a dead end that wastes tokens and tool calls. I also learned not to assume that one implementation of an emerging standard represents all of them. Most importantly, WebMCP is not only useful because a webpage can expose tools. The more interesting capability is that the tool surface itself can change at runtime. That allows a human correction to become part of the application's active contract, which is much stronger than asking the model to remember it. title: ClearHealth AI: Making Healthcare Prices Agent-Ready
pitch: A WebMCP-powered healthcare price transparency agent that lets AI search claims, compare procedure prices, and summarize provider data.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered healthcare price transparency agent that lets AI search claims, compare procedure prices, and summarize provider data.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Healthcare price-transparency data can be difficult to search, compare, and understand through a traditional web interface. I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make an existing healthcare application more useful to AI agents without removing the human experience. 

 The project originally started as a healthcare claims and Machine-Readable File (MRF) coding challenge. I extended it for the WebMCP Challenge so that both humans and AI agents can interact with the same underlying healthcare claims data. 

 Why WebMCP is a Strong Fit 

 Healthcare price transparency is a strong fit for WebMCP because users often need to search, compare, and summarize structured pricing information rather than simply browse a webpage. Traditional web interfaces are designed primarily for humans, requiring an AI agent to understand the interface and determine how to perform these tasks. 

 This project exposes three meaningful healthcare capabilities through WebMCP: searching claims, comparing procedure prices, and summarizing provider claims. These operations have clearly defined inputs and structured outputs, making them natural capabilities for an AI agent to invoke. 

 For example, instead of an agent navigating the application to compare prices for a procedure, it can call compare_healthcare_prices with a procedure code and receive the relevant billed, allowed, and paid statistics. Similarly, an agent can search claims or obtain a provider summary without relying on UI navigation or screen scraping. 

 This creates a human-and-agent experience in which people can continue using the visual healthcare application, while agents can directly access its core capabilities. WebMCP therefore transforms the website from a human-only interface into one that can be used by both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does 

 ClearHealth AI is a healthcare price-transparency application enhanced with WebMCP. 

 A human can use the web application to explore healthcare claims and pricing information. An AI agent can access the same data through three read-only WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_healthcare_claims — searches claims using structured filters such as provider name, procedure code, and place of service. 
 compare_healthcare_prices — calculates billed, allowed, and paid price statistics for a procedure, including averages, minimums, maximums, totals, and amount differences. 
 summarize_provider_claims — provides an aggregate summary of a provider's claims, including claim count, billed, allowed, and paid amounts, average allowed amount, and associated procedures. 
 

 For example, an agent can search for claims associated with Michael Poole, compare prices for procedure s5301 , and then summarize Michael Poole's claims without having to navigate the application's user interface. 

 How I built it 

 The application is built with React and TypeScript and uses a healthcare claims data layer to provide structured data to the WebMCP tools. 

 The WebMCP implementation is located in: 

 frontend/src/webmcp/tools.ts 

 I check whether WebMCP is available and register the tools through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool provides a unique name, human-readable title, description, structured input schema, read-only annotation, and asynchronous execution function. 

 The tools are read-only and reuse the application's healthcare claims data without modifying the underlying dataset. 

 I also use Mantine for UI components, Tailwind CSS for styling, PapaParse for CSV parsing, AG Grid for data presentation, Zod for schema validation, MobX for state management, and React Router for navigation. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The main challenge was deciding which application capabilities would provide real value to AI agents. 

 Instead of exposing simple UI actions, I focused on meaningful healthcare operations with clearly defined inputs and structured outputs. I also needed to make the WebMCP layer work alongside the existing human-facing application rather than replacing it. 

 Another challenge was designing the tool outputs so that an agent receives useful structured information that can be directly interpreted and communicated to a user. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I successfully extended an existing healthcare claims application with an agent-facing WebMCP layer. 

 The application now provides three distinct healthcare capabilities that an AI agent can discover and invoke: 

 
 Search healthcare claims 
 Compare healthcare prices 
 Summarize provider claims 
 

 I'm especially proud that the same underlying healthcare data can support both a traditional human interface and direct agent interaction. 

 I also kept the WebMCP tools read-only so that agent interactions do not modify the underlying claims data. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can provide a structured interface between a web application and AI agents. 

 I learned that an effective agent-facing interface is not simply about exposing more functionality. The capabilities need to represent meaningful user tasks, have clear inputs and outputs, and be easy for an agent to invoke. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can complement a human-first interface: people can continue using the application visually while agents can directly access the application's capabilities. 

 What's next for ClearHealth AI: Healthcare Price Transparency Agent | WebMCP 

 My next step is to expand the agent capabilities while maintaining clear, read-only boundaries around healthcare data. 

 Future improvements could include additional healthcare analytics tools, richer natural-language interactions, stronger validation and error handling, and additional ways for humans and AI agents to collaborate when exploring healthcare price-transparency information. 

 My goal is to continue evolving ClearHealth AI into an application where healthcare data is accessible through both intuitive human experiences and well-defined agent capabilities.

title: Firebro
pitch: A WebMCP incident console where agents investigate production failures and humans stay in control of remediation.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP incident console where agents investigate production failures and humans stay in control of remediation. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Incident response is one of those workflows where an AI agent could genuinely save time, but it is also a workflow where giving an agent unrestricted control would be a terrible idea. During an outage, engineers jump between service health, deployments, logs, traces, alerts, runbooks, and incident timelines while trying to answer a few basic questions: What changed? What is actually failing? What evidence supports that diagnosis? And what is safe to do next? I wanted to explore what incident response looks like when the agent can work inside the same operational console as the human instead of operating through a separate chatbot or a disconnected API. That became Firebro . The design principle behind the project is simple: Agent capability, human authority. What it does Firebro is an incident response console built around WebMCP. An agent can investigate an active incident by checking service health, dependencies, recent deployments and changes, logs, traces, alerts, metrics, runbooks, and the incident timeline. It can correlate that evidence, identify a likely cause, and propose a remediation. For example, one incident starts with degraded checkout performance after a bad deployment. The agent can compare service metrics, inspect traces and logs, find the deployment that introduced the regression, and propose rolling it back. But the agent cannot simply execute a consequential remediation on its own. Actions such as a rollback can require an approval tied to the exact proposed action. The approval has to come from a real human interaction in the console before the action can proceed. Once remediation starts, the simulated production environment reacts. Metrics recover, logs change, and the incident moves through recovery and monitoring before it can be resolved. Firebro includes multiple deterministic incident scenarios so the correct response is not always "roll back the latest deployment." Some incidents involve resource exhaustion, feature flags, memory leaks, or even third-party failures where the best action may be to wait rather than make an unnecessary production change. How I built it Firebro is built as a web-based incident console with a WebMCP capability layer on top of the same operational state visible to the human operator. The system exposes tools across the full response workflow: incident discovery, service health, dependencies, deployments, recent changes, logs, traces, metric comparisons, alerts, runbooks, incident notes, remediation actions, approvals, and incident resolution. One of the main implementation goals was avoiding a separate "agent version" of the application. When an agent investigates something, the console reacts too. A service can be highlighted in the topology, log views can focus on relevant entries, metric comparisons become visible, traces can be surfaced, and approval requests appear next to the operational evidence the human needs to make a decision. Tool availability also depends on context. Capabilities can change based on the selected incident, current incident state, and what actions are currently valid. The backend runs a deterministic incident simulation. Each scenario has a known underlying cause, but that ground truth is intentionally hidden from the WebMCP tools. The agent has to diagnose the incident using the same observable evidence available through the console. Mutations and incident events are persisted so the UI and tool layer stay synchronized as the incident evolves. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the environment realistic enough that the agent actually had to investigate. If every incident simply had an obvious error message pointing to the answer, there would be no real diagnostic workflow. Firebro includes misleading signals and plausible alternatives so the agent has to correlate evidence instead of choosing the loudest symptom. Another challenge was tool design. Returning thousands of raw log lines or metric samples makes an agent less useful, not more useful. The tools needed to expose enough evidence to support a diagnosis without turning every response into an unstructured data dump. I also had to think carefully about approvals. A generic "approved: true" flag would not be enough for a real operational workflow. Approval has to be tied to the exact action being proposed so an approval for one operation cannot silently authorize another one. Keeping the simulation deterministic was another important challenge. The same incident needs to behave consistently enough for automated evaluation while still looking like a live operational system. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Firebro feels like one shared workspace rather than a dashboard on one side and an agent on the other. The agent works with the same incident, graphs, logs, services, and actions the human is looking at. Investigation has visible consequences in the interface, and consequential actions pass through an approval workflow instead of bypassing the operator. I'm also proud of the incident simulation itself. Different scenarios require different forms of reasoning, and remediation does not always produce an immediate perfect recovery. Some actions only partially help, some have no effect, and the system can regress if the diagnosis was wrong. That makes it possible to evaluate more than whether an agent can successfully call a tool. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agentic interfaces need more than a large tool list. The useful part is the structure around those tools: when they are available, what evidence they return, how their effects appear to the human, and what happens when the agent is wrong. I also learned that human approval is much more useful when it happens next to the evidence supporting the action. Asking someone to approve a rollback in isolation is very different from asking them while they can see the deployment, affected metrics, traces, and the agent's proposed action in the same console. WebMCP also made browser context much more important than I originally expected. The agent is not operating a remote service in the abstract. It is operating the application the human currently has open. What's next for Firebro The current version uses deterministic simulated infrastructure so incidents can be reproduced and evaluated reliably. The next step would be connecting the same interaction model to real observability and incident-management systems while keeping the approval boundary intact. I'd also like to expand the scenario set, add more complex multi-service failures, improve automated agent evaluations, and explore richer policy controls for actions with different levels of operational risk. The long-term idea is not an autonomous system that replaces the incident commander. It is an incident console where an agent can do far more of the investigation and coordination work while the human keeps authority over decisions that can affect production. title: Fluent Notebook
pitch: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you.
about_excerpt: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Product WebMCP Inspiration During my time working heavily in quantitative research and portfolio construction, I kept hitting the same friction: context switching. Jupyter is the industry standard for index research and data analytics, but jumping between the notebook to write boilerplate, browser tabs to hunt for dataset documentation, and terminal windows to manage environments breaks the analytical flow. I wanted an environment that respects deep work. By combining WebMCP with a strict, distraction-free UI, the goal was to turn the static notebook into an active research partner. What it does Fluent Notebook is a Jupyter-style Python notebook that runs entirely in the browser. Python executes in Pyodide (WebAssembly) with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib and %pip install via micropip, so there is no kernel server and no data leaves the machine. Around that kernel sits a Fluent UI workspace: a code editor with IntelliSense and Jupyter command mode, an Explorer with Python, Markdown, CSV and JSON files, a Problems panel fed by pyflakes, a Data Wrangler for DataFrames and CSVs, a Variables panel, interactive charts, and a Python terminal. The page registers 49 WebMCP tools , so a browser agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can read and edit cells and files, insert cells between cells, run cells and .py files, install packages, inspect kernel variables, find bugs, open a DataFrame in Data Wrangler, restyle and explain charts, write per-cell summaries, import notebooks from .ipynb JSON, rename, move and delete files, restart the kernel, and save or load the user's cloud workspace. Every tool returns real notebook state; nothing is mocked. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A notebook is not a page you can scrape. It is a live kernel, an editor, a file tree and a set of outputs. Screenshot-and-click agents cannot reliably "run cell 2" or "read the table under cell 3". WebMCP lets the notebook hand the agent the same levers a person has, each with a JSON schema, read-only and untrusted-content hints, and a structured result the agent can chain: add_python_cell → run_python_cell → get_cell_table . Because Python runs in the tab, the person and the agent share one kernel, one file tree and one problem list, with no server round trip. How it creates a better experience Ask "how expensive is the S&P 500 versus its own history?" and the agent writes the pandas cell, downloads Shiller's monthly data inside the kernel, drops the months with no valuation data, runs it, charts CAPE against its long-run average, and reports the answer, while you watch it happen in the notebook. That is the demo video, recorded live in the ChatGPT app. Ask "find bugs in analysis.py" and the agent runs static analysis, reads the Problems panel, edits the file with a find-and-replace, and re-checks. Ask "summarize each cell" and the agent pins its own two-line summaries under every cell and in the Outline. Every agent edit is badged with the tool that made it ( Agent · add_python_cell ) and keeps a one-click Revert until you edit the cell yourself. The WebMCP panel lists every call, linked to the cell it touched. What people and agents can do together now The person keeps the editor, the keyboard and the judgement; the agent gets the same kernel, files and problem list. Debugging, data cleaning and documentation become a shared loop inside one tab instead of a copy-paste relay between a chat window and a notebook. Cell and file tools resolve only once the change is on screen, so the agent can chain calls without racing the UI, and the person can step in at any moment: rerun, edit, revert, or keep going by hand. How I implemented WebMCP Each of the 49 tools is declared once and registered with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }) . The page falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome's flag and keeps checking briefly for hosts that inject the context after load. execute calls the same functions the toolbar buttons use (insert cell, run cell, find bugs, rename, restart kernel), then awaits the React state flush, so results describe what is actually on screen. Results are structured JSON: cell ids, table summaries, chart specs, problems, file paths. Tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations and support abort signals. A tracking wrapper records every call for the status chip and the WebMCP panel, and tags cells the agent touched so the UI can show the badge and the Revert button. Tech stack React 19 in a Next.js-style app on Vite (vinext), Microsoft Fluent UI v9, Recharts for interactive charts, a custom code editor with Python IntelliSense; Pyodide with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, micropip and pyflakes; static export hosted on Azure Static Web Apps (Free tier) with a managed Azure Functions API that stores each signed-in user's workspace in Azure Blob Storage behind optional GitHub or Microsoft sign-in. Challenges I ran into Running Python entirely in the browser brings sandboxing limits: no git clone , and CORS blocks many dataset hosts. I turned that into a showcase for tool use: the agent fetches what the page cannot and passes it in through import_notebook_from_json or create_project_file , or downloads inside the kernel with pyodide.http.open_url . The other hard part was timing: tool calls have to wait for React state to land, or a chained run_python_cell runs a cell that does not exist yet. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The human-agent loop feels fluid. Python IntelliSense sits alongside the agent's edits, so manual changes to a generated pandas DataFrame or chart script are smooth, and the agent can read a traceback from the Problems pane and inject the fix without the user leaving the keyboard. In the demo, ChatGPT completes a full market-valuation analysis with seven tool calls. What I learned Structured tool access beats open-ended prompting. Giving an agent specific, well-defined tools, such as converting a GitHub URL to raw .ipynb JSON and parsing the cells, produces faster and more deterministic help than letting it guess its way through a UI. What's next for Fluent Notebook Expanding the WebMCP tool set for data pipelines: tools for zero-copy business-intelligence queries, so the agent can explore large remote databases and stream aggregated results into the local browser session for visualization. title: Inkling
pitch: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP
about_excerpt: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates fun doodle made by ai best diagrams with the help of ai ai as a fun partner for your daily notes Inspiration A canvas is the hardest thing to hand an agent. There's no form to fill in, no buttons to click, nothing textual to grab onto. Just position, size, spacing, and whether the result actually looks right. That's what made it interesting. If WebMCP could handle a drawing surface, where the agent has to measure its own work and fix what it gets wrong, it could handle most things. So I built one and gave the agent real eyes on it: not a screenshot, but the actual scene, with the ability to check its own overlaps, spacing, and alignment before calling it done. What it does Inkling is a hand-drawn canvas that an AI agent can see and draw on, live, on the same page you're looking at. The agent can: See the real canvas. It reads actual element positions and sizes, not a picture of them. Check its own work. Built-in measurements catch overlapping shapes, crossing arrows, and clipped labels, so it can spot its own mistakes. Draw properly. Shapes, arrows, colored pen strokes, real service icons, and images. Describe a system in plain English and it builds the diagram, laid out automatically. React to you. If you edit something, it notices and responds without being asked again. Read comments off the canvas. Select a region, pin a note to it like "add a WAF here," and the agent picks it up with the exact elements it's attached to. No re-explaining what "this" means. Be undone. Every agent change is logged, and you can jump back to the state before any one of them. Same tool for a scalable AWS architecture and for a weekend to-do list with a doodle next to the fun part. How I built it React and Next.js running on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for saving canvases and R2 for uploaded images. The canvas is hand-rolled SVG with a rough, sketchy ink style. Used Chatgpt site to host the app. The WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Underneath sits a layered-graph layout engine and a small flowchart parser, which is what turns "a client hits a CDN, then a load balancer, then three app servers" into an actual arranged diagram in one call. Challenges I ran into There's no way for the page to notify the agent. WebMCP only goes one direction. So "react when the human edits something" had to be built as a journal the agent parks a call against, waiting to be woken. Same for comments. Tool descriptions are the entire UX. There's no system prompt in WebMCP, so the tool descriptions are the only place to shape behavior. My first attempt at telling the agent a personal canvas could be "looser" produced scattered, disconnected layouts. It read "loose" as "messy." I had to separate "loose in style" from "loose in layout" explicitly. fill="none" vs fill="transparent" . Visually identical. But one is clickable and one isn't, and it silently made every uploaded image impossible to drag. A CSS animation quietly broke a toolbar's position. A shared fade-in animation overrode the element's positioning transform for its entire lifetime, so it never anchored where the code said it did. I only found it by measuring the real rendered position against the math I expected. What I learned In WebMCP, the tool description is the product's personality. There's nowhere else to say "be precise here, playful there." Writing those turned out to be much closer to UX writing than API documentation. I also underestimated the primitives. Given explicit permission to take its time, the agent drew a full colored illustration out of nothing but freehand pen strokes. title: Vouchsafe
pitch: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records
about_excerpt: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration To find out whether a household qualifies for heating assistance, food assistance, or a childcare subsidy, a caseworker needs facts held by three separate agencies, and those agencies are forbidden to share them. The restriction is legal rather than technical, which is why the usual answer (put it all in one database) is not available. So the household becomes the courier: a portal and a login for every agency, documents printed and re-keyed into six forms that all ask the same questions. Benefits go unclaimed because the process is exhausting instead of people not being able to qualify. WebMCP is the first thing that fits the actual shape of that problem. It lets a site offer a capability without handing over the data behind it, and it expresses consent as something the browser already understands: an origin. A server-side MCP integration cannot do this, because the agencies would have to trust a central integrator with the records themselves, which is the exact thing the law forbids. What it does Vouchsafe is a benefits screening workbench for a caseworker. They ask one question in plain language, and six programs are determined across three agencies in seconds, with the reasoning shown requirement by requirement. Each agency keeps its record at its own origin and answers only predicates. attest_income_below(threshold, tax_year) returns {attested: true}, never 34200. The release of information a client signs is expressed as exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app']: this site may ask, and no other site may. The office ends up safer than before, not merely faster. A disclosure ledger shows every question that crossed an origin boundary, which field stayed at the agency, and what came back. After a full screening, it reads eleven questions asked, zero record fields disclosed. A caseworker who never had the income figure cannot leak it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An assistant can compose a decision across mutually distrustful origins that will not share data, and none of them has to trust the assistant, the broker, or each other with a record. Three things follow: Determination without disclosure. Utility Arrears Relief comes back eligible having asked nobody anything, because it is categorically eligible via heating assistance. The determination is derived entirely from another determination. Consent that is revocable mid-session, from the UI. Withdraw a release at the agency and its AbortController fires, toolchange reaches the broker, and the tool stops existing. The assistant does not refuse the question; there is nothing left to call. An honest third answer. Programs that needed the departed agency turn indeterminate, never ineligible. Absence of proof is not proof of ineligibility, which matters when the output is somebody's benefits. How we built it Four separate origins. Plain ES modules, no build step, zero npm dependencies. The three agencies register attestation tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app' ], signal }), each returning a minimal-disclosure envelope of {attested, predicate, agency, ref, ts} and nothing else. Revenue also registers get_income_record without exposedTo, as a control case: the broker cannot see it, and a "Probe the boundary" button demonstrates that live. The broker is a composer, not a forwarder. It discovers agency tools with getTools({fromOrigins}), calls them with executeTool(), and re-syncs on toolchange. It then registers six tools of its own for the assistant, so the agent sees one coherent surface rather than a pile of forwarded predicates, and never sees an agency tool at all. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is young, and most of the real work was discovering how it actually behaves rather than how we assumed it would. Six findings are documented in smoke/RESULTS.md. The three that shaped the architecture: getTools({fromOrigins}) is additive, not exclusive. It returns the caller's own tools alongside those of the requested origins. Before we caught it, the broker's own facades landed in every agency's bucket, so agencies read as online while their tools were missing. The broker now partitions results by tool.origin. executeTool() takes a JSON string and returns a JSON string, not objects, so arguments and results both need serialising and the response needs parsing twice. Registering a tool that already exists throws InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name. Our toolchange handler was not awaiting its own callback, so two refreshes could overlap and the second collided with the first. Verification was its own problem: WebMCP does not exist in headless Chrome, so a normal headless test captures an empty, broken page. Every check drives a real headful Chrome over the DevTools Protocol instead, and cross-origin iframes are out-of-process, which needs Target.setAutoAttach with flatten: true to reach them at all. Accomplishments that we are proud of The central claim is measured rather than asserted. tools/verify-agent.js walks the entire agent path and scans every byte the assistant can see for the record values: leakedSecrets: [] across 9,940 bytes. tools/verify-revocation.js proves the revocation path against production, not a mock. ?selftest=1 runs seven assertions inside the live page, so a judge can check the claims without reading any code. Thirty-six unit tests cover the program graph and the envelope. The control case is the part we would point at first. A tool registered without exposedTo is not merely undocumented or unlisted; the broker genuinely cannot reach it, and the page lets you try. What we learned The important design decision was making the broker compose rather than forward. Proxying twelve agency predicates straight to the assistant would have been less code and a worse product: the agent would carry the burden of knowing which agency holds what, and every question would cross the boundary individually. Six facades that each consult several origins gave a better agent experience and a smaller disclosure surface at the same time. The second lesson was that a privacy claim is worth only as much as its instrumentation. "No records are disclosed" is easy to write and easy to break by accident, so the ledger counts real crossings and the verifier greps the agent's own view for the secret values. What is next for Vouchsafe The predicates here are hand-written per agency. The natural next step is a declarative attestation schema, so an agency can publish which predicates it answers without writing a tool by hand, and a signed attestation reference, so a determination can be re-verified later by a third party from the ref alone. Beyond benefits, the same shape fits anywhere a decision needs facts that are legally forbidden to pool: clinical eligibility, immigration casework, school enrolment, tenancy checks. The interesting property is not that the data stays put. It is that the consent to ask is a browser primitive an ordinary person can withdraw.
